evidence_items.summary: Counterfactual explanations improve the interpretability of graph neural networks (GNNs) by identifying small structural or feature perturbations that alter model predictions. They are especially useful in applications sensitive to relational changes, including molecular property prediction, fraud detection, and recommendation systems. However, existing methods often rely on local importance scores or heuristic search, limiting their ability to capture global graph structure and generate prediction-relevant graph edits. We propose LLM-CFExplainer, a general framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to assist counterfactual generation for GNNs. The framework extracts neighborhood-level influence information from a trained GNN and converts it, together with the original graph information, into structured prompts. The LLM then performs relational reasoning and proposes counterfactual edits subject to prediction-flipping, domain consistency, and basic topological constraints. A lightweight verification module evaluates the validity of the proposed edits and ensures consistency with the original graph. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show that LLM-CFExplainer improves counterfactual validity, coverage of perturbable regions, and coherence of generated explanations. These results demonstrate the potential of LLMs as reasoning tools for enhancing the interpretability of graph learning models. Our code is available at https://github.com/tanhaochen001-ux/LLM-CFExplainer .
evidence_items.title: LLM-CFExplainer: A Large Language Model-Guided Framework for Graph Counterfactual Explanations

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, law, education, and scientific research, where factual accuracy is paramount. However, LLMs frequently generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect statements, a phenomenon widely known as hallucination. Existing detection approaches are constrained by significant practical limitations: white-box methods require access to model internals that are inaccessible from commercial APIs; self-consistency sampling incurs prohibitive inference overhead ($k\times$ additional LLM calls); and perplexity-based signals fail to distinguish factual errors from genuinely novel correct statements. In this paper, we propose RAG-CS (Retrieval-Augmented Consistency Scoring), a post-hoc, model-agnostic hallucination detection framework requiring no access to LLM logits, weights, or sampling distributions. Given any LLM-generated response, RAG-CS first sentence-segments the output, then retrieves the top-$k$ evidence passages per sentence from a knowledge corpus using a dense bi-encoder retriever indexed with FAISS. A cross-encoder natural language inference (NLI) model computes pairwise semantic consistency scores between each response sentence and its retrieved evidence. Finally, a lightweight logistic regression classifier aggregates these scores, including statistical features over the score distribution, into a binary hallucination label and per-sentence fine-grained indicators. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on four hallucination benchmarks (TruthfulQA, HaluEval, FEVER, and FaithDial) and demonstrate that RAG-CS achieves F1 scores of 87.3\%, 84.6\%, 89.1\%, and 83.7\%, respectively, outperforming strong baselines including SelfCheckGPT-NLI, SAPLMA, and FActScore by 4.1--9.8 percentage points.
evidence_items.title: Retrieval augmented consistency scoring for model agnostic hallucination detection in large language models

evidence_items.summary: Manual aerobics scoring is sensitive to evaluator experience, while a single sensing modality cannot fully represent posture, dynamics, and musical timing. This study develops an intelligent evaluation model that encodes video, skeleton, inertial, and music-rhythm data in parallel and integrates them through cross-modal attention, reliability-aware fusion, temporal attention, and multi-task scoring. The dataset contains 8,466 valid sequences from 60 adult athletes. On a participant-independent test set, the model achieved an MAE of 3.18 points, R2 of 0.946, and macro-F1 of 0.925 for four-class primary deviation recognition. Performance declined under cross-site and cross-device testing, with MAE increasing to 4.28 and 4.47 points, respectively. A four-week pilot involving 18 athletes and four teachers indicated shorter video-review time, but it was not designed to establish long-term technical improvement or deployment readiness. The model therefore provides an auxiliary source of quantitative evidence for training diagnosis rather than a substitute for expert judgment.
evidence_items.title: Optimization of an intelligent evaluation model for aerobics performance using artificial intelligence and multimodal deep representation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract AI-assisted development weakens the meaning of a green continuous-integration (CI) check: generated tests may execute realistic code and pass while replacing semantic oracles with tautologies or coarse smoke checks. We introduce CI-DeceptiveTest, a Python execution-paired benchmark and Gatekeeper protocol for detecting such low-assurance tests. Its 600 pairs originate from real tests in 12 open-source repositories; each source-control test is paired with a candidate produced by controlled oracle weakening, yielding 1200 label-free static-binary views. Construction combines deterministic validation, execution evidence, a 20% manually annotated slice, random inspection of 30% of AI-assisted records. The evidence is GPT-5.5-first: GPT-5.5 supports construction, review, and full-dataset validation. Labels are transformation-defined, not model-assigned. On the full benchmark, transparent static rules achieve 0.928 low-assurance recall but a 0.458 false-block rate on accepted source-control tests. mimo-v2.5-pro is retained as an auxiliary external cross-check; it reaches 0.885 macro F1 and reduces false blocking to 0.048. Bounded mutation analysis over 42 pre-specified source/candidate pairs further supports the paired construction. The central stress result is that weak-oracle detection remains hard: plausible coarse assertions retain execution while losing semantic constraint. The benchmark enables CI gatekeeper evaluation in a controlled, reproducible setting.
evidence_items.title: CI-DeceptiveTest: An Execution-Paired Benchmark for Test Assurance in AI-Assisted Development

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Conversational agents that retrieve documents and call tools are being deployed to operate buildings, campuses and other intelligent environments, yet engineering teams rarely have labelled data with which to test them before real users arrive. Synthetic test generation is widely offered as a remedy, but there is little evidence on whether synthetic suites detect faults, which generation strategies matter, and whether automatically produced ground truth can be trusted. We present an inverse retrieval-augmented generation pipeline that turns knowledge-base context into persona-conditioned questions with verifiable answers, expands them along multi-hop, linguistic, edge-case, adversarial and privacy dimensions, and filters them with a claim-level critic. In a controlled study with a deterministic tool-using agent and a grammar-based teacher, synthetic suites of 100 tests detected 93% of fifteen design faults, against 29% for a rule-based suite and at most 40% for re-implemented Ragas- and PyRIT-style generators. On faults independent of the generator design the advantage was smaller: 92% versus 75-77% of 312 automatically generated code mutants, and 70% versus 54-62% of twelve faults from external taxonomies. Fault-level hypothesis tests confirmed the advantage on design faults and code mutants (Holm-adjusted ≤ 0.022), but not on the underpowered held-out set, and the code-mutant advantage lost significance when mutants were aggregated by function. A claim-level critic removed injected label errors in the structured corpus, but on paraphrased, outdated and cross-referenced documents it had to route 41% of items to human review to stay error-free.
evidence_items.title: Inverse-RAG Synthetic Test Generation for Agentic AI Assistants in Intelligent Environments: A Mutation-Based Evaluation of Fault-Detection Effectiveness

evidence_items.summary: The Federated Governance Benchmark Dataset v1.0 (FGBD) is a reproducible synthetic benchmark dataset for evaluating governance latency, review complexity, evidence coverage, escalation behavior, approval workflows, and control coverage across simulated federated enterprise operating models. The dataset contains 10,000 programmatically generated synthetic governance records representing centralized, federated, and hybrid operating models under controlled benchmark conditions including low latency, high review complexity, missing evidence, escalation, policy exceptions, cross-business-unit coordination, and conflicting control requirements. The dataset is designed for research and benchmarking of enterprise AI governance, decision intelligence, governance operating models, control effectiveness, auditability, and workflow analysis. Derived metrics are calculated from documented underlying fields using deterministic rules. All records are synthetic and were generated programmatically using a fixed random seed for reproducibility. The dataset contains no customer, employee, patient, financial-account, government, or production enterprise records and does not represent observations from real organizations.
evidence_items.title: Federated Governance Benchmark Dataset v1.0

TRUSTWORTHY QUANTUM AI FOR REHABILITATION RESEARCH F076-F080 | SCIENTIFIC TECHNICAL NOTEBOOK | RESEARCH WORKING EDITION Prospective | Nonclinical | Falsifiable | Reproducible | Unbuilt Research Concepts 33 x STARLI OPENING ESSAY | THE AUTHORITY A MODEL DOES NOT HAVE A predictive score is a statement about a model conditional on the data and assumptions that produced it. It is not evidence that the model has identified a causal neural mechanism. It is not permission to issue a physical command. It is not a clinical outcome. This family studies the boundaries between those three categories. The central object is a synthetic offline audit environment, designed so that the model may succeed, the ordinary rival may win, or a safety policy may correctly refuse the request. Five separate flagship questions meet at the same test bench. F076 tests the intervention fidelity of explanations; F077 asks whether unfamiliar inputs can be recognized before acceptance; F078 audits the source lineage and disparate failures that can manufacture attractive evaluation scores; F079 gives authorization a separate and explicit place in the decision path; F080 measures the usefulness of quantum-labelled computation after whole-pipeline cost. Each flagship has its own failure conditions. Their coupling is useful only if interfaces are causal, auditable and independently replaceable. Interpretability is especially vulnerable to beautiful output. Heatmaps, feature masks and counterfactual diagrams can look precise while merely expressing local correlation or an approximate post hoc surrogate. A serious explanatory claim tells the next investigator which feasible feature intervention will change the prediction and which independent witness can confirm it. A neural feature that was never intervened on cannot be declared causal from the color of a plot. Distribution shifts change the meaning of confidence. The familiar recording can be transformed by a new electrode montage, a different clock, an unknown class or missing-channel patterns. A detector that recognizes only the noise signatures on which it was trained may appear successful while failing precisely where a reliable refusal is needed. This is why F077 preserves selective risk, coverage, false acceptance and the full latency of the veto, not just aggregate classification accuracy. Leakage often survives a superficial audit. A synthetic source can be transformed into many nearly identical examples. The copied signals may receive new filenames, be presented as a different session or pass through a normalization fitted on the entire dataset. A high score on this partition does not demonstrate that the proposed quantum model has learned generalizable neural dynamics. F078 requires source ancestry, label availability at inference time, group balance and versioned data contracts before model comparison. Human authorization has a different grammar from prediction. A permission token may be valid for one task and forbidden for another; a model version may change while a previously signed policy does not. An operator may revoke consent after inference begins. These are not situations to be resolved by increasing confidence thresholds. A correct engineering design makes the action envelope an intersection of scope, role, time and safety, independently auditable after both successful and refused requests. In this book the commands remain inert simulations. Quantum performance remains an open empirical question for the present application. A systematic review of quantum machine learning in digital health, DOI 10.1038/s41746-025-01597-z, did not find a consistent empirical advantage over classical methods. That does not forbid the search for new architectures. It does require clean experiments. Encoding overhead, noisy operations, repeated runs, queueing, mitigation, hardware drift and classical tuning all belong to a practical utility comparison. A result below the preregistered benefit threshold must be allowed to stop the search. The five-stage parallel spacetime method organizes scientific uncertainty into origin questions, mathematical proposals, competing explanations, bounded stress worlds and independently reconstructable evidence. This phrase describes intellectual branches, not physical travel through alternative universes. The stages are most useful when a late counterfactual changes what we thought we knew at the beginning. No stage gives special permission to call a hypothesis established. A technical notebook does not repeat an entire research monograph line by line. It attempts to show why a researcher would care about an experiment, how instruments might mislead, and what interpretation could survive a fair adversary. Repeated concepts are welcome when their role deepens; recycled paragraphs masquerading as new research are not. This notebook uses Mechanism, Measurement and Refutation not as decorative labels but as obligations that make one another more exact. The research is deliberately nonclinical. It uses synthetic and authorized nonclinical proxies, inert test-bench decisions and invented stress scenarios. The proposal does not support diagnosis, implantation, robotic stroke rehabilitation or therapeutic claims. Clinical translation would require a separately approved, prospective, human-subject program with its own risk and endpoint design. Neither this document nor its figures can supply that evidence. The future reader may inherit much better hardware and different methods for causality, uncertainty or governance. If our circuits look primitive, the questions remain: what was actually measured, which part was guessed, where did the permission come from, what ordinary explanation could prevail, and who can reproduce the result? A living research civilization does not demand that its first equations remain sacred. It tries to leave an apparatus for self-correction. THE FIVE DISTINCT FLAGSHIP CONTRACTS F076 | Explainability of Quantum AI Models for Rehabilitation at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: test whether feature-level interventions change model explanations and predictions consistently under a frozen causal hypothesis. Declared primary observables: counterfactual fidelity [1], explanation stability [1], calibration gap [1], audit time [s]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that a saliency map follows correlated noise or a post hoc surrogate rather than the model decision. The concealed discriminating test should blindly perturb one neural feature while preserving its nuisance-correlated partner. Instrumental evidence: frozen synthetic EEG-like feature traces [normalized], plausible intervention support [1], explanation audit logs [1] and independent causal labels [1]. A strong baseline is feature ablation, sparse logistic models, calibrated gradient boosting and causally constrained classical surrogate explanations under identical data and access. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment. F077 | Out-of-Distribution Detection in Quantum Rehabilitation AI at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: detect unfamiliar EEG acquisition regimes and refuse unsupported inference before any simulated control action. Declared primary observables: OOD AUROC [1], selective risk [1], false-acceptance [1], refusal latency [s]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that shift scores measure recording artifacts or test-set tuning rather than genuinely unsupported states. The concealed discriminating test should hide a center-specific acquisition defect and replace a high-impairment synthetic test subgroup. Instrumental evidence: held-out sensor arrays [mV], acquisition timestamps [ms], unseen-site shift manifests, accept/reject flags [1] and dispatch times [s]. A strong baseline is deep ensemble and conformal selective prediction, classical density models and transparent acquisition-quality rules with equally tuned thresholds. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment. F078 | Data Leakage and Bias Control in Quantum Rehabilitation AI at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: separate individual/session/center provenance and audit false performance improvements across synthetic subgroups. Declared primary observables: leakage exposure fraction [1], subgroup calibration gap [1], false-positive disparity [1]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that participant overlap, batch identity or label timestamp leaks the holdout answer. The concealed discriminating test should plant blinded duplicate source fingerprints and evaluate a locked independent subgroup. Instrumental evidence: source genealogy hashes, session identifiers, timestamp manifests [ms], subgroup sizes [count] and sealed evaluation outcomes [1]. A strong baseline is grouped nested cross-validation, strict temporal split, classical feature leakage audits and equal-cost subgroup calibration analysis. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment. F079 | Human Oversight and Authorization of Quantum Rehabilitation Decisions at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: enforce a versioned authorization-policy intersection before any model suggestion can be executed in an inert test sandbox. Declared primary observables: unauthorized action rate [1], revocation latency [ms], false-denial rate [1], audit trail coverage [1]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that human consent is inferred from a stale token or a policy exception hidden in the interface. The concealed discriminating test should expire a synthetic authorization and revoke permission during an otherwise successful trial. Instrumental evidence: synthetic signed policy tokens, scope lists, version hashes, consent expiry clocks [ms] and complete inert action logs. A strong baseline is ordinary role-based access policy, signed consent records, deterministic fail-closed interlocks and human stop procedures. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment. F080 | Practical Quantum AI Advantage and Research Stopping Conditions at the Limit Falsifiable proposed mechanism: compare candidate quantum/hybrid inference and matched tuned classical methods using end-to-end performance, safety and resource accounting. Declared primary observables: task utility gap [1], total wall time [s], energy [J], safety refusal error [1]. The ordinary or confounded world proposes that encoding, queueing, mitigation or retraining overhead erases a solver-only apparent gain. The concealed discriminating test should blindly add data-loading and queue costs while allowing a tuned classical model to win. Instrumental evidence: raw input bytes, preprocessing and circuit simulation logs, queue durations [s], modeled hardware power [W] and matched classical results. A strong baseline is strong tuned classical SVM, gradient boosting, calibrated neural networks and full-metered classical optimization matched for safety and data. These are plans and measurement contracts only, not records of achieved effect or human treatment.

evidence_items.summary: Purpose Accurate dose calculation is a fundamental component of modern radiotherapy, enabling precise tumor irradiation while sparing surrounding healthy tissue. With the increasing adoption of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-guided radiotherapy and growing interest in real-time adaptive radiotherapy, there is a demand for fast and accurate dose calculation techniques on both computed tomography (CT) and MRI. To facilitate research in this area, the DoseRAD2026 dataset and accompanying challenge introduce a publicly available benchmark dataset comprising paired CT and MRI data with corresponding beam-level photon and proton Monte Carlo (MC) dose distributions, enabling the development and systematic evaluation of advanced dose calculation and prediction methods. Acquisition and validation methods The DoseRAD2026 dataset comprises paired CT and MRI data from 115 patients (75 training, 40 testing) treated on a hybrid MRI-linear accelerator (MRI-linac) for thoracic or abdominal lesions and is derived from the SynthRAD2025 dataset. Image pre-processing included deformable image registration, air-cavity correction and resampling. Ground-truth photon (6 MV) and proton dose distributions were generated using open-source MC dose calculation algorithms and resulted in a training dataset of 40,500 photon beams and 81,000 proton beamlets. Data format and usage notes The dataset is organized into photon and proton subsets, each comprising paired CT-MRI images, beam-level dose distributions, and JSON files specifying patient-specific beam configurations. Data are provided in compressed MetaImage (.mha) format with standardized naming linking dose files to beam parameters in the JSON files. The dataset is released under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license, with the training set available from April 2026 and the test set withheld until March 2030. Potential applications The DoseRAD2026 dataset enables benchmarking and development of fast dose calculation methods for radiotherapy applications.
evidence_items.title: DoseRAD2026: A benchmark dataset for AI‐accelerated photon and proton dose calculation in radiotherapy

This dataset constitutes a Wikipedia link graph where all the article identifiers are normalized to Wikidata Q-ids. It contains the normalized links from all Wikipedia language versions. Detailed link count statistics are attached. Note that articles that have no incoming nor outgoing links are not part of this graph. The format is as follows: Q-id of linking page (outgoing) <tab> Q-id of linked page (incoming) <tab> language version - dump date (20261101) This dataset was used to compute Wikidata PageRank . More information can be found on the danker repository, where the source code of the link extraction as well as the PageRank computation is hosted. evidence_items.summary: The Trust-Calibration Benchmark (TCB): 60 yes/no items across five domains with gold labels and a per-item label audit, per-trial responses of nine models under three administration protocols, repeated-sampling, confidence-elicitation manipulation and transfer-study data, cached LLM responses, analyzers that reproduce every number in the paper offline, and the camera-ready paper materials. Adds the 54-item computable-gold battery used in the transfer study and the full 5,700-entry response cache from the project folder. Dataset accompanying the paper Qualification by Calibration: A Readable Benchmark for Admitting Language Models to Human-Computation Tasks, 2026 ACM Conference on Human-AI Complementarity and Alignment (HCOMP 2026) (https://doi.org/10.1145/3834580.3838735). Paper abstract. When several language models are wired together into a human-computation pipeline, the system routes, arbitrates, and escalates work according to how confident each model says it is, so a team builder needs a way to screen candidate models the way crowdsourcing has long screened human contributors: with a small, inspectable qualification test. We present such an instrument, a compact battery of yes-or-no questions across everyday domains on which a model reports an answer and a confidence, with every gold label independently audited. Our central contribution, however, is the audited harness and the interface properties it measures, not accuracy discrimination: qualification verdicts for model workers are only as valid as the harness that administers them. Evaluating a diverse panel of contemporary models under three administration protocols, we show that a naive harness, with a fixed token budget and an unaudited parser, manufactures failing workers out of competent ones, misreading a model that answers essentially every item correctly as badly inaccurate, answer-biased, and overconfident.
evidence_items.title: Trust-Calibration Benchmark (TCB): dataset for "Qualification by Calibration: A Readable Benchmark for Admitting Language Models to Human-Computation Tasks"

evidence_items.summary: Synthetic worked example for the headroom decision procedure: worked-headroom, planning-headroom, severity-scaled and guard-sensitivity result tables, and the scripts that generate them. Dataset accompanying the paper Headroom Before Protocol Effects: A Decision Procedure for Human-Agent Evaluation, Human-AI Coevolution Workshop (HAIC) at NeurIPS 2026 (https://openreview.net/forum?id=odOgsQYleZ). Paper abstract. A team protocol has no interpretable benefit without a matched no-protocol baseline and decision-relevant headroom. We present a reporting method that tests admissibility, identifies the marginal contrast, evaluates opportunity, and maps paired uncertainty to an operational action. It distinguishes exact headroom on a fixed battery from uncertain population headroom used in planning. A published meta-analysis of human-AI experiments illustrates why the estimand matters: the same evidence supports augmentation relative to humans alone but contradicts synergy relative to the better constituent. Neither comparison identifies a coordination protocol without a matched no-protocol team. An executable synthetic application further shows that a promising point estimate can remain operationally unresolved once paired uncertainty is considered, and that near-perfect pilot performance does not by itself make a modest benefit impossible. Several inherited multi-model summaries fail the method's artifact gates, so they do not validate it. This is a bounded position and reporting contribution rather than an adoption-ready standard. Human-facing claims still require direct human outcomes, and we introduce no new human experiment. Known limitations. All tables are synthetic illustrations; the five earlier pilots audited in the paper have no retained raw data. License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Source code files are released under the MIT License.

evidence_items.summary: Tracking and interpreting finger and hand movements provides valuable information that can help clinicians assess the recovery progress of patients undergoing physical therapy. In this study, a two-stage data collection process was carried out for the assessment of basic orthopedic hand problems using two generations of a resistive flex sensor data glove. In the first stage, a dataset of 3,096 samples covering sixteen movement classes was collected using a commercial reference glove, and the prototype signals were compared with those of the same system. In the second stage, a fifteen-channel prototype measuring three joints of each finger independently was designed, and a dataset of 2,268 samples covering ten movement classes was collected. Both datasets were obtained from healthy volunteers under ethics committee approval, and their separability was evaluated through classification experiments. The datasets were subsequently used for orthopedic hand movement recognition.

evidence_items.summary: The"sim-to-real"gap introduced by hardware impairments motivates realistic experimental platforms for AI-native research in Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN). This paper presents an open-source UAV-to-Ground measurement testbed built on the OpenAirInterface (OAI) stack and commodity Software Defined Radios (SDRs), enabling direct extraction of raw Sub-6 GHz Channel State Information (CSI) synchronized with flight telemetry. Through real-world flight campaigns, we observe a velocity-bandwidth decoupling effect: under unguided, measurement-only ridge extraction, dominant spectral ridges deviate strongly from the theoretical kinematic Doppler trajectory, whereas guided tracking substantially reduces this mismatch. This indicates that Doppler information is present, but not dominant, in the raw observable dynamics of commodity SDR-based measurements. We further benchmark representative deep learning predictors on this hardware-inclusive dataset and show, through a case study, that their behavior differs substantially from idealized expectations. By open-sourcing the testbed and dataset, we provide a realistic foundation for training and evaluating AI models for practical aerial network deployments.
evidence_items.title: Empowering AI towards 6G: Realistic UAV Channel Data Acquisition using Open-Source Solutions

4D MICROROBOTIC NEURAL SIGNAL SENSING F126-F130 | FAMILY 26 | FIVE-FLAGSHIP SCIENTIFIC TECHNICAL NOTEBOOK 33 × STARLI | The companion to the 819-page nonclinical research monograph EVIDENCE BOUNDARY: all 3D sensitivity surfaces and neural-like waveform scenarios are synthetic analytic examples. The manuscript reports no patient investigation, no demonstrated therapy benefit, no quantum advantage and no automated clinical decisions.   A LETTER FROM THE TWENTY-SIXTH RESEARCH FAMILY A measured voltage is not yet a neuronal event. In a sealed saline-tank phantom, the five flagships test whether a known injected source is separable from common-reference pickup, whether multipoint timing is genuine, whether filtering preserves true events, whether calibration survives sensor-version changes, and whether a confident false event forces rejection. Each mechanism requires a different adversarial test and independent witness. F126 separates known injected microvolt waveforms from electrochemical and shared-reference artifacts. F127 measures independently verified interchannel lag under hidden clock slips. F128 tests waveform preservation under electromagnetic interference and aggressive filtering. F129 challenges frozen calibration across wetting histories and sensor revisions. F130 demands explicit abstention on high-confidence counterfeit electrical events. Their common platform is a sealed saline-tank phantom with nonliving electrodes and known injected voltages; no patient or neural recordings are represented. The companion PDF preserves the 819-page research architecture: 30 dimensionally stated candidate equations, 42 reproducible synthetic 3D sensitivity grids, 82 chapters of six progressive pages, 200 Research Gates and 33 unbuilt Phoenix research concepts. This notebook develops each test and counterworld in scientific prose, beginning with nine title-led descriptions suitable for a research listing. The public five-stage parallel spacetime name is a reasoning workflow, not literal spacetime physics. I. NINE TITLE-LED SCIENTIFIC DESCRIPTIONS AND FIVE FURTHER PRELUDES 01 | Flagship Identity — The Five Neural-Sensing Questions The title of this family, 4D Microrobots for Neural Signal Sensing, contains five independent claims that should not be collapsed into a single attractive recording. F126 asks which part of a microvolt waveform originates from an isolated injected source rather than microprobe motion or electrode polarization. F127 asks whether two time-aligned traces are truly synchronized or simply share a misleading clock. F128 challenges the familiar assumption that the smoothest denoised waveform is the most faithful one. F129 treats calibration as a time-limited statement that must survive changes in sensor version. F130 asks whether a high-confidence electrical event should be rejected when the physical witness is missing or contradictory. The common minimum instrument is a sealed saline tank, a deformable nonliving microelectrode, a known synthetic source and at least one independently calibrated reference. Source, detector, clock and adjudicator must be physically distinguishable. The central question is source and measurement integrity at laboratory scale, not the presence of genuine neuronal action potentials. Any improvement must be reported against an ordinary, well-tuned electrical and computational comparator under equal acquisition resources. Five flagship identities therefore create five failure denominators: unexplained voltage, source-lag error, lost genuine waveform structure, long-horizon offset drift and forbidden false acceptance. Each denominator must count failed as well as successful trials. This family makes no claim about implanted devices, patient brain activity, treatment outcomes or quantum computational advantage. Its useful inheritance would be independent refutation routes that future laboratories can rebuild. 02 | Core Three-Coupling — Sensor Motion, Independent Electrical Truth and Contested Attribution A valid coupling cannot consist merely of a deformable microelectrode beside a neural-looking trace and a sophisticated classifier. The first system is a time-varying probe or microactuator with measured geometry and motion. The second is a controlled input and its independent voltage-and-time reference, kept inaccessible to the tested estimator during blind evaluation. The third is a decision about whether the observed waveform can be attributed to that input despite electrochemical offset, common-mode pickup, motion artifact, synchronization leakage and drift. In the candidate voltage relation, the observed potential contains source, motion, electrochemical and common components, all in compatible microvolt units at a validated time. The same single recording can be explained by different mixtures. Consequently a deformation trajectory does not prove improved neural sensing, and a calibration reference that shares the candidate amplifier cannot establish independence. The interventional test changes one nuisance source while holding injected voltage fixed, then asks whether the model predicts the hidden change before the source is revealed. The coupling succeeds only within its nonclinical claim boundary when a simple external source, independent clock, ordinary fixed electrode and blind rival experiments all agree about the cause of any measured gain. If magnetic drive adds electromagnetic contamination, the candidate may look better in a familiar scenario and fail under a reversed actuation schedule. Such a loss is evidence about the coupling, not a reason to conceal the trial. 03 | Core Research Question and Scientific Boundary — What a Saline-Tank Signal Can Mean The core research question is whether a deformable microelectrode can distinguish deliberately injected electrical signals from self-generated artifacts, at a preregistered bandwidth, source amplitude, sampling rate, sensor motion and calibration history. The second part of the question is as important as the first: what observation would make the attractive explanation untenable? A separate voltage source, a blind multipoint delay, an unseen interference spectrum, a swapped sensor revision or a fabricated high-confidence event should all be able to challenge the candidate model. The permitted experimental domain is nonclinical. A sealed saline tank, inert electrode coupon and synthetic known-potential generator can approximate selected electrical boundary conditions. They cannot reproduce neuronal tissue, implant biocompatibility, inflammation, therapeutic engagement or functional stroke recovery. Even a system that perfectly recovers every injected waveform can claim only bench-source reconstruction under those particular tested conditions. Any biological interpretation requires a different approved study, different specimens, separate ethics and an independently defined clinical endpoint. Before testing, record every allowed contact state, power budget, waveform amplitude, electromagnetic interference condition, clock offset and stop trigger. Scientific refusal follows uncontrollable contact, missing calibration, invalid reference or a violation of the nonclinical scope. A strong measurement model should remain capable of saying that the source cannot be identified. 04 | Six Falsifiable Claims and Thirty Candidate Equations — A Geometry of Possible Failure The thirty candidates are organized as six per flagship and are not presented as discovered physical laws. F126 develops voltage source decomposition, reconstructed amplitude error, SNR, common-mode rejection, probe-motion coupling and an attribution margin. F127 defines lag, clock drift, jitter, phase, lag-estimator bias and synchrony admissibility. F128 develops reconstruction error, SNR improvement, true-peak preservation, false-event rate, filtering delay and a bounded loss. F129 measures offset drift, gain residual, temperature compensation, forecast error, calibration availability and cross-version discrepancy. F130 quantifies calibration error, selective risk, false acceptance, coverage, hard admissibility and abstention latency. Dimensional analysis is a requirement rather than an ornament. Voltage error is measured in microvolts; lag in microseconds or milliseconds; drift in microvolts per hour; SNR in decibels; probability and coverage as dimensionless fractions. For example, translating microsecond lag into a phase at frequency f in hertz requires the factor 10^-6 seconds per microsecond. A confusion between these units could manufacture a magnificent frequency dependence that is entirely a bookkeeping error. The corresponding 3D diagrams vary two dimensionless synthetic nuisance parameters and display a dimensionless analytical proxy. Exact recomputation of the plotted 31-by-31 grid shows that the code works; it says nothing about living neurons. Six falsification obligations apply to each flagship: identify the mechanism, forecast a hidden temporal case, beat a fair baseline, separate a rival explanation, refuse an unsafe or unsupported signal, and enable another laboratory to rebuild the failure. 05 | Five-Layer Research System — From Source Identity to Independent Reconstruction Layer one fixes the scientific object: electrode identifier, waveform generator, isolated saline chamber, measured geometry, allowed motion, legal and ethical scope and hard stop authority. A probe can move without being permitted to claim neural function. Layer two freezes traceable electrical and timing calibration, with microvolt sources, reference gain, sampling rates, environmental history and a second independent instrument. A measurement derived from the same clock or amplifier is not automatically a second witness. Layer three creates the contest. A standard microelectrode, fixed-reference acquisition, conventional clock correction, ordinary digital filtering and simple statistical calibration receive the same time, data, bandwidth, energy and tuning budgets as the proposed 4D architecture. The fourth layer blinds all contestants to deliberately concealed faults: shared common-mode error, clock jump, narrowband interference, version-induced drift or counterfeit waveform. The controller must stop or abstain when a necessary witness is invalid. Layer five places source signals, raw and corrected traces, rejected records, calibration versions, stopped trials and reproducibility code in the hands of an independent laboratory. The five layers should produce a result even when the claim is false. The scientific point is not a polished demonstration but a reconstructable decision about why a waveform was trusted or rejected. 06 | Five Research Depth Axes — Source, Synchrony, Spectral Integrity, Drift and Trust The first depth axis perturbs source identity through controlled probe movement, electrode polarization, common-mode voltage and magnetic-drive contamination. The question is whether a supposedly recovered signal remains attributable to a known independent electrical generator. The second axis challenges temporal meaning through hidden source delays, clock steps, jitter, buffering and channel exchanges. High coherence or zero-lag agreement is not evidence of a neurological network without validated timing provenance. The third axis protects waveform fidelity against the temptation of excessive artifact suppression. It introduces hidden true peaks alongside electromagnetic interference and probe-motion noise, then scores original source reconstruction, true-event preservation and false-event rates under an identical digital-compute budget. The fourth axis extends time through temperature changes, wetting history and sensor-version replacement; a calibration that depends on seeing held-out data must be reported as unverified. The fifth axis makes abstention a measurable engineering outcome. Missing independent witnesses, contaminated validators and counterfeit high-confidence events require refusal instead of confident classification. These five depth axes are related but not exchangeable: better waveform SNR cannot compensate a lost reference clock, and lower drift cannot validate a fabricated source. Each axis supplies its own unit-bearing measurements and a different research door for the next generation. 07 | Measurable Endpoints and Minimum Prototype — Voltage, Time, Waveform and Abstention The minimum prototype uses an inert microelectrode in a sealed saline tank and an isolated known-potential source. A physical source signal and an independent acquisition chain are retained even when the candidate sensor or processing algorithm is turned off. F126 is scored on injected-source amplitude error [microvolt], SNR [dB] and source-motion coupling [microvolt/mm]. F127 uses known relative lag [microsecond], jitter [microsecond RMS] and timestamp continuity. F128 preserves waveform morphology and reports reconstruction RMSE [microvolt], filter delay [ms] and false events per hour. F129 follows offset drift [microvolt/h], gain calibration error, temperature [degC] and the fraction of measurement intervals with valid calibration. F130 requires false-acceptance probability, selective risk, coverage and hard-stop delay. Every outcome needs a frozen sampling period, complete assigned denominator, calibration state, model version and uncertainty account. A favorable average must not erase a rare missed event or an interval lost when the calibration chain failed. The crucial distinction is between a measurement of an injected artificial electrical input and a demonstration of valid human neural-signal sensing. The proposed prototype can test the former. It cannot establish the latter, and even a perfectly recomputed synthetic 3D surface remains a mathematical illustration until an independent physical experiment challenges it. 08 | Strong Baselines, Rival Mechanisms and Stopping Conditions — Let Ordinary Electronics Win A good research title makes clear which simpler approach is allowed to defeat it. Strong baselines here include an independently calibrated stationary microelectrode, conventional differential acquisition, known-lag clock correction, well-tuned notch or adaptive denoising, scheduled reference recalibration and a conservative quality-mask detector. Each receives equal source examples, bandwidth, latency budget, compute allowance and evaluation time. Changing those resources after inspecting results would invalidate any technology-specific advantage. The leading rivals differ by flagship. F126 can be explained by a shared reference error or actuation-generated electromagnetic pickup. F127 can inherit common triggers, hidden buffer latency or resampling leakage. F128 can score high by deleting the very event it was meant to recover. F129 can appear stable only because its calibration is refitted using later test blocks. F130 can look trustworthy while confidently accepting injected fake signals whose source was absent. Each rival must be represented by a blind, physical or algorithmic counterfactual. The hard stop is independent of average performance. Invalid microelectrode contact, missing external reference, lost timestamp provenance, calibration outside its validity range or high-confidence counterfeit acceptance must trigger refusal according to prespecified rules. The most honest null result may show that ordinary electronics performs just as well. That finding should survive publication and transfer. 09 | Research Gates and Phoenix Inheritance — Two Hundred Doors to Future Experiments The research doors are neither slogans nor a list of compliance checks. Each door begins from a concrete unresolved observation: an unexpected microvolt peak, a synchronized pair of independent channels, an oddly clean denoised trace, a calibration that worked only on the first sensor batch or a model that was most confident about a nonexistent event. The door asks why the observation mattered, what competing physical world could explain it and what a future laboratory should test next. The two hundred Research Gates span five orientations: origin of the signal question, physical counterworld, independent witness, noncompensatory refusal and successor reconstruction. Every door retains Origin, Extreme Extrapolation and Future Research Plan. For an inspiring question to remain scientific, the counterworld needs a distinct measurable prediction or an explicit reason the original two mechanisms cannot be identified. The future plan names a blind input, strong baseline, reference instrument, failure ledger and stop condition rather than merely inviting hope. Thirty-three Phoenix concepts are not built devices but revisable proposals: known-source observatories, hidden-lag injectors, waveform-preservation courts, cross-version drift sentinels and high-confidence false-event traps. Their diagrams distinguish source, rival, external witness and refusal. A future generation may replace every present sensor and equation and still inherit something meaningful—the complete record that allows it to prove us wrong. 10 | Neither a 4D label nor a quantum label is evidence The public five-stage reasoning name and the 4D device concept organize testable design hypotheses. Neither licenses claims of real spacetime compression, verified quantum speedup or living neural sensing. Take trustworthy sensing and abstention as a specific case. The candidate says source provenance, independent calibration, out-of-distribution checks and a physical rejection gate can distinguish an admissible proxy signal from a confidently wrong synthetic signal. The rival explanation says a model may give high confidence to a fabricated event because it shares contamination with its own validator or because rejected trials were removed. A research team should blind-inject a high-confidence false event and a missing calibration witness, require an explicit rejection rather than a plausible classification and report false accept probability [1], selective risk [1], calibration ECE [1], missed veto [count], stop latency [ms]. Only a blinded difference that survives a strong comparison could justify a narrower technical claim. The most important practical inheritance is an independently clocked signal auditor with authority to force abstention when its witness is missing. Compare with thresholded fixed-reference detection, independent second-instrument validation, classic anomaly detection and simple quality masks at equal input budgets. Preserve sensor batches, artifact transients, calibration, exclusions and all test attempts; refuse if high-confidence false acceptance, calibration invalidity, missing reference chain or an unsafe continuation after the stop trigger. Any proposal involving people or implanted electrodes would require an entirely new ethics, biocompatibility and medical-device review.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Fuzzy decisions may vary with measurement errors and admissible benchmark choices, including thresholds, weights, membership shapes, and aggregation rules. Existing fuzzy uncertainty representations and post-hoc sensitivity analyses do not generally certify decision invariance under their joint variation. This study proposes Benchmark-Multiverse Robustness-Certified Fuzzy Learning (BM-RCFL), integrating benchmark-conditioned fuzzy inference, conservative class-score bounds, object-level robustness certification, fragility diagnostics, and safe benchmark pruning. The evaluated implementation uses a fixed prototype-based reference model rather than end-to-end certificate-aware training. On synthetic data, BM-RCFL achieved an accuracy of $$1.0000$$ , a mean certified radius of $$0.3538$$ , and a certified decision rate of $$99.29\%$$ at $$\rho i \ge 0.20$$ . On a Statistics Indonesia welfare panel with constructed reference classes, reference agreement was $$0.6404$$ , the mean certified radius was $$0.2028$$ , and $$57.02\%$$ of cases met the same threshold. No sampled perturbations within the certified regions changed decisions, providing an empirical implementation-consistency check rather than a mathematical proof. Full-enumeration verification using the same conservative bounds produced identical certificates, while benchmark pruning accelerated certification by factors of $$1.93$$ and $$3.14$$ on the respective datasets. Adversarial search identified decision reversals beyond the certified regions, and sensitivity analyses demonstrated dependence on benchmark widths and perturbation-metric scaling. BM-RCFL therefore provides an interpretable, assumption-dependent decision-stability assessment rather than a guarantee of decision correctness.
evidence_items.title: Interpretable fuzzy decision stability modeling for decision engineering under measurement and benchmark uncertainty

evidence_items.summary: Closed-context question answering (QA) requires a system to generate an answer strictly supported by a supplied passage, or to abstain when the passage lacks adequate evidence. SQuAD 2.0 is a widely used benchmark for this setting, scored by Exact Match (EM) i.e., character-level agreement with human reference spans after lexical normalization. For generative large language models (LLMs), however, an EM failure may reflect a valid paraphrase or an alternative passage-supported answer rather than a hallucination. The best prior leaderboard EM is approximately 91%, but evaluating generative models requires separating lexical divergence from factual error. We introduce SAGE-QA (Semantic-Aware, Grounded Evaluation for Question Answering), a multi-tiered framework combining reference-based Semantic Equivalence Scoring (SES) and passage-based Re-Validation Scoring (RVS). On a fixed set of 10,000 SQuAD 2.0 validation examples, we compute EM and decision-matrix F1 from TP, TN, FP, and FN counts for zero-shot closed-weight frontier models and for open-weight models, untuned and fine-tuned. Zero-shot, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro reach 85.21 and 86.66 EM, outperforming untuned Llama 3 8B (56.88), gpt-oss-20b (66.28), and Llama 3.3 70B (71.39). Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adds 21.19 to 34.06 EM points, raising these models to 90.94, 87.47, and 94.24 EM, respectively. Auditing the frontier models with SAGE-QA and an external LLM judge yields dataset-wide SES scores of 92.81 for Claude Opus 4.6 and 91.67 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and hybrid RVS scores, which combine benchmark credit with passage-based judge assessments, of 97.96 and 98.02. Fine-tuned open-weight models perform best, with fine-tuned Llama 3.3 70B surpassing the previous best known EM.
evidence_items.title: SAGE-QA: Semantic-Aware, Grounded Evaluation for Closed-Context Question Answering on SQuAD 2.0

rationale: Matched: deduplication, evaluat, preference data, synthetic data
evidence_items.summary: Post-training of large language models typically combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with preference-based fine-tuning such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Human-annotated and synthetically generated preference data differ substantially in per-sample cost, but prior work typically holds sample count fixed when comparing the two. In this work, we explicitly study the interplay between cost and performance by comparing the effect of post-training with human and synthetic preference data under a fixed, dollar-matched annotation budget. We train and evaluate multiple base model families across helpfulness and summarization tasks. We find that synthetic data is far more cost-efficient at low-to-moderate budgets, achieving high win rates with as little as \$200--\$400. On helpfulness, human data closes the gap only at budgets roughly two orders of magnitude larger; on summarization, it does not close the gap at any tested budget. We also find that human-annotated data varies in reliability: one widely used human preference source substantially underperforms another, and the gap persists even after standard remedies such as domain restriction and deduplication.
evidence_items.title: Human or Synthetic? What a Fixed Budget Buys for Post-Training

evidence_items.summary: Decentralized training of deep learning models keeps training data local and supports on-device learning over networks. In realistic scenarios, heterogeneity across agents'local data poses an optimization challenge and can severely degrade test accuracy, especially on sparse communication graphs. Building on recent advances in centralized primal averaging, we propose Decentralized Primal Averaging (DPA), a decentralized learning algorithm that combines primal averaging with a local quasi-global momentum buffer. DPA maintains three coupled sequences for optimization, gradient evaluation, and output averaging, while using consecutive mixed iterates to construct a network-aware momentum direction without transmitting an auxiliary tracking variable. For smooth nonconvex objectives, we establish a convergence bound for DPA and identify conditions for linear speedup in the number of agents for sufficiently many iterations. We also introduce DPA-1G, a variant that uses one communication round per iteration and matches the per-iteration communication cost of DSGD-style baselines. Experiments following the GUT decentralized image-classification benchmark show that DPA compares favorably with DSGD, gradient tracking, QG-DSGDm, momentum tracking, and QG-GUTm across datasets, architectures, topologies, and heterogeneity levels, with the largest gains under high heterogeneity on sparse rings. At the same total communication cost, both DPA variants achieve higher mean test accuracy than the best baseline on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-20. Our code is publicly available.
evidence_items.title: DPA: Decentralized Primal Averaging with Quasi-Global Momentum for Highly Heterogeneous Data

evidence_items.summary: Machine learning and data science education overwhelmingly relies on pre-cleaned, statically curated benchmark datasets from repositories such as the UCI ML Repository and Kaggle. These datasets are ill-suited to teaching the realities of production data pipelines, which invariably contain missing values arising from mixed mechanisms, domain-specific typographic errors, format inconsistencies, and embedded fraud of varying sophistication. This paper presents a configurable framework for generating synthetic imperfect datasets tailored to four United Kingdom financial domains: banking transactions, mortgage lending, insurance claims, and investment and trading. The framework offers three alternative generators, one selected per request: a \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\beta $$\end{document}-Variational Autoencoder (\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\beta $$\end{document}-VAE) with KL annealing, a Wasserstein GAN with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP) and their hybrid, with a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) fitted to the VAE latent space as an optional prior, all implemented entirely in pure NumPy so that every operation is an explicit array computation. A probabilistic error injection layer introduces nine distinct corruption types—covering MCAR, MAR, and structural errors—allocated via a Dirichlet prior over a user-specified global error budget. A domain-aware fraud injection layer encodes archetypes drawn from UK Finance, Payment Systems Regulator, Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) and Association of British Insurers (ABI) taxonomies. Evaluation across the four domains, against external baselines fitted to the same training splits, shows that the \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\beta $$\end{document}-VAE attains a mean Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic of 0.104 against a held-out partition of the rule-based seed corpus, ahead of CTGAN and TVAE on the same target at 1/34 and 1/9 of their respective fitting times, and that a structureless independent-marginals generator matches every marginal while destroying the correlation structure, so marginal fidelity alone does not discriminate between generators. A zero-cost smoothed bootstrap of the seed corpus attains a better statistic still on both marginal fidelity and correlation error, and a Gaussian copula is ahead of the \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\beta $$\end{document}-VAE on categorical divergence and correlation error at a fifth of its fitting cost, so the case for the generative stage is not made on fidelity to the seed corpus and is not made here. Validation against real record-level data shows close agreement for bounded quantities and substantial disagreement in the tails, so the framework is characterised as generating plausible rather than realistic records. A detector transcribed from the documented fraud injection ranges and fitted to nothing attains AUROC 0.994 when archetypes overwrite records outright, which motivates an overlap-controlled injection scheme introduced here that makes archetype separability a declared continuous parameter; at its default expression coefficient \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\lambda = 0.25$$\end{document} the same detector falls to 0.609, while a trained classifier reaches 0.948. Error injection realises a stable and monotone but systematically low fraction of the requested rate, averaging 0.596 of it, and the missingness mechanisms are verified to be correctly instantiated when isolated from the default allocation. Generation scales to 100,000 records in 7.0 min on two commodity CPU cores without GPU acceleration. No evidence involving learners or instructors is presented; a protocol for the evaluation that would be required is specified in full.
evidence_items.title: Controlled Synthesis of Imperfect Datasets for Machine Learning Education: A Variational Autoencoder, Wasserstein GAN, and Gaussian Mixture Model Framework with Domain-Aware Fraud and Error Injection

evidence_items.summary: Thermal infrared (IR) imaging enables drone detection with reduced dependence on ambient illumination, supporting continuous surveillance beyond the limitations of visible-spectrum sensing. However, substantial and often undocumented variability in camera systems, processing pipelines, and annotation practices across public IR drone datasets complicates the assessment of detector performance and cross-domain generalization. To examine these sources of variability and their implications for drone detection, we systematically characterize existing IR datasets and establish an artifact taxonomy reflecting their origins across the acquisition and processing pipeline, encompassing optical and sensor effects, tone mapping and image enhancement, and recording-related artifacts. Focusing on long-wave IR data, we investigate the impact of training data composition and model characteristics on YOLO-based detection performance, generalization, and condition-dependent failure modes. Our results demonstrate that detection performance is governed more strongly by training data composition than by YOLO generation or model capacity, while cross-dataset generalization exhibits pronounced asymmetries. Even the best-performing configuration fails to detect over 40\% of drones, with elevated miss rates for very small targets, cluttered urban backgrounds, and thermal crossover, highlighting the shortcomings of existing datasets.
evidence_items.title: What Limits Thermal Infrared Drone Detection? A Cross-Dataset Benchmark Analysis

evidence_items.summary: This record contains the replication dataset, Python scripts, figures, tables, and supporting diagnostics associated with the manuscript entitled "Photovoltaic market-value erosion in Spain’s day-ahead electricity market: Evidence from captured prices and penetration-based operating states". The study examines photovoltaic (PV) market-value erosion in the Spanish peninsular day-ahead electricity market over 2016–2025. The analysis focuses on technology-specific captured prices, capture ratios, price spreads relative to the all-hours pool benchmark, and operating states defined by PV penetration. The replication package includes: A consolidated hourly dataset constructed from electricity market and power-system series obtained from Red Eléctrica de España's ESIOS platform. Seven Python scripts (00–06) for data preparation, descriptive figures, captured-price calculations, PV operating-state analysis, regression tables, and independent regression diagnostics. The numerical outputs underlying Tables 1–3 and Figures 2–5 of the main manuscript, together with Tables S1–S2 and Figures S1–S7 of the Supplementary Material. Documentation describing the input data, processing conventions, computational environment, and execution sequence. The analysis defines 20 global PV-generation-weighted penetration bins, grouped into four operating states: Low, Medium, High, and Very High. Daily regression specifications include renewable penetration measures, electricity demand, calendar controls, and event indicators, with HAC/Newey–West standard errors. A robustness exercise excludes the months with the highest daily-price volatility. The main README provides instructions for reproducing the results using Python 3.11.9. Figure 1 of the manuscript is an editable methodological diagram prepared separately and is not generated by the Python scripts. Data source: Red Eléctrica de España (REE), ESIOS platform.

evidence_items.summary: Postmarketing pharmacovigilance relies on spontaneous adverse event reporting and labor-intensive observational studies, which suffer from underreporting and delayed risk detection. Large language model (LLM) agents could automate real-world evidence generation, but generalist agents make ad hoc analytical decisions that compromise epidemiological validity and reproducibility. Here we present MedCheckpoint, a multi-agent LLM system for automated postmarketing pharmacovigilance. MedCheckpoint grounds each analytical stage in a curated, source-traceable medical knowledge base, locks core study-design parameters before execution, performs patient-level analyses with human-written deterministic statistical tools, and enforces checkpoint rules that abort infeasible analyses, with optional human-in-the-loop review. We evaluated MedCheckpoint using a 54-question benchmark on a dual-purpose simulated electronic health record (EHR) testbed of 2.7 million individuals, designed with reliable clinical signals to evaluate routine analytical accuracy alongside spurious signals to stress-test system rigor. Across the benchmark, MedCheckpoint outperformed two coding-agent baselines in report quality across five dimensions rated by three independent LLM judges (overall means 4.81-4.88 versus 4.25-4.55 and 4.02-4.29) and yielded higher run-to-run consistency (mean within-question standard deviation 0.116-0.186 versus up to 0.440). Crucially, while baselines failed on up to 2 of 21 runs when handling infeasible comparisons or unmeasurable outcomes, MedCheckpoint produced no misleading failures across all seven stress-test trap questions with known data limitations. MedCheckpoint enables reliable, auditable, and scalable pharmacovigilance analysis.
evidence_items.title: Automating postmarketing pharmacovigilance with large language model agents
