evidence_items.summary: Abstract. Machine-learning approaches for soil moisture modelling are expanding rapidly, but their comparison remains difficult because studies often use different target data, predictors, preprocessing methods, and evaluation strategies. Here we present SoMoBench, a quasi-global benchmark dataset that provides standardised predictor inputs and soil moisture targets for data-driven modelling. The targets are derived from in situ observations provided by the International Soil Moisture Network and Brazil’s CEMADEN network. Sub-daily measurements are aggregated to daily values and assigned to a common 0.25° grid for three nominal soil layers (0–10, 10–30, and 30–50 cm). To reduce site-dependent offsets while retaining observation-derived temporal variability, each station series is adjusted to the mean and standard deviation of collocated ERA5 soil moisture. Target series are constructed only for grid cells containing at least one eligible station, and no spatial interpolation is applied. For each grid cell and layer, the longest station record is used as the primary series, and temporal gaps are filled with validated secondary-station record from the same grid cell when available. The current release spans 2001–2024 and includes 1,445 grid cells with at least one target layer, along with daily ERA5 meteorological predictors for 2000–2024. We characterise the spatial and temporal properties of the targets and illustrate their use with climatology-based and Ridge regression models. The release also includes a Python example notebook and baseline performance results to support reproducibility. SoMoBench is designed as a reusable community resource for observation-informed benchmarking and model intercomparison in soil moisture modelling. The dataset is available for peer review through Zenodo; access information is provided in the Data availability section.
evidence_items.title: SoMoBench: a quasi-global benchmark dataset for data-driven soil moisture modelling with in situ-derived targets

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Image-based artificial intelligence models for pediatric fracture localization may exploit demographic signals that are correlated with fracture distribution. Quantifying the discrimination available from demographic metadata alone provides a reference for interpreting image-only and multimodal models. Methods We performed a secondary analysis of the open PediURF dataset, preserving its original patient-level training (n = 4,212) and test (n = 1,053) split. Only age and sex were used as predictors. Logistic regression (LR), Gaussian naive Bayes, radial-basis-function support vector machine, random forest, and gradient boosting were tuned exclusively in the training set. Standard training, inverse-frequency cost-sensitive training, and a post hoc equal-prior decision rule applied to standard LR were compared. The primary discrimination measure was macro one-vs-rest ROC-AUC. Test uncertainty was quantified with 2,000 bootstrap resamples. Paired ΔAUC comparisons were Holm-adjusted. Calibration, class-specific recall, and a training-estimated saturated age-by-sex reference were also evaluated. A test-label-derived saturated model was reported only as an optimistic empirical oracle reference, not as a deployable or theoretical upper bound. Results Among 5,265 children with confirmed fractures, 64.1% were distal, 25.1% midshaft, and 10.9% proximal. Standard LR achieved a test macro AUC of 0.704 (95% CI 0.674–0.734), comparable with the training-estimated saturated reference (0.698). Random forest (0.701) and gradient boosting (0.699) were within the prespecified analytic equivalence framework relative to LR, whereas SVM was lower (0.648; ΔAUC − 0.056; Holm-adjusted p < 0.004). Standard models had poor proximal-class recall. Cost-sensitive training increased proximal recall to 0.450 for most algorithms but worsened probability calibration.
evidence_items.title: Demographic Baseline for Pediatric Forearm Fracture Localization: A Machine- Learning Benchmark Using the PediURF Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Improper segregation of biomedical waste allows infectious and otherwise hazardous material to enter general waste streams, with consequences for public health and the environment. Reliable automatic classification at the point of generation could support safer segregation and disposal. Deep learning has been applied to this task, but the public image datasets used for training and evaluation are commonly distributed in a pre-augmented form, in which each source photograph appears as many transformed copies. A conventional random train–test split then places near-identical copies in both sets, so the reported accuracy partly reflects memorisation rather than generalisation. We study automatic classification of 23 biomedical waste categories (15,600 background-removed images) with explicit attention to this issue. Because the dataset carries no ground-truth labelling of duplicates, a leakage-free partition cannot be certified; instead, visually near-identical images are grouped from image content using ORB keypoints with RANSAC geometric verification and kept within a single split, and this controlled estimate is compared against the fully mixed random split, which is known to be leaked, as an optimistic reference. Across four transfer-learning backbones, ConvNeXt-Tiny performs best, reaching a macro-F1 of 0.847±0.007 under the controlled split against 0.958±0.003 under the random split, so naive evaluation is optimistic by about eleven points. Mapping the categories onto World Health Organization hazard streams yields a disposal-bin accuracy of 0.892, with 1.76% of hazardous items misrouted to general waste. The study offers a benchmark and a more realistic basis for reporting automatic biomedical-waste classification.
evidence_items.title:
Automated Biomedical Waste Segregation Using
Deep Learning: A Duplicate-Aware Classification
Benchmark and Disposal-Safety Assessment

evidence_items.summary: Natural language explanations promised by modern Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) offer autonomous driving systems a path toward detailed scene description and interpretable decision making on the road. While recent benchmarks have begun assessing these models on driving scenes, they mainly target routine traffic conditions and general comprehension tasks based on existing driving datasets and therefore fail to evaluate model performance on the rarest and most safety-critical driving events, also known as"corner cases". To provide a comprehensive evaluation of Video LLMs on precisely these scenarios, we introduce DashBench, a benchmark testing 25 Video LLMs on 1,709 carefully curated driving videos spanning not only collision-related corner cases but also rare non-collision ones. Through extensive prompts and open-ended question answering, we expose a critical capability gap: all evaluated models perform substantially below the threshold required for safety-critical driving applications, frequently misjudging or missing dangerous events on the road ahead and hallucinating non-existent agents or actions in their explanations. We believe DashBench, combining an extensive dataset with a rigorous evaluation toolkit and a detailed diagnosis of current model limitations, drives progress toward safer, more explainable autonomous driving systems. The code and data will be shared at: cornercase-dashbench.github.io
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Video LLMs'Understanding of Corner Cases in Autonomous Driving

evidence_items.summary: Physical AI aims to learn transferable physical knowledge from real-world experience to understand, predict, and act in the physical world. Internet videos and embodied demonstrations provide complementary observations of motion, interaction, and state evolution. A foundational data challenge is to measure and preserve this physical information as training supervision. In video-language pretraining, captions express observed processes in language, yet a semantically correct description can omit the interactions and transitions that define those processes. Rich physical experience in video does not automatically translate into sufficient language supervision. This gap calls for a yardstick to assess annotation quality, compare captioning strategies, and guide training-data refinement. Motivated by our data construction for world-model pretraining, we introduce PhysCapBench, to our knowledge the first unified physical-caption benchmark spanning all three domains: third-person scenes, egocentric manipulation, and handheld-gripper demonstrations. It provides human-verified annotations for 1,500 video sequences and evaluates accuracy and coverage through seven physical dimensions. We examine downstream utility through video reconstruction and manipulation-policy fine-tuning. Physical captions reduce reconstruction LPIPS by 8.6-9.5% on third-person videos and 26.9-30.9% on egocentric videos relative to metadata captions. Training-instruction enrichment improves both PhysCapBench scores and policy success, including a 7.5-percentage-point gain for pi0.5 on a RoboTwin 2.0 subtask. PhysCapBench makes the physical content of language supervision inspectable and comparable, providing a cross-domain basis for its evaluation and improvement.
evidence_items.title: PhysCapBench: A Cross-Domain Benchmark for Physically Grounded Video Captioning

evidence_items.summary: Autograders are a standard tool for evaluating student submissions in programming courses. However, proof-based and short-answer questions characteristic of Computer Science theory courses make grading a substantially more complex and labor-intensive task. In courses such as Discrete Mathematics, teaching assistants and instructors may dedicate several hours per week solely to grading, reducing the time available for higher-impact student interactions such as office hours. Large language models (LLMs) present a promising avenue for alleviating this burden, though their efficacy in this domain remains insufficiently studied. In this work, we evaluate a suite of LLMs for Discrete Mathematics grading. We introduce IADMD (Instructor-Annotated Discrete Mathematics Dataset), a benchmark of over 100 problems drawn from a second-year undergraduate course. To mitigate privacy concerns, synthetic student responses are generated by an LLM and subsequently edited and graded by a current Discrete Mathematics course instructor. A second expert grader separately annotated 12% of the examples to establish inter-rater reliability. Our findings indicate that LLMs can match or even exceed agreement observed between two human graders, suggesting their readiness for real-world integration into course grading workflows. We nonetheless advise instructors to assess model suitability for their specific course before adoption.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Language Models for Discrete Mathematics Grading

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents, i.e., language models run by a harness, can now write, run and debug software autonomously. This raises the question of whether they can also carry out control system design. In this paper, we consider control system design as a task for LLM agents and grade the designed controller as control engineers do: the controller is given in a single Python file mapping measurements to actions, evaluated on held-out seeds against an ordered set of requirements, under specified physical perturbations and structural certificates, without using neural networks. We formulate the task as a chance-constrained feasibility problem and instantiate it in ControlHarbor, a benchmark of 44 tasks over 13 plants, which includes network consensus, vehicle platooning, the MuJoCo hopper, walker and humanoid. The tasks are packaged in the Harbor format, so that any agent harness can be run against them, and the same environments also serve learning algorithms other than LLMs, such as reinforcement learning (RL), under the same evaluation. With ControlHarbor, we observe that the controllers designed by three frontier coding agents, Claude Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Sonnet 5.5, reach the RL return on every parity task, but only in a minority of sessions. We also observe that the controllers certified for return alone usually fail under perturbations. When robustness is part of the specification, a structured design meets it at the RL return on the humanoid task, where domain-randomised RL does not; under large pushes, domain-randomised RL succeeds and no designed controller does. The benchmark, the controllers, and their grades are released.
evidence_items.title: ControlHarbor: A Benchmark for Control Design by Coding Agents

evidence_items.summary: LLM-based peer review is now used at production scale, but its evaluation remains limited. We introduce a benchmark that injects objective, localisable errors of four types (general issues, mathematics, numerics, citations) at three severity levels into real papers and measures each reviewer's detection rate by error type and severity, together with its false-positive rate on clean copies. We also present Skepthical, a multi-agent reviewer that verifies citation-backed claims by retrieving the cited papers, mathematics with computer algebra, and numerical claims with executed code. We apply the benchmark to two corpora of 15 recent arXiv preprints each, one in astrophysics and one in machine learning (ML), injecting a total of 357 errors, and evaluate twelve reviewer systems: six single-LLM reviewers, two Claude Code configurations, three publicly available reviewers, and Skepthical. The choice of model has the largest impact on detection rate: given the same prompt, three frontier LLMs differ by about 50 percentage points in total detection on both corpora. Tools and scaffolding help when they contribute what the model cannot supply on its own. In particular, on astrophysics, Claude Code improves on a single Claude call in mathematics and numerics detection, and enforced citation retrieval gives Skepthical the highest citation error detection rate of all systems by a large margin. This citation lead, however, is not observed on ML, where the models appear to know the literature better and Skepthical's citation detection rate is statistically indistinguishable from that of the best single LLM. False-positive rates are below 10% for most systems, but vary with prompt, model, and scaffolding, with mathematics flags the main source of false positives. The evaluation pipeline, the injected errors, and the adjudication logs are released as a benchmark.
evidence_items.title: Auditing AI peer reviewers: a benchmark on real scientific papers

organizations: Kalasalingam Academy of Research and Education
evidence_items.summary: Indian Sign Language recognition is important for accessible human-computer interaction, yet constrained by limited datasets, signer variability, and difficulty converting frame-level detections into coherent words. This paper presents a framework for real-time finger-spelled Indian Sign Language word recognition from video. Our system focuses on character-level detection and temporal word construction, not continuous sentence-level ISL. The system integrates multi-source dataset construction, size-aware augmentation, lightweight detection, video processing, parameter optimisation and word-building for repeated letters and temporal inconsistencies. A 50,000-image dataset covering 36 classes (0–9, A–Z) combines public ISL data with custom recordings. Tiered augmentation improves robustness: moderate for large datasets, stronger for small subsets. The model uses real-time object-detection, evaluated by precision, recall, and mAP. Results show high detection performance: precision 99.74%, recall 98.43%, mAP@50–95 99.40% on validation. However, signer-independent accuracy drops to 68% on unseen signers, highlighting cross-signer generalization challenges. The system includes video-quality enhancement and parameter tuning for cross-user testing, achieving 15–20 FPS with low latency. The study demonstrates feasibility of detection and post-processing for finger-spelled ISL, highlighting need for stronger validation and benchmarking.
evidence_items.title: Real-time Indian Sign Language word recognition through visual detection and temporal word construction

evidence_items.summary: LiDAR is a core sensor for autonomous driving, yet it is highly vulnerable to fog. Fog scattering produces strong backscatter near the sensor and attenuates reflections from objects behind it, so weak object returns are often discarded by the peak detection that converts received signals into point clouds. Full-waveform LiDAR (FWL), which records the received optical signal before peak detection, retains these weak returns, but the lack of suitable data has prevented research on recovering fog-hidden objects from FWL. We present Fog-FWL, a dataset foundation for this task that consists of a real-world benchmark, Fog-FWL-Real, and a large-scale synthetic training set, Fog-FWL-Sim. Fog-FWL-Real contains 7,527 real foggy FWL frames from 8 scenes and 58 sequences, which is 579x larger than the only existing real foggy FWL data, together with histogram-level Object/Fog/Noise labels, 10,719 3D bounding boxes, and three difficulty levels defined by the attenuation of object reflections. Fog-FWL-Sim contains 12,000 frames generated by our physics-based simulator, Fog-FWL-Simulator, which integrates spatially heterogeneous fog density fields, time-resolved light transport including multiple scattering, and a photon-counting SPAD receiver model. The two subsets share the same sensor format and annotation protocol, enabling a strict sim-to-real evaluation in which no real waveforms are used for training. Our analysis shows that, under the hardest condition, object returns are included in the three strongest peaks for only 34.9% of object rays, underscoring the need for waveform-level recovery. Fog-FWL-Real, Fog-FWL-Sim, and the Fog-FWL-Simulator will be publicly released to facilitate research on fog-robust LiDAR perception.
evidence_items.title: Fog-FWL: A Large-Scale Full-Waveform LiDAR Dataset for Recovering Fog-Hidden Objects

evidence_items.summary: Recommender systems, which retrieve items of interest to users based on their interaction histories, have recently witnessed several key technological advancements, benefiting from the semantic representation space and model-data scaling. Nevertheless, practitioners and researchers have frequently encountered critical inconsistencies between simple offline evaluations and complex online results, and this gap still exists in the era of large models. In this work, we address several key factors that contribute to this inconsistency: 1) the \textit{large-scale continual learning challenge} that assumes a practical demand to maintain long-term model effectiveness under dynamic item pools and distributional shifts; 2) the \textit{combinatorial diversity challenge} that requires the generation strategy to solve the accuracy-diversity trade-off in both the finer token level and the holistic item level; and 3) the \textit{multi-task reward balancing challenge}, which is particularly critical for modern generative models that can accurately model the sequence distribution but are less controllable for the multi-task demands. To address these challenges and further pave the way for the development of more realistic recommendation solutions, we introduce KuaiRecV2, a deliberately constructed benchmark with industrial-level datasets from Kuaishou. Specifically, we provide a large-scale interaction dataset with million-scale multi-modal item information and long-term interaction records across 30 days, with a dynamic video candidate pool. Additionally, we provide a rigorous benchmark that evaluates retrieval accuracy, diversity, and multi-task performance in one rubric system, where an effective advancement occurs if and only if the new method improves all metrics. The code is available at https://github.com/cxli2333/KuaiRecV2
evidence_items.title: KuaiRecV2: Benchmarking Large-Scale Continual Learning for Diversified and Multi-task Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) enables the model to invoke external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporate returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities. We open-source the model weights and inference code.
evidence_items.title: AURA 2.0: From User-Driven Responses to Model-Initiated Conversations in Streaming Video

evidence_items.summary: We present EvenVLM, the first text and multimodal (VQA) dataset for Even (Lamut), an endangered Northern Tungusic language spoken by approximately 6,800 people in Siberia. Our dataset comprises 50,521 structured Even-Russian entries extracted from dictionary and phrasebook sources via GPT-4o Mini-based parsing, from which we synthetically generate 107,543 training examples spanning translation, grammar, reading comprehension, and semantic classification. To address tokenization inefficiency on Even's agglutinative morphology, we propose a three-step tokenizer expansion algorithm that adds Even-specific graphemes (eng, oe, o-umlaut), whitelisted vocabulary, and BPE merges, reducing average tokens per word by 27% (4.99 to 3.64). Using LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen3-VL-4B, we adapt the model for text tasks (0.53% trainable parameters, rank 32) and separately for visual question answering (rank 64, frozen vision encoder). Our best configuration achieves 11.4% exact match and a 13.6 weighted score on text benchmarks, 0.1283 chrF for sentence translation, and 65% accuracy on VQA (up from 0% for the base model and text-only fine-tuning). We release our datasets, evaluation benchmarks, and training pipeline to support further research on Even and other low-resource languages.
evidence_items.title: EvenVLM: A Text and Multimodal Dataset for the Even Language with Vision-Language Fine-Tuning

evidence_items.summary: Identifier naming is a fundamental aspect of code quality and a recurring challenge for novice programmers and this paper addresses how to provide scalable feedback on it. To this end, we develop a fine-grained taxonomy of naming issues and compile a dataset of 337 manually labeled identifiers drawn from novice code. Using this dataset, we investigate how reliably large language models (LLMs) can detect poor identifiers in an introductory programming context, and we compare their labels with human annotations. Our evaluation shows that LLM–human agreement is comparable to agreement between human raters. We argue that human agreement provides a more realistic benchmark than exact label matching - since humans do not always agree, we cannot expect an LLM to always agree with a human annotator. Our findings demonstrate that LLMs can feasibly provide naming feedback to novices, and furthermore, our study informs refinement the proposed taxonomy and highlights opportunities to integrate naming-focused feedback and discussion into programming instruction.
evidence_items.title: Poor Identifier Names in Introductory Programming: A Taxonomy and LLM Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming formal theorem proving. Yet further progress remains constrained by the lack of a transparent and effective data recipe for systematically improving theorem-proving models. In this work, we argue that effective agentic provers require strong mathematical skill priors to ground theorem proving and agentic trajectories to enable long-horizon, interactive proof construction. To this end, we synthesize an agent-native 33.7B-token mid-training corpus covering decomposition, search, self-verification, and revision, together with verifier-grounded agentic trajectories. We further introduce the daVinci-Prover harness, which enables models to construct proofs and interact with a Lean verifier in an isolated workspace, and use it to collect approximately 36K high-quality agent trajectories for supervised fine-tuning. Our mid-training recipe yields an average improvement of 13.7 points over the matched Qwen3-8B SFT-only baseline across MiniF2F, FATE-M, and ProofNet. When applied to the Qwen3.5 series, our approach also yields strong performance across theorem-proving benchmarks and achieves near-saturating MiniF2F performance with memory compaction. The results highlight agent-native mid-training as an effective foundation for developing stronger interactive theorem-proving agents.
evidence_items.title: daVinci-Prover: Agent-Native Mid-Training for Formal Theorem Proving

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent claims that are unsupported by a given source document, motivating accurate and efficient document-grounded factuality detection. Existing LLM-based evaluators often require repeated inference and incur high computational cost, whereas compact factuality detectors are efficient at inference time but commonly rely on large labeled or synthetically generated corpora. We propose CPIL (Cross-Paraphrastic Invariance Learning), a two-stage Siamese framework that converts a small labeled set into relational supervision without acquiring additional factuality labels. CPIL constructs positive pairs from distinct label-preserving paraphrastic views of the same document-claim instance and negative pairs from opposite-label examples associated with the same source document. It further introduces quantile-aware semi-hard negative mining, which derives a boundary from the positive-pair similarity distribution and balances informative negatives with broader coverage. In the two-stage training procedure, Stage 1 learns an encoder from these task-aware pairs, and Stage 2 jointly fine-tunes the encoder and a linear classification head for binary factuality prediction. At inference time, CPIL requires no paraphrase generation, pair construction, or Siamese comparison and uses only one encoder-classifier forward pass. On the 11-task LLM-AggreFact benchmark, CPIL-2% and CPIL-3% achieve macro-F1 scores of 81.04 and 81.60 while using only 2-3% of the FactCG-released labeled pool. Both settings outperform all compared compact detectors and two vanilla LLM references. Ablations and sensitivity analyses support the contributions of task-aware pair construction, dynamic negative mining, and multi-pivot paraphrasing.
evidence_items.title: Label-Efficient Document-Grounded Factuality Detection via Cross-Paraphrastic Invariance Learning

evidence_items.summary: While language-model agents excel at long-horizon coding and terminal tasks, this success relies on two conditions: explicit text specifications and immediate execution feedback. However, neither condition holds in real-world problems where critical information exists only in images, leaving it unclear whether long-horizon capability transfers from text to visual reasoning. In such visual settings, because rules and clues resist text transcription and lack test-case feedback, agents must repeatedly inspect images, simulate spatial transformations, and autonomously cross-check clues. Despite this challenge, existing evaluations fail to capture such capability: visual reasoning benchmarks largely reduce tasks to single-turn, short-chain question answering, whereas agent benchmarks focus on text-based environments or interactive states that permit trial-and-error. To bridge this gap, we introduce Visual Cipher Bench, a collection of 40 original visual puzzles across four categories: spatial manipulation and simulation, logical constraints and planning, rule induction, and knowledge-based decoding. Each puzzle provides only one to three black-and-white line drawings and a minimal submission instruction, requiring agents to discover the underlying solving mechanism entirely from the images. Across 29 reasoning-effort configurations of eight frontier models, even the strongest model, GPT-6 Astra (max), achieves only 26.7% accuracy, while five of the eight models score below 1%. Yet on a ten-task subset, providing a single non-spoiler mechanism hint boosts accuracy from 7.8% to 55.6%. This sharp contrast shows that the primary bottleneck of current agents lies not in executing multi-step plans, but in autonomously discovering rules from visual evidence. Visual Cipher Bench thus provides a rigorous benchmark for measuring long-horizon visual reasoning in agents.
evidence_items.title: Visual Cipher Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Visual Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) reason effectively about video content, but whether they perceive its event boundaries in a manner consistent with humans remains unclear. We first investigate this through Generic Event Boundary Detection (GEBD), which identifies event boundaries naturally perceived by humans in continuous video, without relying on predefined event categories. On Kinetics-GEBD dataset, LVLMs miss many boundaries when predicting directly from frames, but effectively refine candidates proposed by an unsupervised discovery method, achieving state-of-the-art unsupervised GEBD performance. We extend this discovery-refinement approach to hour-long egocentric video, where boundary discovery requires a broader semantic scale and whole-video LVLM refinement becomes impractical. We address these challenges through coarse-to-fine temporal discovery and localized LVLM accept/reject judgments. Human evaluation shows that the LVLM's agreement with group consensus falls within the range observed among human annotators, with disagreements concentrated on low-consensus cases. Using this pipeline, we construct EgoBoundary, a benchmark for event boundary detection in hour-scale egocentric video. Representative supervised and unsupervised methods degrade substantially on EgoBoundary, highlighting the challenge of long-horizon event boundary detection.
evidence_items.title: Can an LVLM Perceive Event Boundaries Like a Human?

evidence_items.summary: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared block, offering a parameter-efficient approach to language modeling. However, most existing works directly reuse each loop's output as the next's input, which can lead to hidden-state scale growth and perturbation amplification as recurrence deepens. We propose Rectified Looped Transformer (RLT), which redesigns feedback between loops using an interpolation schedule inspired by flow-based modeling. At each loop, RLT forms the next input by linearly interpolating between the current state and its prediction. Such interpolation distributes state changes across loops, encouraging a smoother trajectory from the initial input to the final output. Theoretical analysis proves that, under appropriate assumptions, RLT keeps state magnitudes uniformly bounded across loops and reduces the worst-case perturbation amplification. We evaluate RLT on language modeling corpora and downstream benchmarks. At matched training and inference depths, RLT consistently achieves lower perplexity than a standard looped Transformer, while exhibiting greater robustness to input perturbations and variance in inference depth. Consistent with the theoretical results, latent trajectory analysis shows that RLT maintains more stable hidden-state norms across loops, which also facilitates extrapolation-based decoding strategies. Notably, RLT achieves these gains without requiring additional trainable parameters or extra recurrent block evaluations, thus providing a simple yet more stable feedback mechanism for looped Transformers.
evidence_items.title: Rectified Looped Transformer

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
Automated classification of glioblastoma (IDH-wt, WHO CNS Gr.4) histopathologic sub-regions in whole slide images (WSI) is essential for quantitative tumor characterization, but faces substantial challenges from intra-tumoral heterogeneity and inter-observer annotation variability. The AI-RANO & RANO-Pathology working groups organized BraTS-Path 2024, representing the first international benchmarking environment and publicly available spatially annotated dataset, towards promoting the development and fair evaluation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models to classify specific sub-regions: cellular tumor, pseudopalisading necrosis (PN), microvascular proliferation, geographic necrosis, infiltration into the cortex, and white matter penetration (WM).


METHODS
Multi-institutional H&E-stained WSIs had reference standard samples generated by eight expert neuropathologists, following a rigorous peer review protocol, resulting in 309,118 data samples (training/validation/hold-out testing: 96,485/62,387/150,246). Quantitative performance evaluation of six AI approaches was conducted based on multiple metrics, including Accuracy and Matthew's correlation coefficient (MCC). A robust statistically-aware ranking strategy offered statistical significance of the final rankings.


RESULTS
Top-performing approaches employed common strategies, including large pre-trained models, ensembling, and extensive data augmentation, reporting Accuracy=0.69 and MCC=0.58. Key challenges included severe class imbalance, hampering minority class performance, and inter-annotator variability, especially for ambiguous sub-regions such as PN or WM.


CONCLUSIONS
BraTS-Path represents a valuable public resource for glioblastoma histopathologic sub-region assessment. Our findings indicate the specific task remaining an open research problem, highlighting the influence of rare sub-regions, the absence of a consistent "gold standard" annotation protocol, and the potential of foundation models to improve generalization, guiding future research toward developing more reliable AI tools for quantitative neuropathology.
evidence_items.title: AI Assessment of Heterogeneous Histopathologic Brain Tumor Sub-regions: the RANO MICCAI BraTS-Path 2024 Challenge.

rationale: Matched: data quality, evaluat, training data
evidence_items.summary: To help students understand Human-In-The-Loop in AI and how human biases affect AI outcomes, we developed an AI4K12 software called WiseSpend AI. This is a browser-based educational game that places middle school students in the role of data labeler and AI trainer. Students classify household items as financial Needs or Wants to train a rule-based classifier, then evaluate that classifier's autonomous decisions across a simulated 30-day budget challenge. This game provides students with a first-person experience in training data quality, model generalization, and human-AI trust. We tested the game in a middle school setting and analyzed 15,567 logged interaction events from 89 students across 117 sessions combined with 143 pre-activity survey responses. Our findings show that students learned best by actively training the AI, and their outcomes were driven more by the quality and balance of that training than by prior AI knowledge or in-game spending. They also tended to over-trust the AI at first, but replay and hands-on iteration helped them improve at both judging the model and improving its behavior. Students showed clear signs of learning during gameplay, with many shifting from personal preference to thinking carefully about what examples the AI actually needed. One student described this as ''starving my robot'' when they realized they hadn't given it enough examples in the ''Need'' category. Features like the real- time Confidence Meter helped students catch and fix their AI's mistakes. These results suggest that simple, browser-based games can effectively build student understanding of data, fairness, and responsibility in AI systems.
evidence_items.title: WiseSpend AI: Engaging K-12 Students in Financial Literacy by Evaluating the Human Role in Training Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: The teaching quality assessment of college Wushu (martial arts) courses has traditionally relied on instructor-based evaluation and individual skill-test indicators, making it difficult to comprehensively characterize students’ learning outcomes across multiple dimensions such as skill, physical fitness, theoretical knowledge, and classroom behavior, and equally difficult to provide early warning for students with lagging learning outcomes. To address this, this paper proposes a multi-branch deep learning framework for quantitative physical education data, MartialSense-Net, which simultaneously performs classification prediction of students’ learning performance levels and regression prediction of their overall performance scores. The framework first partitions the original heterogeneous quantitative features – physical fitness, skill, theory, and classroom behavior – into four semantic branches, and learns low-dimensional representations for each branch independently through a Multi-Branch Feature Extraction (MBFE) module; it then introduces a Cross Feature Attention Fusion (CFAF) module, which models the interactions among the different branches based on a multi-head self-attention mechanism; finally, a multilayer perceptron encoder and multi-task prediction heads are used to output the classification and regression results. The framework is evaluated as a proof of concept on a publicly available general physical education performance benchmark containing 500 student records and 20 original attributes, from which 16 original predictor variables are selected. Because this dataset contains no Wushu-specific measures of routine precision, force expression, rhythm, or posture, the present experiment evaluates the modeling architecture and does not constitute external validation in authentic Wushu courses. The study systematically compares the framework with random forest, XGBoost, support vector machine, and multilayer perceptron baselines using 5-fold stratified cross-validation, and conducts ablation experiments targeting the attention mechanism and multi-branch structure. The reproducible five-fold rerun shows that MartialSense-Net achieves a Macro-F1 score of 0.545, exceeding the plain MLP and the NoMBFE variant but not the NoAttention variant; however, the overall classification performance of the proposed model has not yet surpassed tree-based baselines such as random forest and XGBoost, and the coefficient of determination (R2) for the regression task is negative, indicating that precise regression of the overall performance score remains challenging under the current data scale and feature conditions. This paper further analyzes the limitations of deep learning-based educational assessment under small-scale and class-imbalanced tabular data conditions (samples of “High Performers” account for only 2.4%), and honestly reports all experimental results without any exaggeration of model performance. The findings therefore support MartialSense-Net only as an initial methodological benchmark for structured physical education data. Demonstrating Wushu-specific effectiveness will require multi-institutional records from authentic Wushu courses, direct Wushu skill indicators, and external validation across instructors, course levels, and student cohorts.
evidence_items.title: Deep learning for learning outcome prediction and evaluation in Wushu physical education

evidence_items.summary: Granular spatio-temporal forecasting of socioeconomic risks, particularly regional crime dynamics, is crucial for formulating targeted public policies and optimizing resource allocation under fiscal constraints. This study presents a comparative framework that benchmarks deep probabilistic graph architectures against Bayesian hierarchical models across 52 administrative districts in South Africa, leveraging a unique multi-year dataset from the Governance, Public Safety, and Justice Survey (GPSJS) spanning 2018/19 to 2023/24. Specifically, we evaluate a novel Quantile Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (Quantile TGCN), which integrates spatio-temporal graph convolutions with pinball-loss optimization to generate distribution-free, calibrated prediction intervals. This model is contrasted with a deterministic Standard TGCN baseline and Bayesian spatio-temporal models fitted via Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA), incorporating Besag-York-Mollié (BYM2) spatial priors under both Gamma and log-normal observation models. The evaluation criteria include out-of-sample point forecast accuracy, residual bias profiles, prediction interval calibration, and the ability to rank high-risk spatial hotspots under strict allocation constraints. Contrary to expectations that more complex architectures would yield superior predictive performance, the Bayesian INLA specifications, particularly the log-normal BYM2 model, demonstrated lower out-of-sample errors and stronger discrimination of high-risk districts. Notably, the Quantile TGCN excels in producing well-calibrated, distribution-free prediction intervals, thus offering valuable insights for granular risk monitoring and evidence-based governance in emerging economies. This comparative approach contributes to the development of robust diagnostic tools for socioeconomic risk assessment and intervention planning.
evidence_items.title: Quantile temporal graph convolutional networks and Bayesian hierarchical spatiotemporal models for crime risk forecasting and hotspot identification

evidence_items.summary: Medical image classification in resource-constrained settings must contend with limited annotations and computational capacity. We evaluate four ZACH-ViT variants with linear, Euclidean prototype, Poincare and spherical heads alongside two compact multiple-instance-learning baselines. All models are trained from scratch with fewer than 260,000 parameters across seven MedMNIST+ datasets and three external benchmarks (PCam, ISIC2017 and Shenzhen tuberculosis radiographs). The low-data protocol uses 50 training images per class and five seeds, with validation-selected checkpoints at 23 and 47 epochs; a full-data reference uses one seed. Compact-TransMIL achieves the highest ten-dataset mean test Macro-F1 at 23 epochs (53.34%) and with full data (73.93%). At 47 epochs, ZACH-Linear narrowly leads (57.76% versus 57.54% for Compact-TransMIL). Extending training improves Macro-F1 in 239 of 300 paired comparisons. On ISIC2017, hZACH-Spherical has the highest 47-epoch low-data Macro-F1 (44.09% with SD 4.09%), whereas ZACH-EuclideanProto leads with full data (51.27%). We additionally conduct 40 CPU-only training runs on ISIC2017 and Shenzhen using four CPU threads; model-only single-image inference requires approximately 4-9 ms, while image decoding and preprocessing substantially increase end-to-end latency. The results demonstrate the feasibility of CPU-only training on the tested platform and the task- and regime-dependence of compact medical imaging under strict resource constraints.
evidence_items.title: Towards Democratising Low-Data Medical Image Classification: CPU-Trainable ZACH-ViT and Its Geometric Variants

evidence_items.summary: Electrochemical and photoelectrochemical data are often processed using several stand-alone programs, making it difficult to maintain a consistent workflow from raw data to reported results. Here, we introduce the Researcher Analysis Toolkit, a modular desktop application that brings together voltammetry, Tafel analysis, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), semiconductor and photoelectrochemical calculations, time-resolved photoluminescence fitting, optical band-gap estimation, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy analysis. For EIS, the toolkit supports both user-defined circuit fitting and hierarchical screening of candidate circuits. The fitting workflow includes Lin-KK consistency testing, residual analysis, parameter-bound warnings, and approximate uncertainty and parameter-correlation diagnostics. Users retain control over fitting ranges and analysis settings, whereas calculations and data export follow a common workflow across modules. The software generates processed datasets, figures, tables, and analysis reports. Its operation is illustrated using representative module outputs, predefined synthetic EIS benchmarks, and experimental impedance data from an indium tin oxide (ITO) electrode coated with a cerium oxide-based composite. The integrated workflow is designed to simplify data handling and support documentation of analysis settings and outputs.
evidence_items.title: Researcher Analysis Toolkit for integrated and traceable evaluation of electrochemical, photoelectrochemical, and spectroscopic data.

evidence_items.summary: Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in automating pipeline design, they have been studied almost exclusively in fully supervised settings, leaving them untested in realistic regimes where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), framing SSL as a program search problem and studying how agents navigate this space under limited supervision. We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%. However, our results identify program selection as a critical bottleneck in AgentSSL, where performance drops by as much as 47% when selecting based on the agent's feedback metric. To systematically study this bottleneck, we introduce ProgramSelectBench, a large-scale benchmark with a combined total of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, and evaluate both unsupervised and active program selection methods. We further evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, highlighting the opportunities and challenges of transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?

evidence_items.summary: Existing natural-language-to-SQL benchmarks primarily evaluate queries over bounded relational data, leaving streaming semantics underexplored. We introduce FlinkEval, an execution-grounded synthetic benchmark comprising 3,903 question--SQL pairs across 45 industry domains and 45 semantic labels. We create diverse schemas and domain-plausible, temporally consistent data through iterative generation and validation. SQL patterns collected from the human-written NL2SQL pairs and vendor documentation drive quota-balanced generation, and execution with a repair loop on Confluent Cloud Apache Flink produces reference queries covering windowing, temporal joins, pattern matching, nested types, and data manipulation. The corpus includes paired schema-explicit and business-language requests, with annotations for analysis by query pattern, complexity, and execution mode. A seven-level Question Specification Ladder examines semantics-preserving reformulation and underspecified requests augmented with oracle-derived clues. Baseline evaluations combine execution outcomes with adjudicated LLM judgments, revealing challenges in pattern composition and request specification.
evidence_items.title: FlinkEval: A Synthetic Corpus for Evaluating Natural Language Interfaces to Streaming SQL

evidence_items.summary: AI agents increasingly access enterprise data, invoke powerful tools, and act with limited human oversight. Existing security defenses primarily detect prompt injection, harmful outputs, or suspicious behavior, but do not determine whether an agent remains faithful to the purpose for which it was deployed. An action may contain no attack pattern and stay within granted permissions while still violating the agent's role, organizational constraints, or purpose. We introduce Intent- Aware Security, a framework that treats trusted agent intent as a first-class security object. We define Intent Preservation and Intent Drift, and operationalize them through an Intent Profile: an agent-specific representation extracted from organizational, role, and developer intent. We further introduce an Intent-Aware benchmark of 887 validated samples across 35 agents, built by a generation procedure that fixes ground-truth labels before LLM realization, and four Intent Profile-based protections: pre-execution detection, post-execution detection, input alignment, and system-prompt hardening. Across all evaluations, Intent Profile-based protection outperforms all profile-free baselines on the primary metric. On our benchmark, it raises four-class acro-F1 from 45% to 79% (Out-of-Scope F1 from 8% to 76%). On more than 10,000 executed AgentDojo trajectories, where ground truth comes from environment state, profile-based post-execution detection reaches 0.949 AUROC versus AlignmentCheck 0.909, 0.897 with raw agent configuration and 0.843 without context. Profile-based input alignment improves protection success by 7 points over DataFilter with a comparable benign utility. These results suggest that an agent's intended purpose can serve as a useful security reference for detecting and mitigating deviations from its deployed role and operational boundaries.
evidence_items.title: Intent-Aware Protection for AI Agents

evidence_items.summary: Efficient batch execution of agent tasks is critical to LLM training and development workflows, including benchmark evaluation, synthetic-data generation, and RL rollouts. Since these tasks alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction, we present coordinated optimizations to reduce batch makespan, the time required to complete all tasks in a batch. For hybrid LLMs, a workload-based resource model guides GPU-memory allocation between key-value (KV) cache and recurrent state and provides a reference sample concurrency to exploit parallelism while limiting recomputation. Trajectory-aware routing and scheduling promote cache reuse while balancing worker load. Under constrained environment capacity, we decouple sample admission from environment execution and introduce Chain-Advancing Action Scheduling (CAAS), which prioritizes long chains using observed progress to shorten the batch tail. Controlled replay combines actual inference with recorded environment responses and durations for ablations of individual optimizations. Live evaluations with Ling-3.0-Flash and Ling-3.1-Flash on the BFCL, SWE-bench Multilingual, WideSearch, and MCP-Atlas benchmarks demonstrate makespan reductions of 10.4% to 65.0%, while evaluation scores remain aligned. Furthermore, these methods have been successfully applied to training and evaluation workflows for the Ling-3.x model series, accelerating the model-development cycle.
evidence_items.title: Reducing Batch Makespan for LLM Agent Workloads through Inference-Environment Coordination

evidence_items.summary: We address the problem of whole-body person recognition in unconstrained environments. This problem arises in surveillance scenarios such as those in the IARPA Biometric Recognition and Identification at Altitude and Range (BRIAR) program, where biometric data is captured at long standoff distances, elevated viewing angles, and under adverse atmospheric conditions (e.g., turbulence and high wind velocity). To this end, we propose FarSight, a unified end-to-end system for person recognition that integrates complementary biometric cues across face, gait, and body shape modalities. FarSight comprises four core modules: multi-subject detection and tracking, recognition-aware video restoration, modality-specific biometric feature encoding, and quality-guided multi-modal fusion. Rather than treating these modules as independent processing stages, FarSight coordinates key stage-level decisions around the final biometric objective: tracking maintains identity-consistent temporal evidence, restoration is selectively invoked and optimized for recognition, and modality-quality estimates guide score fusion. This coordinated design supports recognition under degraded image conditions, large pose and scale variations, and cross-domain gaps. Extensive experiments on the BRIAR dataset, one of the most comprehensive benchmarks for long-range, multi-modal biometric recognition, demonstrate the effectiveness of FarSight. Compared with our preliminary system [1] on the Face-Included treatment set of BRIAR EVP 5.0.1, the current system improves 1:1 verification (TAR@0.1% FAR) by 34.4 percentage points and closed-set identification (Rank-20) by 17.8 percentage points, while reducing open-set identification errors (FNIR@1% FPIR) by 34.3 percentage points. Furthermore, FarSight was evaluated in the 2025 NIST RTE Face in Video Evaluation (FIVE), which conducts standardized face recognition testing on the BRIAR dataset. These results establish FarSight as a state-of-the-art solution for operational biometric recognition in challenging real-world conditions.
evidence_items.title: Person Recognition at Altitude and Range: Fusion of Face, Body Shape and Gait.

evidence_items.summary: Parallel mechanisms pose distinctive challenges to large language models (LLMs), as valid reasoning depends jointly on mechanism topology, loop closure, geometry, joint types, and modeling assumptions. Yet existing LLM benchmarks provide little systematic coverage of such domain-specific knowledge, constraint-sensitive analysis, and constructive design. To fill this gap, we introduce MECHBENCH, a 2,541-question benchmark for evaluating LLMs in parallel mechanisms across professional knowledge, mechanism analysis, and design. MECHBENCH contains standard and challenge tiers spanning six capability categories and nine executable analysis and design tasks. It is constructed through MECHFORGE, a domain-grounded framework that combines expert-organized knowledge, LLM-assisted question generation, programmatic instance generation, two-stage expert review, and task-aware scoring with exact matching, rubric-based evaluation, and program verification. We further develop MECHGPT as a diagnostic domain-adapted model. Experiments show that strong knowledge performance does not directly translate into executable mechanism reasoning: leading closed-service models achieve over 95 on the standard tier but only 47-60 on the challenge tier, while domain adaptation substantially improves MechGPT over its Qwen3-8B baselines but leaves a large gap in constrained analysis and design. These results establish MECHBENCH as a systematic testbed for measuring domain-specific LLM capabilities in mechanism science.
evidence_items.title: MechBench: A Domain-Specific LLM Benchmark for Parallel Mechanisms

evidence_items.summary: AfriNTL: A 500 m annual nighttime light dataset for Africa, 2000–2025 AfriNTL provides annual nighttime light radiance for Africa from 2000 to 2025 at 500 m spatial resolution. The dataset contains 26 single-band GeoTIFFs, one per calendar year, named 2000.tif through 2025.tif . Data sources and processing The 2000–2013 layers are model reconstructions based on harmonized historical DMSP-OLS nighttime light observations. Stage I uses radiance-calibrated DMSP-OLS reference data and temporal attention to refine the historical inputs. Stage II reconstructs nighttime lights on a 500 m grid and maps them to a VIIRS-like radiance scale using population, terrain and vegetation information. The 2014–2021 layers are derived from Earth Observation Group (EOG) annual VIIRS Nighttime Lights V2.1, and the 2022–2025 layers are derived from V2.2. The VIIRS-derived layers were preprocessed and aligned to the common AfriNTL grid. Raster specifications Variable: Annual nighttime light radiance, in nW·cm⁻²·sr⁻¹. Format: Single-band, 32-bit floating-point GeoTIFF with lossless DEFLATE compression. Grid: 18,735 columns × 18,427 rows at 500 m × 500 m. All years share the same grid alignment and spatial extent. Coordinate reference system: Africa Albers Equal Area Conic (ESRI:102022). Scale and offset: 1 and 0. Valid stored values can be used directly. Zero and NoData: Zero is a valid stored value and includes background or low radiance suppressed during processing. NoData is encoded as -3.4028234663852886e+38 and marks cells outside the valid data footprint. Retain valid zeros and mask NoData when calculating statistics. GIS previews: Each file includes five internal overview levels generated by average resampling. Use the full-resolution band for quantitative analysis. Quality and supporting files Each annual raster contains 119,532,922 valid pixels, and all 26 years share the same validity mask.
evidence_items.title: AfriNTL: A 500 m annual nighttime light dataset optimized for Africa from 2000 to 2025

evidence_items.summary: Multi-tenant LLM services can reduce serving costs by sharing a full-precision base model and storing compressed fine-tuning updates. Uploaded fine-tuning data can weaken alignment or implant harmful and targeted backdoors, but prior security studies quantize entire checkpoints. We evaluate BitDelta after full-parameter fine-tuning on four open-source models under static attacks, measuring factual utility separately. One-bit delta compression reduces malicious behavior in many tests relative to the full-precision attacked checkpoint. On Llama-2-7b-chat, mean harmfulness Score changes from 3.34 to 1.13 under red teaming and from 2.87 to 1.02 in a harmful-backdoor setting. In a targeted-backdoor setting, triggered ASR falls from 95% to 9%, while untriggered target insertion falls from 54% to 11%. By comparison, full-model GPTQ and int8 leave attack behavior close to the full-precision attacked checkpoint. Across 12 fine-tuning conditions, TriviaQA accuracy decreases by 5.35% on average, with substantial cross-model variation. A preliminary LogitLens analysis links the recovered safety behavior to refusal-token predictions in deeper layers. These findings apply to the tested models and BitDelta configurations; the comparison does not independently separate compression location from compression severity.
evidence_items.title: Delta-Weight Quantization Preserves Alignment in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: This paper investigates the validity of scalar smoothing-error representations in strongly convex Lorentz-cone contact models. An exact three-dimensional counterexample demonstrates that a single scalar multiplier cannot always represent the smoothing error under the examined mathematical formulation. The analysis establishes the failure through unequal spectral multipliers and provides an algebraic mapping to the structured conic equations of Li and Chou (2026). Two spectral generators provide a valid enclosure for separated isotropic cases, while established primal-dual gap certificates offer a conservative general alternative. The computational evaluation includes 240 held-out synthetic problems across five families, six smoothing levels, and paired timing experiments. The study distinguishes exact mathematical counterexamples from numerical implementation effects and preserves unsuccessful and indeterminate results. Neither alternative met the predefined efficiency criterion. The findings concern the specified mathematical model and do not establish physical robot failures. Source code and reproducibility: https://github.com/suneetdungrani2/conebound Complete benchmark archive: https://github.com/suneetdungrani2/conebound/releases/download/v1.0.0/conebound-benchmarks-v1.0.0.zip Supplementary files: Included with this Zenodo record. This manuscript is a research preprint and has not undergone peer review.

evidence_items.summary: Pediatric drug delivery is a significant challenge in pharmaceutical formulation development because children often experience difficulty swallowing conventional dosage forms such as tablets and capsules. Poor palatability and unpleasant taste may further reduce patient compliance and affect the successful administration of medication. Medicated candy represents a promising alternative dosage form that combines acceptable taste, convenience, and ease of administration. The present review focuses on the formulation and evaluation of Piperazine citrate medicated candy as a potential drug delivery system for pediatric patients. Piperazine citrate is an anthelmintic agent used in the treatment of certain intestinal worm infections. Incorporating this drug into a palatable candy formulation may improve acceptability and encourage better medication compliance among children. The formulation involves the selection of suitable excipients, including sweetening agents, flavouring agents, and a suitable candy base, while maintaining drug stability and uniformity. Various evaluation parameters, such as appearance, weight variation, hardness, moisture content, drug content uniformity, in-vitro drug release, taste acceptability, and stability studies, are important for assessing the quality of the developed formulation. Special attention should be given to dose accuracy, pediatric safety, and appropriate packaging to prevent accidental consumption. This review highlights the potential advantages, formulation considerations, evaluation methods, and challenges associated with Piperazine citrate medicated candy. Overall, this dosage form may offer a patient-friendly approach to pediatric anthelmintic therapy; however, its effectiveness, safety, stability, and suitability require systematic investigation and appropriate pharmaceutical evaluation before clinical use.
evidence_items.title: Formulation and Evaluation of Piperazine Citrate Medicated Candy for Pediatric Drug Delivery

evidence_items.summary: When triaging unknown binaries, security analysts must quickly decide which samples to clear as benign, flag as malicious, or escalate for deeper analysis. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support these decisions by interpreting decompiled code, but a binary can contain hundreds or thousands of functions, making exhaustive LLM analysis impractical. We study how current LLMs behave when static triage is formulated as budgeted evidence acquisition: which functions they inspect and how they trade off benign clearance, malware detection, and escalation. To enable a controlled comparison, we implement TRIAGE-CPG, a fixed pipeline over a code property graph (CPG) of a decompiled binary. An LLM-free heuristic selects seed functions, an agent expands the resulting evidence dossier under a fixed budget, and a reporting stage produces a benign, suspicious, or malicious verdict together with a behavioral report. We evaluate eight closed-source and open-weight models on 1,000 Windows PE binaries, using a 600-sample test split and the same zero-shot protocol for every model. We assess the ternary verdicts under both a strict binary reading and triage balanced accuracy (tBA), which credits malware that is flagged or escalated and benign samples only when cleared. After analyzing about 40 of a mean 1,000 functions per binary, the highest-scoring model reaches a strict balanced accuracy of 0.805 and a tBA of 0.855, flagging 65% of malware, escalating another 12%, and clearing 94% of benign samples. The models implement different triage policies: high-specificity models produce small, malware-rich escalation queues, whereas recall-oriented models escalate or flag much more broadly. Both closed-source and open-weight models appear across this spectrum. Our results identify no universal deployment configuration: model choice itself determines the clear/flag/escalate trade-off under limited static evidence.
evidence_items.title: TRIAGE-CPG: A Cross-Model Study of Budgeted Static Malware Triage with Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA)-based embodied agents combine large AI models with physical perception and actuation, creating safety and security risks when unauthorized actions lead to physical hazards. These systems therefore require context-based access control that accounts for runtime conditions while meeting latency constraints. However, existing work has focused primarily on access policies, leaving the system-level implications of alternative access-control designs underexplored. This short paper implements a context-based authorization framework for VLA-based embodied agents and evaluates motion thresholds, session key validity periods, and centralized versus decentralized authorization deployments. Our results quantify how these design choices affect authorization frequency and end-to-end latency and show that decentralized authorization substantially reduces latency and variability.
evidence_items.title: Design Exploration for Context-Based Access Control of Vision-Language-Action Model-Based Embodied Agents

evidence_items.summary: Today, platforms of Model-as-a-Service (MaaS) provides access to various foundation models to users. Users trust that the platform indeed provides the exact service as requested. However, this trust may be misplaced for benign or malicious intentions, where results from providers are not exactly the same as what the user requested. To detect such violations, this paper introduces Espeon, a large language model (LLM) inference verification framework. It enables reproducible deterministic inference through batch-invariant kernels and includes different verification variants for flexible computation and storage budgets of verification. We evaluated Espeon with single-point manipulation cases and Espeon's performance of serving and verification. Espeon can detect such cases, and under the full verification mode it can achieve a speed-up of 4.56X compared to serving time.
evidence_items.title: ESPEON: Verifying the Predestined Execution of Deterministic LLM Inference

evidence_items.summary: The inception of large language models (LLMs) is expected to revolutionize the software security analysis pipeline. However, is it possible to use state-of-the-art LLMs for detecting and reasoning about the attack vector of real-world wireless attacks? In this paper, we propose, design and evaluate AirVScan– a generic workflow to study the current capabilities of LLMs in light of analyzing wireless attacks. AirVScan takes a packet sequence, possibly containing an attack, as input and as an output, it produces the attack vector (e.g., abnormal packet field) with reasoning if the attack is detected. AirVScan differs from works that investigate LLMs to understand the security of source code, as our approach merely takes the packet sequence as an input. We implement the workflow of AirVScan and evaluate it with state-of-the-art LLMs (o3, grok-4, gemini-2. 5-pro) against 40 benign test cases and 128 attack test cases. Among them, 80 attack test cases exploit real-world implementation vulnerabilities in two widely used wireless protocols (Bluetooth and 5G NR). Our evaluation reveals that AirVScan correctly reasons about the root cause of wireless attacks with a rate of 60.7% for Bluetooth but with only 7.7% for 5G NR, highlighting the limitations of current LLMs to reason about attacks on complex protocol implementations. We also evaluated AirVScan to study the effectiveness of LLMs for an unfamiliar protocol that we created by obfuscating Modbus. For such an unfamiliar protocol, AirVScan was mostly ineffective at reasoning about complex, synthesized attacks. However, the inclusion of context improved the attack vector identification to over 82.1%. Finally, we compare AirVScan with AirBugCatcher-a competitive and customized tool for analyzing attack vector of wireless attacks. Our results shed light on the LLMs' current capabilities and required future research for detecting wireless attacks.
evidence_items.title: AirVScan: Are LLMs Capable of Detecting and Reasoning about Wireless Attacks?

evidence_items.summary: Large language models increasingly generate exact operational identifiers such as URLs, UUIDs, and object keys. A single character mutation can invalidate an otherwise correct answer. We identify High-Entropy String Hallucination (HESH), a source-grounded realization failure in which an identifier is absent from the supplied source. Across 5,000 test cases and 12,500 identifier slots, localized HESH increases from 4 slots under Q8_0 to 52 under Q4_K_M and 305 under Q3_K_M. The same aggregate pattern appears on RTX4090 and A100. We then introduce Source-Constrained Identifier Decoding (SCID). It derives valid identifiers from the input and constrains only exact-value spans. In our SCID evaluation, identifier exactness and source membership both reach 100%. Semantic correctness remains 97.9%. The result shows that exact identifier realization can be protected without replacing semantic source selection.
evidence_items.title: High-Entropy String Hallucinations in LLM Inference: Quantization Sensitivity and Source-Constrained Decoding

evidence_items.summary: Almost ten years after the publication of CryptoNets, the field of Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning based on Homomorphic Encryption (HE) has advanced considerably. While the trend moves towards deeper networks and even Large Language Models (LLMs), a thorough understanding of the fundamentals remains essential. Every network relies on matrix-vector multiplications and activation functions, making it crucial to understand the strengths and weaknesses of each implementation. We therefore study these building blocks in detail on small networks, providing insights that can be transferred to larger architectures. To this end, we conduct a performance evaluation of three binary classification neural networks on consumer hardware, demonstrating the impact of selecting the appropriate matrix-vector multiplication algorithm: runtimes differ by up to a factor of three, and memory usage by up to a factor of two. Our results show that high speed and low memory footprint cannot be achieved simultaneously, requiring this trade-off to be weighed carefully. In addition, we propose a novel method for deriving a network's final classification using the binary step function.
evidence_items.title: Classification in the Dark: Performance Insights and Novel Methods for Homomorphic Binary Networks

evidence_items.summary: The Internet hosts billions of publicly accessible services, many of which inadvertently expose sensitive data or allow device manipulation. Historically, understanding the security implications of exposed Internet services required manual analysis or a priori knowledge, neither of which scales to the diversity of devices and services in the wild. In this paper, we show that Large Language Models (LLMs) change this dynamic and can identify security-relevant exposure without predefined rules or fingerprints. After evaluating their efficacy, we leverage LLMs to conduct the first large-scale measurement of HTTP(S)-based exposure and RTSP camera feeds. We use LLMs to build a hierarchical taxonomy of services and develop a multi-stage pipeline that combines lightweight ML classifiers with targeted LLM analysis to identify and triage security-critical exposure. We examine five types of security-critical exposure: directory listings, business applications and dashboards, IoT device interfaces, pages showing stack traces, and camera feeds. Our approach identifies thousands of dangerously exposed services, including healthcare management systems, financial documents, API keys, and private cameras.
evidence_items.title: Exposure is All You Need: Using LLMs to Identify Critical Endpoints at Internet Scale

evidence_items.summary: Large language models can generate programs that compile and pass functional tests, but these outcomes are insufficient for evaluating code in secure multi-party computation (MPC). MPC programs must also follow the target interface's programming constraints, implement the requested algorithm, and satisfy the stated secure-operation efficiency criteria. Using NLMPC, a staged code-generation framework, we conduct an empirical study of 3,600 C++ programs generated by three LLMs for three algorithms under four generation settings that vary API instructions, explicit programming constraints, and iterative repair. We evaluate each program along four dimensions: functional correctness, MPC conformance, algorithmic adherence, and MPC efficiency. Although 59.2% of the generated programs passed the functional correctness tests, only 31.0% satisfied all four criteria. Functional testing alone did not establish conformance, adherence to the requested algorithm, or compliance with the stated efficiency criteria. Adding MPC-specific constraints revealed trade-offs: aggregate functional correctness and MPC conformance increased, while algorithmic adherence decreased. Validation-guided repair had a higher observed overall pass rate than single-pass generation, but this improvement was not statistically significant after correction. Its recorded token use, including LLM-validator calls, was 1.77×-3.19× that of single-pass generation. These findings show that passing functional tests does not establish the overall quality of LLM-generated MPC code, and that additional constraints and repair do not necessarily improve all evaluation dimensions. They motivate separate checks for functional behavior, MPC programming constraints, algorithmic invariants, and source-level efficiency, rather than relying on compilation or functional testing alone.
evidence_items.title: Multidimensional Evaluation of LLM-Generated MPC Programs

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in generative AI (artificial intelligence) have enabled the creation of highly realistic visual content, posing significant challenges to image authenticity verification. Existing detection methods predominantly rely on supervised learning of generator-specific artifacts, potentially limiting their ability to generalize to unseen generation models and image manipulation scenarios. In this work, we propose a training-free framework for AI-generated image detection based on perturbation-induced representation coherence. Instead of measuring the response to a single perturbation, we construct multiple complementary residual-guided perturbation families and analyze the internal coherence of their feature representations extracted by a frozen DINOv3 model. Furthermore, we extend the proposed coherence analysis across network depth by introducing a layer-wise coherence trajectory, capturing the evolution of representation consistency throughout the hierarchical feature space. Extensive experiments on both fully AI-generated images and images locally modified using AI models demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves the highest mean AUROC among the evaluated training-free methods, while remaining competitive with training-based approaches.
evidence_items.title: Training-Free Detection of AI-Generated Images Based on Coherence Analysis of Image Representations

evidence_items.summary: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has democratised content creation while scaling systemic threats in Deepfakes, Deception, and Disinformation (D3). As traditional content detection and watermarking are increasingly bypassed, this paper presents a position and baseline synthesis of Reverse Prompt Engineering (RPE) as a defensive capability. RPE inverts the generative pipeline to infer plausible instruction prompts and support, rather than definitively proving source-model attribution. Grounded in threat telemetry, we synthesise representative RPE frameworks while explicitly delineating the evidentiary limits of prompt recovery, attribution, and content provenance. We further evaluate RPE across public information, legal, and policy/governance viewpoints, analyse key technical limitations such as cross-modal generalisation, and outline a research roadmap to establish RPE as a cornerstone of digital provenance and AI accountability.
evidence_items.title: Reverse Prompt Engineering in Generative AI: A Baseline for Deepfake, Deception and Disinformation Mitigation

evidence_items.summary: We report the Lagrangian-based Koopmans ionization potential (IP)/electron affinity (EA) method, denoted Koopmans-IP/EA, for the gradients and Hessians of singly ionized and electron-attached states starting from a closed-shell restricted Hartree-Fock (RHF) reference. By exploiting Koopmans' theorem, the method avoids spin contamination inherent to unrestricted approaches and provides a description of pure doublet states without the need for an explicit open-shell treatment. Analytic first and second derivatives of the Koopmans-IP/EA Lagrangian with respect to nuclear displacements and external electric fields are derived and implemented in the koala program package, enabling geometry optimizations, harmonic vibrational frequencies, and infrared intensities of doublet states at a computational cost comparable to a ground-state Hartree-Fock Hessian. The method is benchmarked against unrestricted Hartree-Fock, restricted open-shell Hartree-Fock, and equation-of-motion IP coupled cluster singles-doubles (EOM-IP-CCSD) reference data for a set of open-shell systems, including C2H4+, CH2O+, NH3+, NO2, and NO3. Qualitative disagreement with EOM-IP-CCSD is only found for certain cases with pronounced orbital relaxation, e.g., for CH2O+. The computational overhead of the Koopmans-IP/EA Hessian relative to the ground-state RHF Hessian is assessed for a chloro bay-substituted CF3-tetraazaperopyrene-Cl4 anion, yielding an overhead of ∼121%, demonstrating that the method is applicable to systems of realistic size, avoiding spin-contamination.
evidence_items.title: Molecular vibrations of doublet states obtained using Koopmans' theorem.
