evidence_items.summary: Abstract This viewpoint addresses developers and evaluators of large language model (LLM)–based clinical decision support systems. Although recent benchmarks increasingly evaluate multiple clinical reasoning domains, many still rely substantially on reference decision agreement—whether model outputs conform to predefined decisions. Our aim is to clarify when such agreement remains useful, when it becomes insufficient for complex or preference-sensitive decisions, and how it can be complemented by reasoning-centered assessment. Clinical decision-making often depends on structured reasoning under uncertainty, integrating probabilistic evidence, contextual constraints, and patient values. Using oncology as an illustrative domain, we argue that some decision variability is a structural feature of clinical reasoning rather than noise or error. Used alone in such settings, single-reference benchmarks may conflate reasonable divergence with incorrectness and reward answer imitation over transparent reasoning. We conclude that reference decision agreement should be retained for tasks with stable ground truth but supplemented by evidence grounding, reasoning quality, patient-centeredness, and safety checks for open-ended clinical decision support. This multidimensional approach is intended to support safer and more clinically meaningful evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Challenges of Single-Reference Benchmarks for Clinical Reasoning in Large Language Model–Based Decision Support

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are extensively used for many Natural Language Processing tasks such as question answering, natural language inference, document summarization, etc. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting compels LLMs to generate step-by-step reasoning chains. While some of the reasoning chains may follow a correct thought process, they can also suffer from hallucinations, leading to errors in answer generation. Recently, many articles have targeted the problem of verifying these reasoning chains from various aspects. Despite this recent attention, to the best of our knowledge, no comprehensive survey currently summarizes these studies on reasoning chain verification. This work addresses that gap by presenting a detailed overview of the methods for verifying reasoning chains and categorizing them according to their methodology. This paper introduces a novel taxonomy of existing reasoning chain verification methods and mainly divides them into approaches that assess entire chains versus those that examine individual steps. This paper also reviews benchmarks for evaluating reasoning chains and verification methods and further discusses the challenges and future directions associated with these methods. By compiling and analyzing these approaches, our survey aims to advance the understanding and development of robust reasoning techniques in LLMs.
evidence_items.title: Verifying Reasoning Chains Generated by Large Language Models: A Survey

evidence_items.summary: Exact, deterministic preparation of an arbitrary dense n-qubit state is the data-loading step for quantum signal and image processing, and, without ancillae, a generic target needs at least ⌈(2n − n − 1)/2⌉ controlled-NOT (CNOT) gates. We evaluate the two new Quantum Signal-induced Heap Transform (QsiHT) syntheses, Real and Complex, built on the discrete signal-induced heap transform (DsiHT), inside a nine-configuration benchmark drawn from the uniformly controlled rotation, multiplexor, isometry, Schmidt, and Quantum Shannon Decomposition (QSD) families. Qiskit’s StatePreparation is the only method benchmarked as shipped rather than re-implemented. Every configuration reproduces its Haar-random targets to machine precision, with the Real Synthesis confined to sign-bearing targets. Under noise, one coarse tier is stable, set by the executed two-qubit count; the O(2n) frontier stays well below QSD’s O(4n), and no finer order reproduces across two IBM Heron r2 processors at n = 3. Both syntheses reach the 2n − n − 1 multiplexor-family floor. That count matches StatePreparation and, as built, undercuts every other from-scratch construction from n = 3 up. Under a uniform optimization-level-3 pass Plesch–Brukner falls below it at n = 4 and on real targets at n = 6, and as built, it keeps the lowest constant on complex data among the from-scratch methods above that floor. At large registers, the Real Synthesis has the cheapest build-time cost and the Complex Synthesis handles arbitrary targets.
evidence_items.title: A Unified Benchmark for Exact Dense Quantum State Preparation

evidence_items.summary: The physics programs of current and future collider experiments necessitate the development of surrogate simulators for calorimeter showers. While much progress has been made in the development of generative models for this task, they have typically been evaluated in simplified scenarios and for single particles. This is particularly true for the challenging task of highly granular calorimeter simulation. For the first time, this work studies the use of highly granular generative calorimeter surrogates in a realistic simulation application. We introduce DDML (4hep with machine learning), a generic library which enables the combination of generative calorimeter surrogates with realistic detectors implemented using the 4hep toolkit. We compare two different generative models—one operating on a regular grid representation and the other using a less common point cloud approach. In order to disentangle methodological details from model performance, we provide comparisons to idealized simulators which directly sample representations of different resolutions from the full simulation ground truth. We then systematically evaluate model performance on post-reconstruction benchmarks for electromagnetic shower simulation. Beginning with a typical single-particle study, we introduce a first multiparticle benchmark based on diphoton separations, before studying a first full physics benchmark based on hadronic decays of the tau lepton. Our results indicate that models operating on a point cloud can achieve a favorable balance between speed and accuracy for highly granular calorimeter simulation compared to those which operate on a regular grid representation.
evidence_items.title: First full physics benchmark for highly granular calorimeter surrogates

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Visual Foundation Models (VFMs), such as DINO and CLIP, excel in semantic understanding of images but exhibit limited spatial reasoning capabilities, which limits their applicability to embodied systems. As a result, recent work has incorporated some 3D tasks (such as depth estimation) into VFM training. However, VFM performance remains inconsistent across other spatial tasks, raising the question of whether these models truly possess spatial awareness or overfit to specific 3D objectives. To address this question, we introduce the Spatial Relation Recognition Task (SpaRRTa) benchmark, which evaluates the ability of VFMs to identify static directional relations between visible objects. Unlike traditional 3D objectives that focus on precise metric prediction (e.g., surface normal estimation), SpaRRTa probes a fundamental capability underpinning more advanced forms of human-like spatial understanding. SpaRRTa generates an arbitrary number of photorealistic images with diverse scenes and fully controllable object arrangements, along with freely accessible spatial annotations. Evaluating a range of state-of-the-art VFMs, we reveal significant disparities in their ability to encode directional spatial relations. Through our analysis, we provide insights into the mechanisms that support or hinder this form of spatial awareness in modern VFMs. We hope that SpaRRTa will serve as a useful tool for guiding the development of future spatially aware visual models. Our project page can be found at https://sparrta.gmum.net/ .
evidence_items.title: SpaRRTa: A Synthetic Benchmark for Evaluating Spatial Intelligence in Visual Foundation Models

evidence_items.summary: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) silence target genes through RISC-mediated hybridization and cleavage, but can silence unintended transcripts and cause toxicity or complicate regulatory approval. In drug development, empirical assessment by qPCR and RNA-seq is slow, forces early candidate prioritization, and is limited by available species- and genome-appropriate cell models. While extensive empirical screening remains standard practice, there is a significant opportunity for modern AI methods to change this paradigm. We introduce DeepRNAi, a deep learning model that accurately predicts on- and off-target knockdown from siRNA and mRNA sequence. Trained on 16 million siRNA-transcript pairs from 2,031 siRNAs designed to interrogate known siRNA failure modes, and incorporating transcript context from biological foundation models, DeepRNAi is the first in silico method that approaches experimental accuracy. It generalizes across cell models, transcripts, genomes and species, and in a small study distinguishes approved therapeutics from hepatotoxic candidates. The value of DeepRNAi for prioritizing better candidates up front improving likelihood of success later in development is evidenced by a genome-wide survey of 24.4 million siRNAs targeting 7,946 genes, which indicates that 90.1% of the 100 most potent siRNAs have at least some off-target concerns. To support the community, we are publishing a training and benchmark dataset containing 1.84 million siRNA-transcript pairs from 240 siRNAs.
evidence_items.title: DeepRNAi: Predicting on- and off-target siRNA activity and establishing a benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Terraces play a vital role in mitigating runoff and intercepting sediment. Large-scale, high-precision extraction of terraces from remote sensing imagery is essential for environmental monitoring and soil erosion control. However, accurate spatial identification of terraces still presents significant challenges, including scale variability, shadow interference, and complex geometric configurations. To address these issues, we propose DETS-Net, a dual-encoder network that integrates CNN and Transformer architectures. The network employs ResNet-34 as the CNN encoder for local feature detail extraction, utilizes a Transformer encoder to strengthen long-range dependency modeling, and incorporates an adaptive feature fusion (AFF) module for the dynamic integration of the two feature branches. We develop the THDIR dataset, which covers four typical terrain types, namely, plateau mountains, hills, and mountain-basin transition zones, and contains 9,336 standardized 256 × 256 pixel images. We conduct systematic comparisons with eight representative deep learning models. Experimental results demonstrate that DETS-Net achieves an overall accuracy (OA) of 89.91%, a mean intersection over union (MIoU) of 81.28%, and an F1-score of 87.99% on the THDIR dataset, outperforming current mainstream methods in segmentation precision. We apply the optimized model to 2023 remote sensing imagery of Luotian County in the Dabie Mountains, Hubei Province, and generate a high-precision county-level terrace spatial distribution map. This framework supports the assessment of soil and water conservation benefits through area statistics, slope distribution data, and high-precision boundary extraction and provides a reproducible technical pathway for automated terrace mapping using high-resolution remote sensing imagery in complex mountainous regions.
evidence_items.title: A comprehensive benchmark and dual-encoder baseline for terraced field extraction in complex mountainous regions

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Text-to-SQL systems allow users to query databases in natural language, yet existing benchmarks cover English and a small number of well-resourced languages, and no resource has been reported for Kurdish. This paper presents SoraniSQL, a novel dataset and benchmark that is, to the best of current knowledge, the first for Text-to-SQL in Central Kurdish (Sorani). The dataset contains 7,518 question-SQL pairs from 609 query types, systematically constructed over a nine-table retail point-of-sale database with four database instances for test-suite execution accuracy (EXₜₛ); a five-member native-speaker panel rated a stratified sample of 200 questions at 4.9 out of 5 for fluency and 4.9 for adequacy. Dedicated splits separate new values, unseen phrasings, unseen combinations of query components, unseen SQL constructs and spelling variation. Experiments with retrieval, template, compositional, neural and pretrained models, all tuned on development data, show that a template classifier reaches 97.1% EXₜₛ on new values but 0.7% on unseen combinations, where a compositional model reaches 97.7%. A 1.5B-parameter code model fine-tuned with quantised low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) reaches 95.0% on unseen combinations on a laptop central processing unit (CPU), and the structure split and the orthographic-noise sets form the most demanding conditions of the benchmark. A Windows application, DanaText2SQL, demonstrates offline use of the benchmark's best fast model with Microsoft SQL Server.
evidence_items.title: SoraniSQL: A Novel Synthetic Text-to-SQL Dataset and Benchmark for Low-Resource Central Kurdish (Sorani)

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) is based on accumulated precipitation, but there is a difference between the scale of accumulation and the forecast lead time. When a forecast is issued at month t and verified at t+h-1, each post-issue month during the target accumulation period must either be forecast or be provided via a specified alternative. Although the method for constructing the SPI from observed and forecast precipitation is well established in operational practice, its impact on comparisons of lead times across different models has rarely been quantified. We assess three accumulation methods; a full-trajectory forecast, a climatology-gap operational baseline, and a perfect-intermediate-information (PII) diagnostic. This study uses a dataset comprising 10 stations with complete records from Bangladesh, six expanding rolling-origin folds, ten forecasting techniques, SPI values of 3, 6 and 12 months, and lead times of 1, 3, 6, 9 and 12 months. Sensitivity analyses were carried out on a 34-station dataset with variable records and an empirical SPI. For the Gamma SPI-12, the difference between the PII and full-trajectory approaches increased with lead time and reaches +0.760 F1, +0.732 PR-AUC, and +1.873 R2. No method performed best in all criteria and simple baselines of climatology and residual-trees were highly competitive. This shows that the accumulation protocol can qualitatively affect the conclusions about lead-time skill and model performance.
evidence_items.title: Multi-Horizon SPI Drought Forecast Skill under Alternative Accumulation Protocols: A Rolling-Origin Benchmark for Bangladesh

evidence_items.summary: Abstract De novo drug design must balance global drug properties with local structural determinants of target specificity. However, existing methods often reduce both objectives to local geometric optimization, relying on blind, reward-driven perturbations that can disrupt essential scaffolds and compromise overall drug-likeness. To resolve this destructive optimization trap, we propose CadreAI, a semantically decoupled agentic de novo drug design framework. CadreAI explicitly decomposes the entire drug design process into two independent subtasks: target-oriented semantic planning and plan-conditioned molecular generation. This strict separation mitigates potential task interference, allowing each module to focus exclusively on its dedicated objective without mutual disruption. Crucially, the strategic logic of how to formulate these target-oriented plans is driven by Simulation-Guided Insight Consolidation (SGIC). To eliminate trial-and-error guessing, this persistent memory mechanism translates transient numerical docking feedback into reusable textual heuristics, allowing the agent to continuously learn and logically deduce subsequent structural edits. Evaluated on the CrossDocked2020 and DrugGen benchmarks, molecules generated by CadreAI achieve superior docking performance with suitable drug-likeness and synthetic accessibility. Additional Boltz-2 evaluations provide orthogonal computational validation of predicted structural plausibility and binding affinity. These results demonstrate that semantically decoupled reasoning offers a highly controllable and practical route for in silico therapeutic design.
evidence_items.title:
CadreAI: Agentic
AI for Semantically Decoupled Protein–Drug
Design and Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Securing the Internet of Things (IoT) requires detecting and responding to evolving threats across distributed devices with limited computing and communication resources. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret security alerts and help investigate incidents. Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) extends these capabilities by combining reasoning, planning, memory, and tool use to coordinate security actions. Existing studies offer a fragmented account of how these capabilities fit IoT architectures, what risks arise when agents act autonomously, and how to evaluate their performance. This survey addresses these gaps by tracing the transition from LLM-assisted analysis to agentic defence across threat detection, triage, investigation, and response. We develop a unified taxonomy covering IoT infrastructure, LLM-driven and agentic security, trust and resilience, application domains, and evaluation methods. We compare hierarchical, orchestration-based, distributed multi-agent, and cognitive architectures by examining where security decisions are made, how agents coordinate, and where actions are executed across device, edge, fog, and cloud layers. We also examine threats introduced by agentic operation, including prompt injection, memory poisoning, privacy leakage, and compromised trust between agents, together with corresponding defences. Our synthesis finds that limited attack testing and dataset coverage leave uncertainty about how well these systems generalize, while coordination failures and inference overhead constrain deployment. These findings motivate research on trustworthy orchestration, privacy-preserving collaboration, explainable security decisions, and efficient edge inference.
evidence_items.title: From Large Language Models (LLMs) to Agentic AI for IoT Security: A Survey

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Public sector agencies increasingly seek to use artificial intelligence in complex administrative workflows, yet guidance on process architecture for AI integration remains limited. We present an action design research study of an AI-augmented grant evaluation process in a Singapore enterprise development agency. Across three architectural iterations, we moved from an agentic AI approach, through a layered extraction-evaluation pipeline, to a workflow-based design that models grant evaluation as a directed acyclic graph of typed process nodes (data ingestion, AI processing, and deterministic computation) with mandatory human review checkpoints. Across the iterations, we observed improvements in consistency, debuggability, and governance compatibility. In a three-month pilot with 11 officers and 123 cases, 80 of the 103 outputs produced were accepted (77.7%), and five officers self-reported a 21% reduction in processing time per application. Seven months later, a census of the nine remaining officers found reported routine use and the lowest ratings for judgement-adjacent outputs; none of the six officers who answered both surveys lowered any of four repeated ratings, and officers reported adapting their practices in different ways (process co-evolution). We derive three design principles for AI-augmented business processes: (1) decompose complex processes into typed, bounded workflow nodes rather than delegating end-to-end reasoning to AI agents; (2) separate AI-suitable tasks from deterministic computation and human judgment within the process model; and (3) design conservative failure modes that route exceptions to human handlers. We also argue that research on structured language-model agents supports, rather than refutes, explicit process structure.
evidence_items.title: From Agentic AI to Structured Workflows: Designing Process Architectures for AI-Augmented Administrative Decision Support

evidence_items.summary: Journeyman grades how an agent worked, not whether it passed. It drops an agent into eight small simulated jobs — diagnose a crashed service, assay an alloy at a bench, walk a fogged maze, pick up a night shift from a note that lies — and scores the walk on ten axes: did it keep hitting a wall that had already answered, did it stop when the work's object was served or when the budget ran out, could it name what it could not reach and price it, did it repeat a planted false story as fact. Nothing touches real files; every world is simulated and seed-rebuilt, so a claimed exit never reached is caught by arithmetic. What is unusual is not the grading — it is who is allowed to grade. Calibrating an LLM judge before trusting it is standard advice; almost nobody ships the labels to do it with. Three things follow from taking it literally. The calibration set is inside the package: 82 cases across seven axes, labelled by a three-family council in a blind round and an anonymous evidence-quoted second round, distilled from real agent records rather than synthetic vignettes. A judge that has not passed it cannot score — journeyman qualify grants or refuses a badge, and an unqualified run is stamped NOT COMPARABLE. And the judges that failed are published by name, beside the ones that passed. Two scoring layers, and the boundary between them is enforced. Facts are counted programmatically from the record; the questions no counter can answer go to a pluggable judge, one call per rubric item, with the verdict echoed from a fixed label set. Moving a judgement into a deterministic counter to save a call is a standing prohibition, not a preference. The record of being wrong is shipped with it. The first calibration set taught a lesson that the second retracted: under the earlier questions no judge outside one family read one axis at threshold, and that looked like a finding about judging skill. Under the revised definition every judge screened passes it.
evidence_items.title: Journeyman: a process-quality benchmark for LLM agents

evidence_items.summary: Neural surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are trained and ranked on datasets that each vary one design family in one flow domain. Such datasets cannot test the least that an aerodynamic foundation model must do: predict CFD-quality incompressible flow in seconds for new shapes in new enclosures. On DrivAerML, larger models and longer training barely lower Transolver's error; doubling the training cases cuts it by about 12% up to 400 cases, exhausting the dataset. We introduce AeroZoo, a benchmark and training corpus of 3,815 time-mean solutions to the unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) equations with a transition model, across seven geometry families, eight enclosure configurations and Reynolds numbers from $10^3$ to $10^8$. Each sample poses a well-posed PDE problem in the form a solver receives it: the boundary meshes grouped by condition type, the prescribed values and the fluid properties. The 2,816 samples with a stable time mean form the canonical benchmark: two tasks, engineering metrics and 22 frozen splits, disjoint in geometry, that hold out geometry families, enclosures, boundary-condition layouts and Reynolds ranges. On the random split, boundary-condition tokens cut GeoTransolver's median velocity error from 76.9% to 8.4% of the inlet speed in single-seed runs (uniform inlet flow: 11.0%). ISLA, a transformer for boundary-driven PDEs, reaches 5.3% over four seeds, about 4 times the change from a finer mesh. On the same test samples, a held-out geometry family barely changes ISLA's error relative to uniform flow, and a held-out enclosure or boundary-condition layout raises it 2.4 to 9.2 times. The data and the scoring code will be released.
evidence_items.title: AeroZoo: A Benchmark of Well-Posed Flow Problems for Foundation Models of Aerodynamics

evidence_items.summary: Equipping in-service teachers to teach Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) meaningfully demands more than technical instruction: it requires course designs that connect unfamiliar concepts to existing knowledge and classroom practice. This experience report describes the design and retrospective evaluation of professional development courses delivered to 68 in-service teachers across two contexts, grounded in the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (T-PACK) framework and Bloom's Taxonomy. We report on hands-on learning activities in which participants generated, labeled, and evaluated their own training data - for instance by training a classifier on photographs of their own facial expressions or by teaching a browser-based game to recognize their body gestures - and reflect on why this data-centric, embodied approach seems to be effective at building conceptual understandings. A recurring theme is the value of connecting new AI content to subject-area knowledge that students and teachers already hold, particularly from media education. We also identify a gap in available curriculum materials: resources that explain algorithmic bias not merely as an observable problem but in terms of its technical origins in data collection, labeling, and model training remain scarce. Findings are discussed with reference to embodied cognition, body syntonicity, and experiential learning, and recommendations are offered for practitioners designing AI professional development for teaching staff.
evidence_items.title: Game-Based Course Designs for Teaching Machine Learning Concepts to In-Service Teachers

evidence_items.summary: Large language models have made rapid progress in agentic reasoning and tool use, raising expectations for agents that can take over realistic productivity work from humans. However, current agents still struggle to finish such tasks, where success requires following long-horizon professional workflows, understanding heterogeneous file contexts, and producing usable deliverables under fine-grained requirements. A key bottleneck is the lack of scalable post-training data that reflects real work intent, authentic file environments, and deliverable-level evaluation. To close this gap, we introduce Agent-R^2, a real-source data synthesis framework that scales training data for realistic productivity work. Instead of relying on manually specified workflows or LLM-generated files, Agent-R^2 grounds synthesis throughout the pipeline in real occupational seeds, corpus-derived workflow evidence, and authentic web-sourced files. From 10k web-corpus candidates, Agent-R^2 distills 4k task instances that pair real multi-format attachments with fine-grained, deliverable-level rubrics. On this data, we train Agent-R^2-4B via supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement learning, improving both end-to-end productivity performance and file-grounded reasoning. Trained on only 4k instances, Agent-R^2-4B surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 on both GDPval (51.0% vs. 48.0%) and OfficeQA (14.8% vs. 13.8%). Further analysis shows that Agent-R^2 mitigates shortcut behavior, where agents produce superficially plausible deliverables before sufficiently grounding, constructing, or verifying them, while promoting sustained exploration.
evidence_items.title: Agent-R^2: Scaling Agents for Realistic Productivity Work via Real-Source Data Synthesis

evidence_items.summary: This dataset accompanies the revised manuscript “SCALE: A Systematic Review and Conceptual Framework of Scalability, Cost, AI-Driven Automation, Latency, and Security in Cloud-Based Big Data Pipelines”. It documents a systematic review of English-language, peer-reviewed studies published in 2022–2025 on AI-related cloud, edge and fog pipelines under the stated eligibility and venue criteria.   The corpus contains 291 studies: 28 retained from the submitted version, 31 from the revision database search, 97 from previously unassessed discovery-export records, and 135 from citation searching. The full-text flow comprises 810 reports sought, 371 assessed (291 included and 80 excluded), and 439 not retrieved. The package supplies the protocol and dated amendments, identification and screening records, retrieval decisions, extraction and appraisal records, source-linked coding and quantitative-claim checks, codebooks and mappings, the complete included-study bibliography, synthesis and sensitivity data, author-attested verification records and provenance, and scripts for regenerating the frozen results.   The final audit on 14 November 2026 reviewed 195 remaining title-only exclusions, reopened 17 records and retrieved three of them; three previously unretrieved VLDB studies were also recovered and included. Initial ratings are preserved. These six assessments and the earlier 13-November addition are outside the frozen author-attested verification sample. The final package’s 56 selected generated outputs reproduced byte for byte in an isolated copy.   The package records the actual discovery and AI-assisted revision procedures alongside the authors’ reported reading, methodological discussion and sample verification. It distinguishes original study findings from review-level interpretation and includes a post-hoc retrieved-versus-unretrieved comparison.
evidence_items.title: SCALE systematic review (2022–2025): study data, screening records and reproducibility materials

Biophysical Scope & Mathematical Formulation Extending the conditional boundary-value and non-equilibrium energetic mismatch framework established in Baird (2026a, BioSystems), Baird (2026b, J. Alzheimer’s Dis.), and Baird (2026c, Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys.), we formulate an 11-state cortical sensory-gating Pyramidal–PV+ pyramidal-interneuron network gamma (PING) microcircuit across T ∈ [310.15, 313.55] K (37.0 °C–40.4 °C). evidence_items.summary: Pre-trained encoders fine-tuned on natural language inference (NLI) and other language understanding tasks keep much of their accuracy after the input is perturbed, e.g. by removing all nouns or shuffling the words. Does the same hold for large language models (LLMs), and if so, is it because they have seen the benchmarks during pre-training? In this paper we revisit these perturbation experiments with eight LLMs alongside fine-tuned encoders on GLUE and the three rounds of ANLI. Regardless of model size, every system that answers directly retains 36-72% of its above-chance performance without nouns on MNLI compared to only 14-29% on ANLI. Only a model that reasons before answering departs from this pattern. We also check contamination indicators (including exact $n$-gram counts in the public pre-training data of two of the models) and find no link between exposure and robustness. Our strongest evidence comes from 368 new, human-validated items that none of the models can have seen. All eight LLMs keep more of their performance without nouns on items written in MNLI's style than on items written without its cues. When the perturbation instead removes the function words carrying such cues, this advantage reverses. In light of these results, we argue that robustness to perturbation on familiar NLI benchmarks reflects dataset shortcuts rather than memorisation, and tells us more about the benchmark than about the model.
evidence_items.title: Shortcuts or Memorisation? Revisiting Data Corruption in Natural Language Understanding with Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: The reduced availability of medical datasets represents an important challenge in the development of predictive models for remote healthcare solutions, especially when the available data are imbalanced or difficult to extend through traditional methods. Small Language Models (SLMs) have become a promising alternative to Large Language Models (LLMs) for addressing these limitations due to their lower computational requirements and adaptability to specialized tasks. However, their performance remains highly dependent on the quality and representativeness of the available training data. In this paper, we propose a method for clinical data augmentation based on a fine-tuned Microsoft Phi-2 model that is used to generate synthetic instances, with the purpose of improving deep learning-based model for predicting remotely monitored vital signs. The Phi-2 model was adapted to the medical domain through supervised fine-tuning on the MedQuad dataset, through a Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA)-based method and by applying few-shot prompting techniques. The resulting model was used afterwards in the augmentation of a small-sized dataset, composed of vital sign values and labels associated with pathological and physiological states. The experimental results demonstrate that fine-tuned SLMs improved the performance on medical domain, achieving higher scores for both lexical (ROUGE) and semantic (BERTScore) evaluation metrics compared to the pretrained model. Moreover, the fine-tuned SLM is effective for generating structured synthetic clinical data. When used for data augmentation, the generated dataset improved the performance of a LSTM predictive model, increasing the classification accuracy from 89.0% to 93.7% and showing consistent improvements in precision, recall, and F1-score.
evidence_items.title: Fine-Tuned Small Language Model for Synthetic Clinical Data Generation and Predictive Healthcare Analytics

evidence_items.summary: A multilingual speech recogniser has heard much speech in its own languages. We ask how much of that it brings to a language it was never trained on, when it is fine-tuned on the little that language has. We score 28 open multilingual models untouched on Low-Language-TTS, 50 low-resource languages in 11 writing systems, and fine-tune 24 of them on at most 1,000 clips a language, 82 hours in all, with a dev set choosing every epoch. Fine-tuning lowers every model's macro character error rate (CER), by 16.6 to 53.1 points, to 9.5 at best, and a word language model takes three CTC models 1.2 to 1.4 points lower; WER is still 34.4 at best. On the 12 languages that no model lists, every model starts at 46 or worse and the best ends at 11.7. The same architectures from random weights stay 60 points or more behind, so the gain is transfer, and an encoder left untouched already gives a Whisper or Qwen decoder most of what it needs. It is the language, not the corpus: on FLEURS recordings that ours do not share, the median model keeps 79% of its gain. It costs the languages the models knew, 5.7 points of CER on English, Spanish, French and German in the median model. Low-rank adapters on 4% of the weights come within 1.1 points of tuning everything, and on 2 of 3 models forget less. Seq2seq and language-model decoders are done within three to five epochs, while a new CTC head is still improving at twenty or thirty. Data beats epochs: 25 clips a language take Qwen3-ASR 0.6B from 60.9 to 39.3, and at equal clips presented, ten times the data is worth 9.7 points. A model that first learned forty of the languages learns the other ten no faster. On a public Malay benchmark, untouched Whisper large-v3 scores 8.9 when it detects the language and 14.9 when told the clip is Malay, because it then translates the English that speakers mix in; trained on the Scicom telephony dataset it scores 6.0.
evidence_items.title: Low Language Transfer Speech-to-Text

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous greenhouse management increasingly requires robotic systems that integrate perception, navigation, environmental regulation, and plant-level intervention. This paper presents AgriSense, a framework combining an Isaac Sim virtual greenhouse, a quadruped mobile manipulator, RGB and LiDAR-inertial sensing, environmental control, and supervised vision-language decision support. Frozen DINOv2 and BERT encoders, together with structured environmental inputs, support joint prediction of twelve environmental references, a target zone, and an intervention flag. Checkpoint replay reproduces 41/43 zone decisions. Across five seeds on a source-grouped test set, the full, image-removed, and language-removed configurations each achieve 43/44 correct zone decisions, providing no evidence of incremental multimodal zone-accuracy improvement. The full model achieves mean absolute errors of 0.249 degrees C for temperature, 2.030 percentage points for humidity, and 0.997 percentage points for soil moisture. Sensor-only inputs match full-model zone accuracy, while language-only inputs achieve 68.64%. External real-image benchmarks reveal distribution-shift limitations. Five offline Point-LIO routes yield rigidly aligned trajectory errors of 5.22-17.32 mm. Of 40 virtual-arm targets, 32 satisfy geometric acceptance criteria and eight are rejected at boundaries. Six long-horizon climate cases and fault protocols characterize integration limits. Navigation and integrated treatment rely on simulator-state inputs; physical greenhouse performance and agronomic treatment efficacy remain unvalidated. The contribution is an evaluated decision-support and robotic-intervention framework for a virtual greenhouse.
evidence_items.title: AgriSense: Vision-Language Decision Support and Robotic Intervention in a Virtual Greenhouse Copy title

evidence_items.summary: Millions of Bangla Sign Language (BdSL) users lack reliable automatic translation tools. Existing systems are limited by data scarcity, unidirectional design, and computationally expensive architectures that are not suitable for low-resource deployment. We introduce IsharaBART, a bidirectional generative framework for gloss-sentence translation in BdSL. IsharaBART uses Bidirectional and Auto-Regressive Transformers (BART)-based conditional language modeling with denoising learning objectives. We developed a parallel dataset of 1,000 professionally annotated gloss-sentence pairs, balanced across tenses and structures. We expanded the dataset to 4,831 pairs through four augmentation techniques: rule-based tense transformations, masked token substitutions, back-translation, and one-shot prompting. A compact denoising sequence-to-sequence model was pre-trained from scratch on monolingual Bangla text from six different corpora, then fine-tuned on the annotated and augmented datasets. We compare IsharaBART against four larger baseline models under identical conditions, where it achieves comparable or superior bidirectional performance. On the gloss-to-sentence (G2S) task, it attains Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU-4) score up to 51.7, and on the sentence-to-gloss (S2G) task, it achieves 61.40, outperforming multilingual models despite having fewer than 10% of the parameters. Ablation studies demonstrate that pre-training provides 62.5-90.4% faster convergence and 11.5-118% higher BLEU-4 than scratch. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces trainable parameters by 99.3%, but with 28.0-52.2% loss of BLEU-4 compared to full-parameter fine-tuning.
evidence_items.title: IsharaBART: An efficient BART-Based Framework for Low-Resource Bangla Sign Language Translation

evidence_items.summary: Universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are increasingly used as computationally efficient surrogates for density functional theory (DFT) in high-throughput nanomaterials screening. Systematic softening has been reported for several universal MLIPs when high-energy and far-from-equilibrium configurations are underrepresented in training data. We examine how this behavior appears at under-coordinated edge sites in graphene quantum dots (GQDs), where a vacancy can have pronounced molecular-radical character. Using coronene (C$_{24}$H$_{12}$), a hexagonal GQD with $D_{6h}$ symmetry and three carbon classes, we benchmark SevenNet (7net-omni-i12) against spin-polarized PBE DFT (GPAW) for monovacancy, divacancy, and Stone-Wales defects. Beyond the full site- and bond-resolved landscapes, we perform a controlled matched-reconstruction comparison in which 28 vacancy and divacancy configurations are scored by both engines using self-consistent chemical-potential reservoirs. In this dataset, SevenNet underestimates all 28 vacancy and divacancy formation energies, and the mean deficit increases with under-coordination within each defect family: 0.30-0.74 eV for monovacancies and 0.65-1.11 eV for divacancies as the number of broken edge C-H bonds increases. By contrast, the mean Stone-Wales energies differ by only 0.013 eV. SevenNet also preserves the ordering of three hydrogen-dependent reconstruction basins and reproduces $D_{6h}$-equivalent sites to within a few meV. The within-class symmetry spread therefore provides a practical diagnostic of basin-sensitive relaxations. Within the present coronene benchmark, these results support MLIP-based structure screening and preliminary ranking, while absolute vacancy energies and multi-basin edge configurations still require DFT validation.
evidence_items.title: Edge-scaling softening of a universal machine-learned potential: point-defect formation energies in a coronene graphene quantum dot

evidence_items.summary: Abstract. Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success and demonstrated superior performance across various tasks, including natural language processing (NLP), weather forecasting, biological protein folding, text generation, and solving mathematical problems. However, many real-world data exhibit highly non-Euclidean latent hierarchical anatomy, such as protein networks, transportation networks, financial networks, brain networks, and linguistic structures or syntactic trees in natural languages. Effectively learning intrinsic semantic entailment and hierarchical relationships from these raw, unstructured input data using LLMs remains an underexplored area. Due to its effectiveness in modeling tree-like hierarchical structures, hyperbolic geometry—a non-Euclidean space—has rapidly gained popularity as an expressive latent representation space for complex data modeling across domains such as graphs, images, languages, and multimodal data. Here, we provide a comprehensive and contextual exposition of recent advancements in LLMs that leverage hyperbolic geometry as a representation space to enhance semantic representation learning and multiscale reasoning. Specifically, the paper presents a taxonomy of the principal techniques of hyperbolic LLMs (HypLLMs) in terms of four main categories: (1) hyperbolic LLMs through exp/log maps; (2) hyperbolic fine-tuned models; (3) fully hyperbolic LLMs; and (4) hyperbolic state-space models. We also explore crucial potential applications and outline future research directions. A repository of key papers, models, datasets, and code implementations is available at https://github.com/sarangp2402/Hyperbolic-LLM-Models .
evidence_items.title: Hyperbolic Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: It is common to train Large Language Models (LLMs) for agentic tasks with Reinforcement Learning (RL) from scalar rewards. However, this throws away the fine-grained information about the environment that the agent experienced during the trial (e.g., error logs). To utilize this rich information, recent works wrap the agent in a harness that refines its own inputs through reflection or compaction and hands past experience to future rollouts, but the construction of the handed-off artifacts (e.g., a playbook) is itself not learned. We want the best of both worlds: gradient updates from a scalar reward, while also utilizing environment information to hand off experience. As a concrete testbed, we fix the Agentic Context Engineering () harness and train one model to act, reflect, and curate task-local playbooks. Our method, , evaluates candidate experience-handoff artifacts by their downstream effect on future actor rollouts, and co-optimizes the role-specific behaviors (action generator, insight reflector, and playbook curator) under a fixed scaffold. Across agentic benchmarks,  achieves higher held-out performance than baseline methods. The results suggest that agent training should optimize not only the actions in the current rollout, but also the model-written experience that future rollouts inherit.
evidence_items.title: Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning for Recursive Self-Improvement

evidence_items.summary: While search agents demonstrate impressive capabilities in multi-step question answering, their robustness to poor-quality evidence remains under-explored. Such evidence is rare in benchmark corpora, and resulting failures are hard to reproduce. We propose DeepStress, a dynamic stress-testing framework that subjects agents to degraded evidence at controlled rates. It replaces the retrieval module with a synthetic environment where documents are generated dynamically for each query, under independent control of their trustworthiness, relevance, and factuality. To characterize behavior under stress, we go beyond binary accuracy with a five-way classification of final-answer outcomes and two new reliability-aware metrics, RAS and CoPRAS, which credit cautious behavior and account for computational cost. Evaluating 12 systems on questions from HotpotQA and BrowseComp-Plus, we find that several open-weight agents answer confidently when sources contain obvious credibility red flags, and that many HotpotQA questions are answered from parametric knowledge even when all returned documents are factually wrong.
evidence_items.title: DeepStress: Stress-Testing Deep Search Agents

evidence_items.summary: Video generation models produce visually realistic videos but still struggle with physical dynamics and causal consistency. Learning from generated videos requires fine-grained physical supervision, yet reliable quality judgments, correction pairs, and controlled variations are difficult to obtain. Large language models (LLMs) possess physical knowledge, but struggle to reliably guide video generation models in producing their training videos. We present PhysLoop, a unified harness designed to support physically grounded self-improvement in video generation models. The harness guides and constrains LLMs throughout video generation, selection, and correction, distilling their physical knowledge into physically consistent videos. The framework supports controllable training-data construction and inference-time video repair. By identifying and correcting failures, PhysLoop marks a key milestone toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video generation models with limited human intervention. We release 100K videos spanning diverse, realistic indoor and outdoor scenes, along with generation tools and two evaluation datasets: PhysLoop-Gen and PhysLoop-Repair. We evaluate controllable generation and localized repair on these datasets, respectively, and assess physical behavior on the external Physics-IQ Verified benchmark.
evidence_items.title: PhysLoop: Harnessing LLMs' Physics Awareness for Self-Improving Video Generation Models

evidence_items.summary: Self-evolving agents improve their own skills, memory, and harness code from experience without retraining the base LLM, and group-evolving agents go further by sharing these lessons across agents. Yet most such systems overlook that sharing across users and heterogeneous agents requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private. We present MixUA, a memory system that distills independent user-agent trajectories into lessons and assigns each lesson to a user-agent pair, user, agent, or global scope according to whom it benefits and what it may disclose. For evaluation, we introduce CrossLearnBench, a mixed-user-agent benchmark that pairs established agent tasks with user preferences and privacy probes that test whether private facts leak into memory other users can read. With five users and seven agents, MixUA raises pass rates by up to 16 points over no memory and 5 over a single global memory, even on tasks previously tried only by other users on other agents. It retains up to 90% of previously stated preferences, and at most 0.02% of privacy probes find a planted private fact in a forbidden scope. We hope MixUA offers a scalable path toward a global system where users and agents co-evolve.
evidence_items.title: Who Remembers What? Multi-Granularity Memory Extraction for Multi-User, Multi-Agent Interaction

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate computational fluid dynamics, yet progress is limited by the lack of benchmarks capturing realistic, time-dependent turbulent flows. We introduce TurtLES, a 14 TB dataset of 3D turbulent cylinder wakes in the shear-layer transition regime, computed via high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulations. The dataset contains 400 trajectories of 400 time steps each, with 3-11 million points per frame, spanning variations in geometry, Reynolds number, and angle of attack. Unlike existing datasets, TurtLES combines (i) physically realistic turbulence with an active energy cascade driven by vortex stretching, (ii) dense irregular meshes, and (iii) long-horizon temporal dynamics. We benchmark state-of-the-art neural operators on autoregressive rollouts and identify key failure modes, including temporal instability, loss of small-scale energy, and challenges in learning on large irregular domains. TurtLES provides a new benchmark for evaluating surrogate models on 3D turbulent wakes at industrially relevant mesh resolution.
evidence_items.title: TurtLES: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Turbulent 3D Neural PDE Surrogates

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language model (LLM)-based chatbots are increasingly used for medical information, but their suitability for pheochromocytoma education remains uncertain. We compared four contemporary LLMs for knowledge accuracy, information quality, transparency, and readability. Methods ChatGPT (ChatGPT-5.6 Sol), DeepSeek (DeepSeek-V4 Flash), Gemini (Gemini-3.6 Flash), and Grok (Grok-4.5 Fast) answered 200 pheochromocytoma-related multiple-choice questions across three independent trials. Google Trends and clinician input were used to develop 15 patient-centered questions. Responses were evaluated using DISCERN, EQIP, GQS, JAMA benchmark criteria, and six readability indices. Results Overall knowledge accuracy differed among the four models ( p = 0.0012), with mean accuracy rates of 93.00% for ChatGPT, 91.17% for DeepSeek, 90.50% for Gemini, and 81.67% for Grok. However, after adjustment for multiple comparisons, statistically significant pairwise differences were limited to ChatGPT versus Grok for overall accuracy (adjusted p = 0.0129) and clinical-presentation questions (adjusted p = 0.0088). No significant differences were identified among ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Gemini. Exploratory assessments of 15 patient-oriented questions suggested differences in information quality, transparency, and readability across models. ChatGPT showed comparatively favorable information quality scores, whereas DeepSeek exhibited a more favorable descriptive readability profile. Nevertheless, transparency was limited across all models, and none achieved the recommended sixth-grade readability standard. Conclusion The evaluated LLM-based chatbots demonstrated generally favorable performance on structured pheochromocytoma-related knowledge questions, although statistically significant pairwise differences in accuracy were limited.
evidence_items.title: Comparative evaluation of large language model chatbots for pheochromocytoma education: accuracy, information quality, transparency, and readability

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly support open-ended visual reasoning, yet their behavior in low-resource languages and sustainability-oriented domains remains underexplored. We introduce a controlled English–Bangla plastic-waste VQA benchmark comprising 402 image records derived from 136 base images and 2,412 question–answer pairs across five waste categories and three task types: recognition, visual description, and environmental reasoning. We evaluate GPT-4.1 mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-4B zero-shot using task-specific answer-quality metrics, bilingual consistency, and image ablation. Gemini 2.5 Flash yields the highest recognition point estimate, with 93.5% accuracy and 91.3% macro-F1. Across models, English normalized performance exceeds Bangla by 3.78 points on average, with the largest observed gap for environmental reasoning. Removing the image reduces normalized performance by 66.29 points for recognition, 52.89 for description, and 11.42 for environmental reasoning. The smaller environmental-reasoning ablation gap indicates that, in this benchmark, many environmental questions remain partly answerable from linguistic and domain priors. These results show why answer quality alone is insufficient for multilingual multimodal evaluation and motivate reporting cross-lingual consistency and sensitivity to visual evidence alongside conventional metrics.
evidence_items.title: VisText-VLM2Plastic: A Bilingual Benchmark for Visual Grounding and Environmental Reasoning in Vision-Language Models

organizations: Ph.D., Assistant Professor, Department of Finance and Banking, Gerede Faculty of Applied Sciences, Bolu Abant Izzet Baysal University, Turkey

evidence_items.summary: Type of the article: Research ArticleAbstractManaging customer retention across retail credit-card portfolios remains imperative for containing revenue attrition and safeguarding banking profitability. This empirical study benchmarks five supervised classification architectures to identify observed credit-card customer attrition and investigates the internal attribution mechanisms of the top-performing model using explainable artificial intelligence. Utilizing the BankChurners benchmark comprising 10,127 records across 37 encoded inputs under an unresampled 75:25 stratified split alongside training-only repeated five-fold cross-validation, we evaluated model discriminatory efficacy across threshold-dependent and ranking-based metrics. Gradient Boosting demonstrated the strongest empirical performance on the held-out test split (accuracy = 0.960; weighted F1 = 0.959; ROC–AUC = 0.986; average precision = 0.949), detecting 332 of the 407 observed churners (recall = 0.816; precision = 0.925; F1 = 0.867) alongside 75 false negatives and 27 false alarms, whilst Random Forest yielded comparable ranking capacity (ROC–AUC = 0.984; average precision = 0.934) but lower minority-class sensitivity. Across fifteen repeated training folds, Gradient Boosting achieved mean ROC–AUC of 0.989 (SD = 0.002) and an attrition-specific F1-score of 0.886 (SD = 0.009), while SHAP and ELI5 global attributions on held-out records consistently pinpointed total transaction amount, transaction frequency, and revolving balance as the most decisive predictive drivers. These insights indicate that diagnostic customer reviews can be substantively enhanced by monitoring longitudinal utilization patterns, though retrospective associations must not be equated with prospective warning or intervention efficacy.
evidence_items.title: Classifying credit card customer attrition using explainable artificial intelligence

organizations: Laboratoire Adhésion et Inflammation, Aix-Marseille University UM61, INSERM U1067, CNRS U733, Parc Scientifique de Luminy, 13009 Marseille, France
evidence_items.summary: There is a strong feeling that artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping most human activities, and this is supported by impressive proof-of-concept reports that were published during the last decade. Furthermore, medicine is a prominent candidate for AI development, due to the overload on medical practitioners, and specific features of medical practice including the existence of general guidelines and diagnostic algorithms, development of evidence-based medicine and use of an accurate vocabulary making it highly suited for processing by artificial intelligence models. Thus, the current challenge is not to determine whether the introduction of AI in medicine is beneficial or even acceptable, but to organize this inevitable evolution to optimize benefit and prevent pitfalls. The aim of this paper is to discuss the main challenges that must be met to optimize AI support to medical practice. It is suggested that (i) specific procedures are needed to ensure the reliability, comprehensiveness and availability of medical datasets, (ii) there is a need for specific benchmarks and guidelines to validate AI use with a reliability comparable to that ensured by procedures currently used in medicine and (iii) the selection of an AI model to perform a given task must be examined to achieve an optimal balance between efficiency, feasibility and cost.
evidence_items.title: How Can Artificial Intelligence Alleviate Physician Overload: A Current Issue

evidence_items.summary: Hyperspectral image analysis increasingly depends on large, densely annotated benchmark datasets. A review of widely used benchmarks reveals persistent gaps: an almost complete absence of multi-temporal acquisitions, predominantly controlled acquisition conditions, and sparse semantic annotation. We present a methodological framework that addresses these gaps and lays the foundation for a multi-temporal hyperspectral benchmark. Specifically, we describe (a) data acquisition through two UAV-based hyperspectral surveys over an industrial earthworks site in Germany using a HySpex Mjolnir VS-620 sensor, complemented by in-situ ASD FieldSpec reference spectra and photogrammetric products; (b) a multi-stage processing pipeline that transforms raw push-broom data into georeferenced surface-reflectance mosaics (∼5 cm ground sampling distance, ∼5.5 million pixels, 487 bands); and (c) two complementary strategies for dense semantic annotation: an interactive, prompt-driven image-based annotation tool built on the Segment Anything Model 3 and a spectral-similarity approach based on the Spectral Angle Mapper. Within a human-in-the-loop workflow, the two strategies appear complementary, providing spatial delineation and spectrally consistent labelling across disconnected regions, respectively, and show potential for accelerating dense annotation while supporting semantic consistency.
evidence_items.title: Towards a multi-temporal hyperspectral benchmark: UAV-based acquisition, processing, and semantic annotation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We present a systematic benchmark of MACE interatomic potentials for iron–nickel alloys, focusing on structural, elastic, and finite-temperature properties of chemically disordered body-centered-cubic (bcc) and face-centered-cubic (fcc) phases. The reference dataset comprises spin-polarized PBE density-functional-theory (DFT) calculations for special quasirandom structures (SQS) span-&#xD;ning composition, volume, and shear deformation. A system-specific MACE–sqs model trained on this dataset achieves validation errors of 2.0 meV/atom for energies and 24.3 meV/Å for forces. We compare MACE–sqs with several MACE foundation models, including models trained using Hubbard corrections, through equations of state, equilibrium volumes, cubic elastic properties, and&#xD;thermal lattice expansion. MACE–sqs gives the most consistent overall performance for several zero-temperature structural and elastic benchmarks, although its relative performance depends on property and composition and it does not reproduce all experimental elastic trends. In the finite-temperature comparison, no single model is uniformly superior, and MACE–matpes agrees more closely with experiment for some compositions and comparison metrics.&#xD;Finite-temperature calculations yield reasonable thermal-expansion coefficients near 300 K, while deviations at elevated temperatures and for magnetovolume sensitive compositions highlight the limitation of representing magnetic effects only implicitly through the spin-polarized reference data. These results define the tested application domain in which targeted SQS-based training improves&#xD;upon broad foundation models and identify explicit magnetic degrees of freedom and broader configurational sampling as priorities for future development.
evidence_items.title: Capabilities and limitations of MACE interatomic potentials for Fe-Ni alloys: a systematic benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Interpersonal head-motion synchrony may differ in interactions involving adults with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), but its value for held-out dyadic classification remains uncertain. We reanalyzed 36 structured conversations involving 72 unique participants: 18 typically developing (TD) speaker-TD listener dyads (TD-TD) and 18 TD speaker-ASD listener dyads (TD-ASD). Four established phase-difference descriptors were extracted from 100 Hz forehead accelerometry. H1 predicted lower synchrony density and higher phase-difference standard deviation (SD) in TD-ASD dyads; Hedges g values were −1.20 and 1.01, respectively. For H2, seven classifier families evaluated with fixed and nested-cross-validation-tuned configurations showed no consistent nonlinear advantage (median fold-averaged AUCs, 0.731–0.815); equivalence between families was not established. For H3, density plus SD and density alone yielded leave-one-dyad-out AUCs of 0.793 and 0.790, vs. 0.765 for all four descriptors; these results do not demonstrate superiority, equivalence, or noninferiority. Synchrony events per speaker peak were less frequent in TD-ASD dyads (0.257 vs. 0.421), while chance-corrected coupling differences remained uncertain. These exploratory findings provide an interpretable, internally validated benchmark for prospective studies of dyadic behavioral decision support, not individual ASD diagnosis.
evidence_items.title: Autism Classification in Dyadic Interaction: An Interpretable Machine-Learning Benchmark Using Phase-Difference Motion Synchrony

evidence_items.summary: A response to a question regarding uploaded PDFs is only useful if supporting text can be found and examined. This paper presents the Agentic RAG Document Intelligence Assistant, where a Python controller evaluates retrieval results to either select more search, query rewriting, generation or abstention. The budget consists of three searches, with the eligibility evidence lasting for a given number of attempts. You extract the pages from PyMuPDF each at a time, then split yours recursively on 300 chars with a target overlap of 60 chars. The latter chunk are stored as local SentenceTransformer embeddings which, along with the text and metadata, is persistent in Chroma storage (384d vectors). Query rewriting + answer generation leverages openai/gpt-oss-120b via a compatible API. A cosine-similarity boundary of 0.45 (strong) and 0.15 (weak) can differentiate usable, weak and unusable matches but they need calendarisation to make them more suited for different datasets. To reduce unsupported responses, evidence admission, possible limited number of retries and generation constrained in context. Source identifiers link claims to filenames, and physical PDF pages. These choices are compared with adaptive retrieval, handling of corrective evidence, rewriting, document retrieval and citation assessment in a review of ten 2024-2026 studies. This contribution is not particularly an invention of an algorithm but rather a reproducible integration specification and evaluation protocol. Matched baselines, ablations, threshold analysis, citation checks and latency measurements are planned; no unmeasured outcome is reported as a result.
evidence_items.title: Agentic RAG Document Intelligence Assistant

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for database tasks, yet most work, such as Text2SQL, assumes that the relational schema already exists. We ask whether LLMs can design a schema from natural language requirements (Text2Schema), verbalize an existing schema (Schema2Text), and preserve its structure through a Schema-to-Text-to-Schema round trip. We present SchemaBridge, a benchmark of 902 schemata from three collections, stratified by size and constraint complexity, that scores fidelity separately for tables, attributes, domain (data types and nullability), entity, and referential integrity. Evaluating six open-weight and proprietary LLMs, we find that: (i) human-written requirements under-specify schemata, with no model exceeding 0.27 referential integrity F1; (ii) LLM-generated descriptions carry far more structure when explicitly asked to be complete, raising GPT-5.4-mini's referential F1 on SchemaBench from 0.228 to 0.909, even as BLEU, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore decrease; (iii) controlled experiments show that both constructor and describer choices influence round-trip fidelity under fixed settings; and (iv) masked schema experiments show that structural cues support recovery of keys and relationships, while joint data-type and nullability information is poorly retained through verbalization. Code and data are available at https://github.com/iamsriom/SchemaBridge
evidence_items.title: [Experiment, Analysis, and Benchmark] How well do LLMs comprehend and design relational database schemata?

evidence_items.summary: This paper investigates whether Large Language Models can answer a personality questionnaire as a specific individual would. Given a user's social-media posts, the model completes the BFI-2-60 Big Five questionnaire as that user. The predicted responses are converted into trait scores and compared with the user's actual scores. We evaluate GPT-4, Gemma, Llama 3.1, and Mistral on the MyPersonality dataset. To determine whether predictions reflect information from the user's writing, we compare them with answers produced without user text and with values derived from general population tendencies. We measure prediction error across all users and separately for individuals with low, intermediate, and high trait scores. We also test whether an LLM can express an explicit personality profile when given only the target Big Five scores, without user text, and examine how predictions change as more text is provided. The results show that user text does not consistently improve performance. Models perform better near the middle of the trait distribution, while at the lower and upper ends they often remain close to central values or perform well at one end but poorly at the other. When given an explicit profile, GPT-4 most clearly translates trait information into consistent questionnaire responses, particularly for Extraversion and Neuroticism. Increasing context does not systematically reduce error: open-source models fluctuate more, whereas GPT-4 remains comparatively stable. Overall, the evaluated models do not consistently reproduce the questionnaire behavior of specific individuals.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models as Digital Twins: a Distribution-Aware Questionnaire-Based Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Patient-generated drug reviews offer a large source of real-world evidence on perceived medication effectiveness, yet existing computational analyses predominantly model effectiveness as a single drug-level estimate, ignoring variation across therapeutic indications. This study introduces an integrated four-module natural language processing (NLP) framework that extends patient review analytics from aggregate rating prediction toward condition-aware pharmacovigilance support. Module 1 decomposes drug effectiveness across 1880 drug-condition pairs (623 drugs; 131 conditions), showing that the same medication can differ by up to 4.18 rating points across indications (mean cross-condition range = 0.98 rating points on a 1-10 scale among the 533 drugs observed in at least two conditions). A condition-aware model combining term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) features with linear support vector regression (SVR) achieves a coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.749 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.731-0.767), comparable to a drug-level model (R2 = 0.744), while providing indication-specific estimates. Item-based collaborative filtering imputes unobserved drug-condition pairs with a hold-out root mean squared error (RMSE) of 0.716, no better than a simple additive drug + condition baseline. Module 2 benchmarks patient-derived scores against documented U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) safety actions for 230 matched drugs. FDA-actioned drugs were rated slightly higher (Cohen's d =  - 0.297, 95% CI - 0.431 to - 0.163; area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) = 0.592), but this difference was largely explained by their much higher review volume: it disappeared with unshrunk ratings (d =  - 0.045) and was attenuated after covariate adjustment (odds ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.95-1.31), although a small difference persisted among drugs with at least 50 reviews (d =  - 0.285). Module 3 constructs a composite safety concern score from four lexicon-based dimensions. The score discriminated FDA-actioned drugs modestly (AUC = 0.568, 95% CI 0.516-0.619), including among drugs with at least 50 reviews (AUC = 0.593) and with corrected lexicon matching (AUC = 0.574); discontinuation language was the most consistent discriminating feature. The module flags 141 "blind-spot" drugs combining high ratings with high safety-concern language; many flags reflected lexicon terms that name the treated condition, so blind spots are hypothesis-generating only. Module 4 evaluates robustness to simple text perturbations and template-based fake review injection. TF-IDF with SVR and TF-IDF with Ridge regression yield robustness indices of 0.991 and 0.994, respectively; approximately 50 (SVR) and 61 (Ridge; extrapolated) injected reviews were required to shift a prediction by one rating point for sparsely reviewed target drugs. Condition-aware effectiveness estimates and linguistic safety signals can complement, but not replace, established pharmacovigilance sources.
evidence_items.title: Beyond ratings: a condition-aware natural language processing framework for drug effectiveness decomposition, regulatory benchmarking, safety signal detection, and adversarial robustness assessment using patient-generated reviews.

organizations: Anhui University of Traditional Chinese Medicine
evidence_items.summary: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) demonstrates distinct efficacy in managing gynecological disorders. However, accessing this specialized care in a home setting remains challenging due to the high cost of frequent hospital visits, privacy concerns, and a lack of immediate professional guidance. While general-purpose artificial intelligence offers a convenient alternative, the semantic gap between a patient’s colloquial symptom descriptions and formal TCM diagnostic logic—compounded by the inherent 'hallucination' risks of large language models—prevents these tools from providing safe, actionable advice. To bridge this gap, this study proposes MAGR-TCM, an intelligent home health consultation and triage model. Under expert supervision, a domain-specific knowledge graph was constructed, encompassing 10,231 entities and 32,051 relationships extracted from 741 high-quality clinical case records. Based on this foundation, we developed a Multi-Agent Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework comprising four specialized agents designed to reconstruct the complete TCM 'Disease-Pattern-Therapeutic Principle-Formula-Medicinal' reasoning chain from informal user inquiries. This collaborative architecture simulates the expert diagnostic process to generate logical, evidence-based health guidance. Experimental results demonstrate that MAGR-TCM significantly outperforms all baseline models on both RAGAS automatic evaluation and expert human evaluation. The model achieved 100% sensitivity and specificity on the safety test set, further validating its practical utility in home health settings and its ability to distinguish self-treatable conditions from those requiring urgent hospital care. By transitioning from black-box predictions to transparent, safe, and explainable reasoning logic, MAGR-TCM offers a technological paradigm for patient-centered home health management. It effectively mitigates generative hallucinations, making professional TCM expertise safely accessible for women’s daily self-care and preliminary triage.
evidence_items.title: MAGR-TCM: a knowledge graph-powered multi-agent model for intelligent home health consultation and triage in TCM gynecology

evidence_items.summary: Robotic manipulation often requires both spatial scene understanding and task history. However, many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely primarily on current observations, without explicitly integrating spatial structure and task history. Appearance-based memories can be sensitive to occlusion and viewpoint changes, while spatial representations of the current scene alone do not preserve how the scene has changed during task execution. We introduce STVLA, a framework that incorporates features from a pretrained visual geometry foundation model into temporal memory alongside visual representations. This allows the policy to recall past scene structure as context for current action decisions. To select informative history, STVLA uses a mathematically grounded scoring rule that balances relevance to the current observation with complementary evidence from memory. Across evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Mem, MIKASA-Robo, and SimplerEnv Bridge, STVLA achieves the highest average success rate among the compared methods on each benchmark. On real-world block stacking, object organization, and phone packaging, it improves success over $\pi_{0.5}$ by $58.33$, $30.00$, and $35.00$ percentage points, respectively. These results support integrating scene geometry into temporal memory to improve manipulation requiring both spatial precision and task history. Project website: \href{https://stvla.github.io/}{https://stvla.github.io/}
evidence_items.title: STVLA: Spatial-aware and Temporal-memory forVision-Language-Action Models

evidence_items.summary: Theory of Mind (ToM), the ability to infer mental states in others, is pivotal for human social cognition. Existing evaluations of ToM in large language models (LLMs) mainly focus on static belief attribution and false-belief reasoning, leaving a critical aspect of social reasoning underexplored: can LLMs decide whether perceptual evidence is sufficient to justify another person's belief revision? To address this gap, we present MuSeToM, a human-validated, text-based benchmark for evaluating epistemic belief revision in ToM reasoning. MuSeToM contains 2,415 instances adapted from BigToM and OpenToM, with textual cues spanning six sensory categories, and tests whether models can determine when a protagonist should revise a belief and infer the resulting updated belief state. Using MuSeToM, we systematically evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs under direct and chain-of-thought prompting, revealing a pronounced dissonance: while models often detect that a belief may change, they struggle to identify the updated belief and frequently over-update on perceptually salient but epistemically insufficient cues.
evidence_items.title: MuSeToM: Multi-Sensory Evaluation of Belief Revision with Textual Cues Across Six Senses

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophancy, a tendency to agree with users, flatter or affirm them, and preserve their face, even when independent judgment or critical feedback would be more useful. Prior work has largely evaluated sycophancy through benchmark evaluations, but less is known about how users perceive and respond to sycophantic AI in everyday tasks. We combine benchmark evaluations with two large-scale user studies. We study four personas defined through system prompts: objective (instructed to prioritize accuracy over agreement), soft-sycophantic, hard-sycophantic, and baseline (no persona-specific system prompt). Benchmarks show that even baseline exhibits substantial sycophancy, agreeing with users'stated views 71.7% of the time on NLP Survey, compared with 54.8% for objective and 89.5% for hard-sycophantic. Under conversational pressure on TruthfulQA, accuracy ranged from 81.9% for objective to 59.6% for baseline and 8.7% for hard-sycophantic. Participants were assigned to one of the four personas, and either discussed contested policy topics or collaborated with AI on email writing. Despite its higher accuracy under pressure, objective AI was rated significantly less respectful and satisfying than the other personas, and less trustworthy than baseline. Baseline and sycophantic personas did not differ significantly. Persona did not significantly affect how often participants changed their opinions, although participants who discussed with objective AI had greater odds of reduced confidence. Objective AI prompted greater writing expansion than soft-sycophantic AI, but final writing quality did not differ significantly across personas. These findings highlight a tension between accuracy and user approval: personas with substantially lower accuracy under conversational pressure received more favorable ratings for respect and satisfaction than objective AI.
evidence_items.title: Mind the Accuracy-Approval Gap: How Users Evaluate Sycophantic AI in Everyday Tasks

evidence_items.summary: Do large language model (LLM) migration agents learn from accumulated experience, or do apparent gains reflect retrieval and reference reuse? We evaluate an evidence-graded agent for Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration across four studies. On 1,833 documentation-derived source-reference pairs, persistent memory improved reference conformity (RC) over a no-memory baseline by 0.015 [0.004, 0.025], while policy adaptation added no gain (-0.004 [-0.010, 0.001]). An audit found that 264 of 367 held-out units (72%) shared a PostgreSQL reference with training, and the memory effect on the 103 leak-free units fell to 0.002 [-0.008, 0.011]. A model-free nearest-target copy baseline scored RC 0.222, outperforming all LLM systems (at most 0.163). A reference-grouped split reduced copying to 0.119; a rerun on 374 units in 118 independent target groups found no statistically distinguishable memory effect (0.005 [-0.003, 0.017]) and no policy effect. A separate Oracle-grounded evaluation on 216-224 real PL/SQL units showed that 10-22% of PostgreSQL-accepted units were behaviorally incorrect; a human-gated fix cycle increased demonstrably correct units from 98/216 to 167/224. A write-back study showed a 54% decline in retrieval margin as the knowledge base grew from 12 to 1,200 entries. We derive six evaluation rules that distinguish cross-task learning from reference leakage, copying, metric artifacts, and unstable feedback.
evidence_items.title: Does a Self-Learning Migration Agent Learn? An Audited Evaluation of Evidence-Graded Experience Memory for Oracle-to-PostgreSQL Migration

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents use external skills to reuse task procedures and experience with tools.
