General-purpose skills describe shared execution procedures, while specific tool choices, operating practices, and output requirements vary across users. In long-horizon tasks, subgoals, available inputs, and environmental states change as execution progresses. Agents must select currently applicable skills from an expanding skill pool and prepare candidates for subsequent steps. We propose Skill Adapter, which enables personalized modification and online routing of general-purpose skills. The system distills local adjustments from user requirements and execution feedback and stores them as Adapters linked to general-purpose skills. The routing agent selects general-purpose skills and applicable Adapters based on the current subtask, execution progress, and environmental feedback, incrementally maintaining a task-level online skill library that the main LLM reads on demand. The system preloads candidates for subsequent nodes and rechecks their applicability once actual inputs are determined. Reinforcement learning optimizes the two types of decisions using modification gains and routing outcomes, respectively. We evaluate Skill Adapter on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SkillsBench. Compared with SkillRL, it improves task success rates by an average of 11.43 percentage points and reduces mean execution time on all three benchmarks. Skill Adapter retains its performance advantage when the skill pool grows to 1,000 skills.
evidence_items.title: Skill Adapter: Personalized Modification and Online Routing of General-Purpose Skills

evidence_items.summary: In safety-critical aerospace systems, errors in requirements engineering can lead to significant operational risks, which makes accurate information extraction essential. Named Entity Recognition (NER) plays a crucial role in this process by supporting tasks such as requirements classification and automated test case generation. Despite the emergence of diverse language model–based predictive pipelines across multiple domains for NER, the aerospace software development field has so far witnessed only limited exploration of the capabilities of foundational large language models (LLMs). This study investigates the effectiveness of foundational LLMs, recurrent architecture–enhanced LLMs, and generative models under domain-specific constraints. However, single-model approaches struggle with stability, domain shifts, and difficulty in capturing long-context dependencies, which motivates the need for more robust solutions. To address this, the study proposes a novel meta-predictive pipeline that integrates heterogeneous models for improved robustness. To develop a robust and precise meta predictor, it benchmarks the performance of 15 foundational LLMs, 30 recurrently enhanced LLMs, and 4 generative language models, including DeepSeek, ChatGPT, LLaMA, and Gemini. Finally, 12 distinct meta-predictors were developed based on foundational LLMs and recurrent architectures. The best performing meta predictor on the public AeroBERT-NER benchmark dataset achieved 94.73%, 93.59%, and 94.17% precision, recall, and F1-score, respectively. The key findings demonstrate the potential of the proposed approach to improve reliability and scalability in aerospace requirements engineering workflows.
evidence_items.title: Meta-predictive ensembles of LLM pipelines for automated named entity recognition in aerospace software requirements

evidence_items.summary: In the financial decision-making process of Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) and individuals, integration of forecasting, risk quantification, and advisory generation is a tripartite requirement that is not addressed by existing systems. We present MoneyMind AI, a modular, system integration pipeline-based Financial Decision Support System (FDSS) with tightly integrated components: (i) Data ingestion & preprocessing, (ii) Structured financial analytics engine computing per financial metric like income, expenses, Net Cash Flow (NCF), and Profit Margin (PM) from the transaction-level CSV data, (iii) Machine Learning (ML) forecasting module using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Linear Regression (LR) and Random Forest (RF) ensemble methods, which offers 1, 2, and 3-month ahead financial forecasts, and (iv) a composite Financial Health Scoring (FHS) algorithm that integrates the four primary metrics the PM, Cash Flow Stability (CFS), Revenue Growth (RG) rate, and Expense Volatility (EV) into a tri-class risk stratification schema, (v) A Large Language Model (LLM) driven recommendation engine that supports the generation of action-oriented, natural language-based financial advisory based on a prompt-engineered API call, converting the structured financial summary results. The RF forecasting model benefits the ARIMA(1,1,1) baseline model, with a mean MAPE of 11.2% ± 1.5% (95% CI; MAE ≈ ₹50,400; RMSE ≈ ₹67,100) achieved over a 24-month observations hybrid transactional dataset of 480 transaction records across six expense categories using four-fold cross-validation (walk-forward). The Diebold–Mariano test with HLN small-sample correction indicates that RF is significantly more accurate than the ARIMA(1,1,1) baseline at the 1% level (HLN-corrected DM = 3.94, p = 0.002, n = 12) and then LR at the 5% level (HLN-corrected DM = 2.24, p = 0.046). The FHS risk classifier achieves an overall accuracy of 84.0% and a macro-average F1-Score of 83.9% and a Cohen’s κ of 0.76, showing substantial inter-class agreement. The recommendations of LLM (50 outputs per category from 5 domain experts) result in a mean quality score of 4.19 ± 0.31/5.0 (Krippendorff’s α = 0.79). On a full four-module functional coverage, which it is alone among the four benchmark methods, MoneyMind AI cuts the time required to complete financial analysis tasks by 97.9–99.0% relative to manual financial analysis methods across a small battery of standard tasks. The results presented show the potential of MoneyMind AI as an accessible, replicable, and actionable solution to empower SMEs and individual financial decision-makers with financial intelligence.
evidence_items.title: A unified ML LLM decision support framework for SME financial analytics forecasting risk and advisory recommendations

evidence_items.summary: Planning for a heterogeneous robot team from a scene image and an instruction involves two kinds of decisions. Some must be judged from the scene: which goals are already met, how the task splits, and which robot does what. Others follow from these and can be computed: prerequisite actions, handoffs between robots, and timing. We argue that each kind should go to the component suited to it: a small vision-language model learns the first, and a deterministic solver computes the second. In NSDL (Neuro-Symbolic Division of Labor), the trained model writes its judgments as a plan sketch, which lists the goals that still need action and the intended steps in order, each with a robot. The solver expands the sketch into an executable joint plan. The model calls two tools, a detector for evidence and the solver, and is trained with the solver in the loop. We evaluate on the public VIKI-L2 benchmark and on LOCUS-Bench, a new benchmark that grades the two kinds of difficulty separately. NSDL outperforms end-to-end planners and formalize-then-plan baselines on both benchmarks and with three backbones from 3B to 8B; the 7B model reaches 97.0% out-of-distribution accuracy on VIKI-L2. Ordering and scheduling errors nearly disappear once the solver writes the structure; the remaining failures are misjudged states, and most goals the model misses are ones it never lists. Code, model weights, and LOCUS-Bench are publicly available at https://github.com/Xincheng-Tan/NSDL.
evidence_items.title: NSDL: Neuro-Symbolic Division of Labor for Multi-Robot Task Planning

evidence_items.summary: Visual content in multimedia systems may be resized, compressed, or re-rendered before it is interpreted by a vision-language model. We study a security failure mode in which these transformations change the machine-readable semantics of an image: a textual instruction is not recovered at a $512\times512$ presentation resolution under our evaluation protocol but becomes recoverable after aggressive downsampling. We formulate this behavior as Scale-Induced Semantic Shift (SISS) and develop a closed-loop black-box framework that combines dual-scale verification, selective self-hardening, shallow-layer low-rank adaptation, and pixel-space noise regularization. On a fixed 300-case benchmark, the third SISS refinement round obtains a $58.75\%$ average attack success rate across four closed-source vision-language models, compared with $41.08\%$ for the strongest generation baseline. A controlled sweep bounds the effect to aggressive compression: average success decreases to $17.68\%$, $6.85\%$, and $5.60\%$ at $128\times128$, $224\times224$, and $336\times336$, respectively. In a downstream web-agent study, the generated images increase hidden-instruction perception, but absolute behavioral compromise remains about $4\%$. Generic input transformations provide little protection in a separate defense protocol, whereas the proposed ScaleGuard consistency detector reduces non-adaptive success from $61.4\%$ to $24.3\%$ and one-round defense-aware success from $42.5\%$ to $15.0\%$, with no observed rejection among matched clean controls. The results characterize a bounded but reproducible semantic inconsistency in multimedia preprocessing and motivate scale-consistent visual-language inference.
evidence_items.title: Scale-Induced Semantic Shift in Visual Prompt Injection Against VLMs and Web Agents

evidence_items.summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models through forward-only evaluations, but high-dimensional random perturbations can limit optimization efficiency. Sparse perturbations reduce the search dimension, making the selection of informative coordinates critical. We propose Wanda-Importance Sparsity-MeZO (WIS-MeZO), which uses Wanda weight--activation saliency to construct task-conditioned sparse perturbation masks while keeping the pretrained model dense. We analyze support quality through gradient energy capture and relate it to gradient estimation and convergence. Across 16 benchmarks with LLaMA and Qwen models ranging from 3B to 32B parameters, WIS-MeZO achieves higher aggregate scores than MeZO and reaches comparable validation losses in fewer optimization steps. Comparisons with random and magnitude-based sparse perturbations further highlight the importance of informative support selection.
evidence_items.title: Wanda-Guided Sparse Perturbations for Efficient Zeroth-Order Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Automatic setlist identification aims to identify the songs performed in live concert recordings by matching noisy and variable-quality audio against a database of reference tracks. This task presents challenges beyond conventional music version identification, including substantial arrangement differences, background noise, and the need to process continuous recordings efficiently at large scale. In this work, we evaluate modern music version retrieval methods for setlist identification using the ASID benchmark, comparing the established Re-MOVE system with CLEWS and NAVE, an internal neural audio version embedding model. Our results show that NAVE and CLEWS substantially outperform Re-MOVE. Notably, NAVE uses 256-dimensional embeddings, compared with 1024 dimensions for CLEWS, providing a four-fold reduction in embedding storage while achieving better retrieval performance. We further evaluate music/non-music gating and find modest improvements in detection and temporal coverage, while qualitative analysis suggests that such preprocessing can improve recognition boundaries beyond what the standard ASID metrics capture. Overall, the results demonstrate that segment-level audio embeddings provide a strong basis for scalable setlist identification and that compact representations can achieve strong accuracy under realistic live-concert conditions at much lower storage and serving cost.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Music Version Retrieval Methods for Setlist Identification in Live Concerts

evidence_items.summary: Grammar Error Correction (GEC) has emerged as a critical natural language processing task with applications in educational technology, automated proofreading, and digital communication enhancement. Although current transformer-based methods have shown remarkable results in formal textual settings, they struggle to handle the linguistic diversity and situational ambiguity of informal digital communication, including purposeful abbreviations, code-switching, and intentional grammatical violations. This study presents a hybrid CNN-BART model that effectively merges local pattern recognition with transformer-based contextual understanding for robust text error correction. The proposed system integrates curriculum-based noise injection, multi-scale convolutional encoding, and a comprehensive feature selection pipeline to address the challenges of informal text processing. Experimental validation on three benchmark datasets demonstrates consistent absolute \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$F_{0.5}$$\end{document} improvements of \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$+6.5$$\end{document} points over Pillars of GEC on CoNLL-2014, \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$+10.5$$\end{document} points over T5 on ErAConD, and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$+2.4$$\end{document} points over Pillars of GEC on BEA-2019, representing statistically significant advances (\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$p < 0.05$$\end{document}, bootstrap resampling, 95% CI). This work offers a practical framework for automated writing assistance in both academic and industry contexts.
evidence_items.title: Advancing Grammar Error Correction in informal digital communication: a hybrid CNN-BART approach with adaptive noise modeling

evidence_items.summary: Recent advancements in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLM) enhance X-ray report generation, but often neglect clinical context, overlook workflow integration, and lack explainability, which hinders clinical adoption due to interpretability and reliability concerns. This paper addresses the dual challenges of performance and expert explainability in automated X-ray report generation for clinical AI applications. Our proposed approach, TransXplainRRG, utilises an off-the-shelf Swin Transformer model along with a transformer-based text encoder that incorporates patient medical history to generate a radiology report. Further, we explore an expert-guided `inside-out'approach and extract only abnormal findings for radiology report refinement. Thus, this study bridges the gap between high-performance automation and interpretability critical for clinical practice by combining state-of-the-art transformer-based vision encoders, text encoders, and LLMs. TransXplainRRG is trained and tested on the large-scale MIMIC-CXR dataset and further evaluated on the unseen IU X-Ray dataset to demonstrate its generalizability and robustness. We employed the GREEN metric as a complementary measure of clinical consistency, achieving scores of 0.327 on MIMIC-CXR and 0.605 on IU X-Ray, both higher than those achieved by MAIRA-2 under the same evaluation setting. It also performed competitively across standard evaluation metrics, frequently matching or surpassing state-of-the-art models. Additionally, we introduce qualitative evaluation metrics developed from radiologists'viewpoints and conduct a preliminary radiologist evaluation on 100 generated reports to assess their clinical relevance. Quantitative and qualitative analyses further demonstrate the potential of our TransXplainRRG framework for reliable and explainable radiology report generation.
evidence_items.title: TransXplainRRG: A Radiologist-Evaluated LVLM for Chest Radiograph Report Generation

evidence_items.summary: Quantum software engineering (QSE) lacks validated approaches for translating natural-language non-functional requirements (NFRs) into execution parameters such as shots and transpiler optimization levels. Existing methods emphasize semantic similarity rather than execution outcomes. We evaluate seven large language models (LLMs) against a deterministic heuristic baseline using 540 synthetic and 18 real-world user stories. We assess semantic accuracy and execution outcomes, including time, cost, top-state probability, and two-qubit gate exposure, through Qiskit/Aer simulations. All LLMs significantly outperformed the heuristic in semantic accuracy, achieving 55.6 to 83.3 percent on real-world stories compared to 16.7 percent for the heuristic. However, no LLM demonstrated statistically significant superiority over others on the real-world dataset. Speed- and cost-oriented configurations reduced execution time and cost, but fidelity improvements were not supported. Some failures resulted from provider safety refusals rather than translation errors. Our findings demonstrate the potential of LLMs as middleware for NFR-to-configuration translation in QSE, while emphasizing execution-based validation, human oversight, and careful interpretation of model differences.
evidence_items.title: Non-Functional Requirements to Hyperparameter Translation for Quantum Software via LLMs

evidence_items.summary: The easy access to Large Language Models (LLMs) has made AI-generated texts on the web increasingly ubiquitous, making AI-text detection a crucial task. Prompts greatly influence the generation process, but existing detectors focus solely on the generated texts --- supervised methods learn from labeled texts only, and zero-shot methods rely on the text's probability distributions --- ignoring the underlying generation process, which limits their robustness in open-world scenarios. We introduce SPADE: Soft Prompts for Ai-text DEtection, a novel framework for detecting AI-generated text that transfers better across datasets. Specifically, we measure the prompt's influence and use it as a discriminative signal. We characterize the prompt's influence by introducing a Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) term that captures how much a prompt explains a text. Based on this quantity, SPADE trains one soft prompt per class to amplify the separation, and predicts the class whose prompt best explains the candidate text. Extensive experiments on several benchmarks against various detectors demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of our method, achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets.
evidence_items.title: SPADE: Soft Prompts for Ai-text DEtection

evidence_items.summary:
PURPOSE
Although professional societies provide standardized resources, the reliability of online health content remains inconsistent, particularly as large language models (LLMs) become a growing source of patient information. Therefore, the primary objective of this study was to determine whether patient-focused prompt optimization improves the readability of Generative Pre-trained Transformer-5 (GPT-5) Thinking responses compared with standard prompting while evaluating potential changes in expert-rated factual accuracy using educational materials published by the European Society of Breast Imaging (EUSOBI).


METHODS
All GPT-5 Thinking outputs were prospectively generated in January 2026. The dataset included frequently asked questions (FAQs) and special information notes (SINs) derived from EUSOBI articles, each submitted under two distinct prompts (standard-Prompt 1 vs. patient-focused-Prompt 2). Readability was quantified using four indices with an averaged composite "reading grade level." Accuracy was scored by two radiologists using a 5-point Likert scale.


RESULTS
A total of 48 questions (15 FAQs and 33 SIN-derived questions) were each answered under two prompt conditions, yielding 96 responses for analysis. Prompt 2 produced significantly lower readability levels than Prompt 1 across all indices (P < 0.001). These improvements occurred without significant differences in word count (P = 0.12) or sentence count (P = 0.63). The mean accuracy scores remained high and comparable between prompts for all questions (4.54 ± 0.63 vs. 4.52 ± 0.59, P = 0.75). The inter-rater agreement was almost perfect for both the FAQ and SIN-derived question sets (κ = 0.82 and 0.81, respectively).


CONCLUSION
Patient-focused prompting substantially reduced the linguistic complexity and reading grade level of GPT-5 Thinking responses without a statistically significant reduction in expert-rated accuracy, demonstrating its ability to produce more accessible breast imaging content, although the resulting grade level remained above widely recommended patient-education thresholds.


CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE
A simple, low-cost prompt modification can substantially improve the readability of LLM-generated patient education content in breast imaging without a measurable reduction in expert-rated accuracy, although further work is needed to confirm this translates into improved patient comprehension.
evidence_items.title: Prompt-dependent readability and accuracy of Generative Pre-trained Transformer-5 thinking responses to breast imaging questions derived from European Society of Breast Imaging patient recommendations.

evidence_items.summary: Existing large language models typically rely on massive fine-tuning datasets for safety alignment, which results in higher costs for safety alignment and often leads to the problem of over-refusal. We propose Less is Safer (LIS), a compact yet highly effective dataset for safety alignment, constructed through interpretable feature-guided selection and adversarial synthesis. Specifically, we leverage Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) activations to efficiently select prompts that cover diverse and interpretable safety features. Then, we employ a multi-agent adversarial synthesis framework to generate harmless prompts that nevertheless elicit unnecessary refusals. LIS contains only 2.4K samples, yet outperforms much larger datasets, e.g., TRIDENT-Core (26K), TRIDENT-Edge (19K) and WildJailbreak (262K), in overall performance on four safety and five over-refusal benchmarks. Through ablation experiments, we demonstrate that neither safety data nor over-refusal data alone can achieve optimal results. We also used safety features from SAE, annotated by an LLM, for data filtering, but the results were inferior to those obtained using the pipeline proposed in this paper.
evidence_items.title: Data-Efficient LLM Safety Alignment Guided by Interpretable Features

evidence_items.summary: Protein mutation effect prediction is fundamental to protein engineering and disease variant interpretation, yet experimentally measured mutation data remain accurate but extremely sparse. To provide scalable supplementary mutation signals, we construct a PDB-wide mutation augmentation dataset that exhaustively enumerates single-site substitutions on experimentally resolved protein structures and aligns mutation signals from physics-based energy models, protein language models, and inverse folding models. Large-scale analysis under a unified mutation preference representation reveals substantial differences in the consistency, concentration, and substitution patterns of mutation distributions across models, indicating that disagreement is pervasive and reflects conflicting inductive biases rather than random noise. Motivated by these observations, we propose an unsupervised multi-source mutation preference distillation framework that learns from relative mutation preferences while explicitly modeling cross-source disagreement. Without using any experimental mutation labels during training, our approach achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated zero-shot baselines and naive multi-source fusion strategies on ProteinGym. We release the dataset and evaluation pipeline to support reproducible studies of protein mutation effects.
evidence_items.title: MutAtlas: A PDB-Wide Energy-Guided Atlas of Protein Mutation Effects

evidence_items.summary: Generalized panorama depth estimation has witnessed great advances in recent years. These methods typically achieve robust zero-shot generalization performance using large pretrained models, but their high computational cost makes real-time inference on embedded platforms challenging. In contrast, previous lightweight panorama models have mostly been developed for single-domain evaluations and cannot generalize well due to domain shifts. To reduce the gap between these two types of models, we introduce EG360, an efficient and generalizable panorama depth estimation model. Specifically, building on a lightweight depth model, we design an Adaptive Panorama-Perspective Distillation (APPD) strategy guided by scene geometry, along with a Spherical Cross-Level Feature Fusion (SCFF) module for global semantic perception. As a result, with only 6.593M parameters after reparameterization, EG360 achieves strong zero-shot performance on real-world benchmarks and runs at 35 FPS on a Jetson Orin NX 16GB in MAXN mode, whereas a previous ViT-small model runs at less than 2 FPS. Our code will also be made public for future research.
evidence_items.title: EG360: Efficient and Generalizable $360^\circ$ Depth Estimation via Adaptive Panorama-Perspective Distillation and Spherical Cross-Level Feature Fusion

evidence_items.summary: We run reinforcement learning (RL) with GRPO across four environments, starting from a supervised fine-tuned 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts model covering English and eight Indic languages. We compare the model before and after RL across 34 benchmarks in one evaluation campaign. MATH improves by 36.07 points, and most Indic benchmarks also improve. Yet XQuAD-Indic F1 falls 19.32 points as English answers rise from 8.7% to 91.7%; IndicQA falls 8.64, while English XQuAD gains 11.71 F1. A second RL run from the same supervised initialization adds an Indic environment together with language and repetition rewards. Compared with the released model, it improves both passage-answering and instruction-following benchmarks, along with preserving MATH performance. But it loses ground on reasoning and coding benchmarks. Several training choices changed together, so we cannot isolate the effect of any one of the reward terms. Script compliance remains unresolved. Adding a language reward did not ensure use of the requested script. Passage answering and script compliance therefore need direct evaluation, even when other benchmark scores improve.
evidence_items.title: Indic-Task Gains and Regressions after Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: Adapting general Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to Autonomous Driving (AD) is thought to require heavy 3D spatial priors or intrusive architectural overhauls to compensate for a lack of spatial grounding. In this work, we present a counterintuitive pilot study: off-the-shelf general VLMs already exhibit remarkable adaptability across diverse driving tasks, while precise metric depth remains the primary missing link, a bottleneck readily addressable via onboard sensors and depth foundation models. To this end, we introduce the Triplet Incremental Training Framework, a non-intrusive paradigm that seamlessly instills 3D geometric awareness into a general VLM backbone while fully preserving its open-world capabilities. Driven by automatically constructed (image, depth, QA pair) triplets, our framework operates via a unified tri-stream training pipeline: an unfrozen primary VLM stream to adapt to driving tasks, an auxiliary depth stream that guides the visual backbone to implicitly imagine 3D scene geometry via explicit geometric constraints, and a frozen twin VLM stream employing logit-level KL distillation to prevent semantic drift. Crucially, the auxiliary depth branch is discarded during deployment, ensuring the enhanced geometric awareness comes with zero inference overhead. We evaluate our framework across four major benchmarks targeting four diverse capabilities spanning 3D spatial perception, driving-oriented language reasoning, end-to-end planning, and general multimodal understanding. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art driving VLMs, rivals domain-specific expert models in 3D perception, and successfully retains its original general reasoning capabilities. This demonstrates that Triplet Incremental Training offers a unified, deployment-ready paradigm for transforming general foundation models into robust driving intelligences.
evidence_items.title: From Foundation VLM to Versatile Driving VLM: A Triplet Incremental Training Approach

evidence_items.summary: Time Series Forecasting (TSF) is essential across diverse domains, including finance, supply chain management, environmental monitoring, and healthcare, where reliable predictions support critical decision making. Despite recent progress in Deep Learning (DL) based forecasting, limited data availability and distributional variability often hinder model generalization. Data augmentation has emerged as an effective strategy to mitigate these challenges by increasing data diversity. Existing augmentation methods, such as frequency domain and wavelet based transformations, have shown effectiveness to some extent but struggle to maintain temporal coherence and consistency across varying prediction horizons. To address these limitations, this study proposes Wavelet-guided Frequency-based (WaveFreqAug), a novel hybrid augmentation method that integrates wavelet decomposition with adaptive frequency domain enhancement. The method operates on residual components to enrich spectral variability while preserving long-term temporal structures. Comprehensive experiments conducted on four benchmark datasets (ETTh1, ETTh2, ILI, and Weather) using six forecasting models demonstrate that WaveFreqAug outperforms both the unaugmented baseline, in which the same forecasting model is trained on the original data without any augmentation, and six State-of-the-Art (SOTA) augmentation methods applied to the same data, in the large majority of short- and long-term forecasting settings. These results highlight the robustness and generalizability of the proposed approach for improving deep learning based TSF.
evidence_items.title: Wavelet guided frequency-domain augmentation for robust time series forecasting

evidence_items.summary: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will observe a superposition of gravitational-wave signals, requiring joint inference of an unknown number of sources, parameters, and instrumental noise. To disentangle these contributions, that overlap in both time and frequency, a Global Fit (GF) analysis is needed. We present samsara++, a C++/CUDA sampler designed to address this trans-dimensional GF problem. Building on the continuous-time MCMC framework of samsara, the algorithm combines birth-death processes for adding and removing sources, with mutation moves for parameter estimation. Birth and death are selected through posterior-dependent rates. Shared-memory parallelism, incremental likelihood updates, and indexed storage reduce the computational and memory costs, while parallel tempering improves the exploration of multimodal posteriors. We assess the performance using simulated one-year LISA datasets containing Galactic double white dwarf binaries and stationary Gaussian instrumental noise. Analyses of populations containing 143 and 866 binaries start from empty source models, without preliminary searches or proposals tailored to the injected population. These tests demonstrate source reconstruction and catalog generation, highlighting, at the same time, the importance of source-count, overlapping signals, and incomplete mixing on joint source and noise inference. Then we perform a separate stress test, initialized at the injected parameters, exploring a population of 16,435 binaries, corresponding to 131,480 source parameters. This run completes 15 million iterations in approximately 16 hours using about 3 GB of RAM. All together, these benchmarks show the computational feasibility of birth-death sampling for large Galactic-binary populations, and provide a foundation for extending samsara++ toward a comprehensive LISA global fit.
evidence_items.title: Global Fit Inference for LISA with samsara++

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
Medical school curricula are managed through fragmented, static tools that prevent faculty and curriculum committees from seeing a unified view of content scope, sequence, and licensing examination alignment. Governance relies on manual reporting that is neither timely nor consistent, and no widely adopted platform incorporates a generative AI agent that queries a relational curriculum database to produce tailored, on-demand reports.


OBJECTIVE
This study aimed to design, implement, and evaluate a 4-phase, AI-integrated relational curriculum mapping framework providing faculty self-directed curriculum search; cross-course alignment reports classifying content as redundant, complementary, or a gap, with recommendations; and alignment with United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE) content and accreditation requirements.


METHODS
We implemented the framework during academic year 2025-2026. It captures session learning objectives (SLOs) annually; maps them to program objectives, course objectives, USMLE codes, Association of American Medical Colleges keywords, and Bloom's levels using a large language model with expert verification; centralizes verified data in a relational database (Airtable) with faculty read-only search; and uses a second AI agent via an API to generate on-demand reports on scope, sequence, redundancy, gaps, and USMLE alignment across all 16 preclerkship courses and all clinical clerkship rotations.


RESULTS
Course directors gained self-directed curriculum access through Airtable Extensions search. Cross-course vertical alignment reports identified redundant, complementary, and gap findings and generated course-level recommendations. An analysis of 2 preclerkship courses identified 50 matched SLO pairs across 3 USMLE pathology domains within minutes. A USMLE Step 1 alignment report across all 16 courses identified a curriculum-wide pathology coverage deficit (42% vs a target of 45%-55%) that was descriptively consistent with institutional performance data (not formally tested). An accreditation query identified all preclerkship and clerkship content on a specified topic and generated Data Collection Instrument-ready documentation within seconds. A Medical Education Program Objective coverage analysis across all 9 clinical clerkships, generated within minutes, found documented coverage for 24 of 25 (96%) program objectives and 1 objective with no matching SLO in any clerkship, a gap not previously tracked. In a blinded validation study, 3 independent course directors each coded a 30-SLO sample; agreement with the database (Fleiss κ, 3 raters plus database) was substantial at the exact-code level (κ=0.67, 95% CI 0.55-0.78) and almost perfect at the USMLE domain level (κ=0.94, 95% CI 0.88-1.00).


CONCLUSIONS
An AI-integrated relational curriculum database with a faculty-facing search interface can convert curriculum governance from a periodic, retrospective activity into a continuous, self-service one, producing alignment and gap analyses within minutes rather than weeks. Workload effects have not been formally measured. Extension to assessment items and prospective correlation with licensing examination outcomes are planned.
evidence_items.title: An AI-Integrated Relational Curriculum Mapping Framework for Alignment and Transparency in Medical Education: Implementation Study.

evidence_items.summary:
The emergence of generative artificial intelligence has transformed information retrieval, yet limited understanding of its differences from traditional search engines hinders clarity regarding changes in user search behavior and variations in search effectiveness, thereby impeding guidance for future search interface design.
 
 
 
 We conducted a laboratory experiment comparing two versions of the Bing search engine: the traditional Bing search and the generative-AI integrated Bing (Bing Chat). We interpreted variations in user search behavior through querying, browsing, and clicking data, and established a multidimensional metric framework encompassing user, cost-benefit, and system dimensions to assess search effectiveness. 40 participants with good search skills completed the experiment, resulting in a final dataset comprising 160 observation records.
 
 
 
 The Mann-Whitney U test revealed that users of generative AI search engines exhibited the following characteristics compared to those using traditional search engines: longer queries, more keyboard activity, more frequent query restructuring (including more narrowing queries, more following the system queries, and more changing the syntactic structure queries, with less broadening queries), more browsing during the first search session, and less scrolling and clicking. The results of the Linear Mixed Models show that, compared to traditional search engines, users achieve superior performance with generative AI search on users’ subjective perceptions and search efficiency metrics. Furthermore, we employed machine learning to validate which search behaviors can predict a user’s search effectiveness. The results indicate that the Gradient Boosting Machines are the optimal prediction models. The five most significant indicators for predicting search performance are Avelength. QueryConsTime, TimetofirSearch, ResViewTime and NumbofScroll.
 
 
 
 By revealing differences in user behavior and search efficiency across various search engines, this study deepens our understanding of generative AI search engines at a finer granularity and contributes to building adaptive search platforms capable of optimizing search recommendations.
 
 
 
 By revealing differences in user behavior and efficiency between traditional and generative versions of the Bing search engine, this study deepens our understanding of generative AI search engines at a finer granularity and contributes to building adaptive search platforms capable of optimizing search recommendations.
evidence_items.title: Effectiveness evaluation of generative intelligent search: a comparative study with traditional search engine

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objective Oral lichen planus (OLP) is a chronic inflammatory disorder classified as an oral potentially malignant disorder. Accurate clinical diagnosis remains challenging due to lesion heterogeneity and substantial overlap with other oral mucosal diseases. This study developed an explainable artificial intelligence framework for automated OLP classification using complementary deep feature representations and hybrid feature optimization. Materials and Methods A dataset comprising 1,345 clinical images (747 OLP and 598 non-OLP) was divided into training ( n  = 967), validation ( n  = 189), and test ( n  = 189) subsets using stratified sampling. Images were resized to 224 × 224 pixels, and geometric data augmentation was applied only to the training set, expanding it to 10,000 images while preventing data leakage. Two attention-guided convolutional neural networks, LichenNet-CBAM and Inception-LichenNet-CBAM, were independently trained to extract complementary 512-dimensional deep feature representations. The resulting 1,024-dimensional fused feature space was optimized using a hybrid Grey Wolf Optimizer with Mutation-based Local Search (GWO-MLS) prior to evaluation across multiple machine learning classifiers. Model interpretability was enhanced using Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping), feature importance analysis, and confidence calibration. Results On the independent test dataset, Naïve Bayes and AdaBoost achieved the highest classification accuracy of 94.71%, whereas Random Forest produced the highest discriminative performance (receiver operating characteristic area under the curve, ROC-AUC = 0.981). The Naïve Bayes classifier correctly identified 99 of 105 OLP lesions and 80 of 84 non-OLP lesions. Statistical analysis demonstrated overlapping 95% confidence intervals and no significant performance differences between the best-performing classifier and alternative models. Conclusion The proposed framework provides accurate and interpretable automated classification of OLP by integrating complementary deep feature extraction, hybrid feature optimization, and explainable artificial intelligence. Further validation using large multicenter cohorts is warranted before clinical implementation.
evidence_items.title: Attention-Guided Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Automated Oral Lichen Planus Classification

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in higher education for assessment, tutoring, learning analytics, resource production and academic administration. An emerging area is the use of generative systems for music business education. Artists and Repertoire (A&R) professionals play a central role in finding new musical talent, shaping artistic direction, and connecting artists with songwriters and music producers. Preparing music business students for this role typically requires them to engage with real world artists, with whom they can develop their interviewing and other A&R skills. Using role play during the early stages of teaching can support students with developing their skills before they work with real artists. In this study, Ama, a fictional R&B and neo-soul musician realised through an embodied conversational agent, underwent preliminary design and formative evaluation. The agent was developed as an interactive rehearsal partner for students learning about the artists and repertoire process. Development involved using a combination of generative AI tools, including ChatGPT, Copilot, Kling AI, Suno, Nano Banana, and Adobe Firefly, to develop the artist's lyrics and supporting media, thereby visualising the artist. Her profile was extended into a knowledge base, configuring the agent and refining its responses. The evaluation identified issues relating to response length, answer format, conversational naturalness, generative improvisation and latency. The study presents a prototype developed through iterative design, providing preliminary results and a foundation for further research with students using embodied conversational agents in the classroom.
evidence_items.title: Embodied Conversational Agents as Rehearsal Partners for Developing Music Business Students' A&R Skills

evidence_items.summary: The growing volume of process data generated by screwdriving systems, combined with advancements in computing power, data storage, and algorithms, is facilitating the application of artificial intelligence in this field. Accurately detecting and classifying screwdriving errors is crucial for ensuring product quality, avoiding costly rework in manufacturing, and supporting sustainability by facilitating the maintenance, reuse, and recycling of screw-connected products. In this context, machine learning approaches offer a promising alternative to traditional monitoring techniques, such as window-based methods or envelope curves. This study examines the use of deep learning techniques for anomaly detection and error classification in screwdriving processes. The data corpus consists of multivariate time series capturing process parameters, such as torque and rotation angle. For anomaly detection, the embedding space of a vector quantized variational autoencoder was analyzed. In terms of error classification, four different model architectures were evaluated. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of anomaly detection and confirm that deep learning models can distinguish between multiple error categories beyond traditional binary classification. This extends the capabilities of conventional monitoring approaches, achieving accuracies of up to 100%. Additionally, real-world data material was examined in order to further demonstrate model robustness. Overall the results indicate strong generalization capability and highlight the practical potential of the developed models for use in industrial screwdriving processes, eliminating the need for expert knowledge in error identification and significantly reducing manual effort and analysis time.
evidence_items.title: ScrewSense: Mapping the Invisible - Anomaly Detection and Error Classification in Screwdriving Processes

evidence_items.summary: The major challenge in computational neuroscience arises from the coexistence of temporal fluctuations, long-term dependencies, and complex context-aware dynamics when predicting brain states from multiscale signals. The existing models, including recurrent models (GRU), hybrid models (CNN-BiLSTM), Transformer-based architectures (EEG-PatchFormer), and graph-based models (GLCNet) have demonstrated effectiveness on sequential modeling but may face limitations in capturing hierarchical temporal patterns and adaptive memory modelling across different timescales. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a Unified Context-Aware AI (UCAI) framework that integrates multiscale temporal learning and adaptive memory with context-aware temporal representation, including brain prediction within a single coherent architecture. Unlike conventional sequential modelling approaches, the proposed framework represents neural signals with structured context-aware temporal representations. A mathematically formulated context-aware temporal representation module maps temporal features into higher-level representations through context-aware transformations to enhance decision-making and contextual representations. The experimental evaluation using “EBrains” (12 subjects) and “SEED-IV” (15 subjects) datasets under Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) cross-validation protocol. The UCAI achieves significant improvement in terms of classification performance and under LOSO evaluation (p < 0.05). In addition, cross-dataset and distribution-shift evaluations provide preliminary evidence of transferability.
evidence_items.title: A unified context-aware AI framework for multiscale temporal learning and brain state prediction

evidence_items.summary: Accurate day-ahead forecasting of individual residential electricity demand remains challenging because household consumption is highly variable, nonlinear, and influenced by recurrent behavioral and environmental patterns. This study proposes a multi-input, multi-feature Long Short-Term Memory (MIMF-LSTM) framework for direct 24 hour residential load forecasting at 15 minute resolution. The proposed architecture independently processes two lag-aligned temporal profiles: the immediately preceding 24 hour period and the corresponding 24 hour period one week earlier. Each pathway contains total household load and historical meteorological variables, including air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, and precipitation. The resulting representations are fused with cyclic calendar features to generate a 96-step day-ahead forecast. The framework was evaluated using approximately one year of measurements from a residential household in Tallinn, Estonia. Under a controlled experimental protocol, all benchmark models were provided with the same daily and weekly historical information, input variables, chronological data partitions, and forecasting horizon. Comparisons included seasonal benchmarks, Ridge regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, LSTM, GRU, CNN-LSTM, and attention-LSTM. Across three independent runs, the proposed MIMF-LSTM achieved an RMSE of 0.848 ± 0.005 kW, an MAE of 0.464 ± 0.006 kW, and a MAPE of 63.86 ± 2.69%, yielding the lowest mean RMSE among the evaluated models. Ridge regression achieved a marginally lower MAE of 0.463 kW, although the difference was not statistically significant. Paired daily comparisons showed that MIMF-LSTM significantly reduced both RMSE and MAE relative to GRU, standard LSTM, attention-LSTM, CNN-LSTM, Random Forest, XGBoost, and CatBoost after Holm correction. Ablation analysis further demonstrated that the combined daily–weekly configuration outperformed the individual pathways, whereas adding a 28-day pathway increased model complexity without improving forecasting accuracy. The results indicate that explicit separation of daily and weekly temporal information can improve day-ahead residential load forecasting without requiring additional long-term input pathways.
evidence_items.title: Improved residential load forecasting using multi-feature, multi-layer LSTM exploiting trend and periodic patterns in historical data

evidence_items.summary: Single-cell reference mapping is increasingly central to translating heterogeneous datasets into consistent representations of cell identity. As cell-type atlases expand in scale and complexity, mapping new data to shared references enables reproducible annotation, cross-study integration, and accumulation of biological knowledge. We present MapMyCells, an open-source, high-performance framework for mapping diverse single-cell omics datasets to hierarchical reference taxonomies with minimal preprocessing. MapMyCells currently supports six diverse brain references spanning whole mouse and human brain, Alzheimer's disease and aging cohorts, developing mouse cortex, and a cross-species basal ganglia taxonomy. Across these references, MapMyCells accurately recovers cell identities at broad and intermediate taxonomic levels, remains robust with reduced informative gene panels, and supports transcriptomic, epigenomic, and spatial datasets. Benchmarking shows competitive accuracy with substantially lower computational requirements, enabling datasets and taxonomies containing thousands of cell types to be analyzed on standard workstations. MapMyCells provides a scalable framework for unified, extensible brain cell atlases.
evidence_items.title: MapMyCells: High-performance mapping of cell-by-gene data to reference brain taxonomies.

evidence_items.summary: Contextual anomaly detection in tabular data aims to identify objects whose behavior is unexpected under their contextual conditions. In data-engineering pipelines, this task screens table rows whose measurements violate context-dependent integrity relationships. Most existing approaches rely on either shallow conditional models with limited distributional expressiveness or localized estimators that require per-context modeling, making it difficult to capture complex conditional relationships and scale to high-dimensional settings. We propose Flow-CAD, a new framework for contextual anomaly detection based on Flow Matching. Flow-CAD learns a single global and amortized conditional generative model that flexibly represents behavioral distributions conditioned on context, without assuming simple parametric forms or retraining local models. To enable robust and interpretable anomaly scoring, we introduce a scale-normalized and truncated residual energy derived from the learned conditional flow, which stabilizes anomaly scores, mitigates domination by extreme deviations, and supports feature-wise attribution. We further provide theoretical insights showing that the proposed residual-based anomaly score is stable under velocity estimation error, and that its Monte Carlo estimator satisfies concentration bounds. Experiments on 20 benchmark datasets with 13 competitors demonstrate that Flow-CAD has the best average rank for PR AUC, ROC AUC, and P@n, highlighting its effectiveness and practicality for contextual anomaly detection in tabular data. We provide the source code at https://github.com/ZhongLIFR/FlowCAD.
evidence_items.title: Flow-CAD: Flow Matching for Contextual Anomaly Detection and Explanation in Tabular Data

evidence_items.summary: Integrating heterogeneous single-cell datasets requires aligning shared biological features while preserving meaningful variation across modalities, studies, and species. Here, we present multiVIB, a unified framework combining the variational information bottleneck with probabilistic contrastive learning for horizontal, vertical, and mosaic integration of single-cell multi-omics data. Across diverse benchmarks, multiVIB achieves competitive integration performance while minimizing spurious alignments. Applied to BRAIN Initiative atlas-scale datasets, multiVIB enables incremental integration of nine molecular modalities in the mouse primary motor cortex and cross-species integration of primate basal ganglia transcriptomes, recovering conserved cell identities and species-specific molecular programs. Together, these results establish multiVIB as a versatile framework for scalable, biologically faithful construction and expansion of comprehensive brain cell atlases.
evidence_items.title: multiVIB: A unified probabilistic contrastive learning framework for atlas-scale integration of single-cell multi-omics data.

evidence_items.summary: High-dimensional cyclic multiplexed immunofluorescence (cMIF) enables single-cell phenotyping within intact tissues. Cell annotations rely on a multi-step pipeline involving normalization, sampling, dimensionality reduction, and clustering, but the absence of standardized benchmarks for method selection, especially at the clustering stage, leads to inconsistent and less reproducible phenotyping. To address this, we developed CONCLAVE, a consensus-clustering-based workflow that optimizes upstream steps and integrates results from multiple clustering algorithms retaining only those cell labels supported by at least two independent methods. Through in silico simulations and real-world cMIF datasets, CONCLAVE consistently outperformed single-clustering-method approaches in agreement with expert-curated references, reproducibility, and robustness, with improvements becoming more evident when mapped within spatial tissue contexts. Additionally, CONCLAVE includes a scoring module that flags regions likely to contain unreliable or inconsistent data, facilitating targeted quality control. In summary, CONCLAVE offers a robust framework for cell annotation in cMIF datasets, enhancing the reliability of downstream spatial proteomics analyses.
evidence_items.title: CONCLAVE: A consensus clustering with annotation-validation extrapolation for cyclic multiplexed immunofluorescence data.

evidence_items.summary: Steady-state detection is a central step in software performance benchmarking, yet different detection methods rely on different assumptions and may perform best on different execution profiles. This paper formulates steady-state detection as an algorithm-recommendation problem: given a benchmark time series, predict which of two complementary detectors is more appropriate. The first, CP-SSD, identifies steady state through changepoint-based segmentation of the execution trace, whereas the second, KB-KSSD, uses a kernel-based approach to identify stable behaviour. We propose a data-driven recommender that characterises benchmark time series using automatically extracted features and combines supervised prediction with information derived from groups of time series exhibiting similar behaviour. The approach is evaluated on 407 labelled benchmark time series for which one of the two detectors can be identified as preferable with respect to a reference steady-state index. The proposed recommender selects the better detector correctly for 72.97% of the series, compared with 62.65% when always selecting the detector that performs best most often, corresponding to an absolute improvement of 10.32 percentage points. Paired statistical testing and bootstrap confidence intervals support this improvement. A comparison with a recommender using time-series features alone shows that the cluster-derived information mainly improves interpretability rather than predictive accuracy. Recommendations also remain highly stable when the unsupervised representation is learned from either the labelled subset or the full collection of 5,860 time series. These results demonstrate the feasibility of per-series steady-state detector recommendation while highlighting the need for broader labelled data, particularly for execution profiles favouring the changepoint-based detector.
evidence_items.title: Towards Automated Recommendation of Steady-State Detection Algorithms for Software Performance Benchmarks

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in robotic manipulation have enabled increasingly complex and dexterous behaviors, yet existing benchmarks still focus on simple pick-and-place tasks and lack a systematic framework for measuring progress in robot learning along the axis of task difficulty. We present ManiLadder, a large-scale and organized simulation benchmark for robotic manipulation. ManiLadder contains 112 carefully designed tasks stratified into 4 difficulty levels, with 8 categories in each level, spanning rigid-body and deformable-object manipulation, single-arm and dual-arm settings, and gripper and dexterous-hand end-effectors. To calibrate difficulty, we fix the data amount the same for every task and use a unified flow- matching imitation learning policy under the same training and evaluation protocols, then use its evaluation success rate as an operational empirical difficulty signal. All tasks are iteratively refined until they fall into target difficulty ranges, which are then verified across different random seeds, policies, and agentic learning systems. We further analyze the task properties, compare different policy performances and training settings, analyze task transfer and data scaling behaviors, and conduct real-world experiments showing that the designed tasks preserve their difficulty ordering beyond simulation. ManiLad- der provides a calibrated ladder for measuring, comparing, and advancing robotic manipulation capabilities. More results are available at https://maniladder-benchmark.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: ManiLadder: Benchmarking Robot Manipulation Through a Categorized and Multi-Difficulty Level Task Ladder

evidence_items.summary: The short duration of general insurance contracts leads to rapid distributional shifts in the data, warranting regular model updates. This process may yield a post-update model that differs considerably from the pre-update model in both predictions and structure. Structural stability is upstream of predictive stability, yet existing structural stability metrics are mostly restricted to simple decision trees. Thus, we first introduce the notion of functional transparency, characterising models with a prediction function that can be expressed as a sum of univariate functions for main effects and bivariate functions for pairwise interactions. Then, we propose the Mean Squared Shape function distance, a metric to quantify the structural stability of functionally transparent models, which are particularly relevant in actuarial science. Using three public auto insurance datasets, we present a benchmark study to demonstrate the usefulness of our metric in identifying a stable and accurate transparent model. Generalised linear models with centred numerical covariates are stable, and explainable boosting machines (EBMs) offer a compromise between stability and performance. We also find that stabilisation strategies, such as sequential modelling and fixed hyperparameters, can substantially improve stability for both EBM and XGBoost models, with negligible impact on performance.
evidence_items.title: Quantifying structural stability of transparent models for general insurance pricing

evidence_items.summary: External trial evidence can inform oncology trial design, but broad pooling may produce benchmarks poorly aligned with the planned population. We developed TRACE (Target-Trial Relevance Assessment and Compatibility-Guided Evidence Synthesis), combining eligibility screening, Bayesian compatibility assessment using published baseline characteristics, and hierarchical survival modeling. An integrated compatibility score based on the largest standardized difference in jointly reported characteristics identifies compatible external trials. Their reconstructed control-arm survival data are synthesized using a hierarchical beta-Stacy process to generate a predictive survival benchmark. We evaluated TRACE using eleven randomized phase III trials in first-line HER2-negative advanced gastric/gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma. With KEYNOTE-859 as the target, three external trials were selected. TRACE predicted a control-arm median overall survival of 11.8 months (95% posterior predictive interval, 8.9-15.2), compared with an observed median of 11.8 months (95% confidence interval, 10.9-12.7). In leave-one-trial-out validation, seven targets had compatible external evidence. Predictive intervals contained the observed median for all seven. In comparison, confidence intervals from Kaplan-Meier estimates pooling all other trials'control arms contained it for five. Mean pointwise curve coverage was 92% for TRACE and 59% for pooled Kaplan-Meier. For four targets without compatible external evidence, TRACE returned a weakly informative prior predictive benchmark. TRACE provides a transparent approach to selecting relevant external evidence and generating benchmarks for oncology trial planning.
evidence_items.title: TRACE: Target-Trial Relevance Assessment and Compatibility-Guided Evidence Synthesis

evidence_items.summary: To overcome the challenges arising from strong nonlinearity, complex multi-factor coupling, and the limited interpretability of conventional methods for blast-induced peak particle velocity (PPV) estimation, a hybrid model integrating a multi-strategy improved greylag goose optimization (MSGGO) algorithm with random forest (RF) is proposed. The MSGGO algorithm is developed by incorporating multiple enhancement strategies into the standard greylag goose optimization (GGO) framework, which enhances its ability to perform global exploration while improving convergence behavior. MSGGO is subsequently used to optimize the RF hyperparameters to enhance PPV prediction performance. Comparative experiments on 12 benchmark functions demonstrate that MSGGO generally achieves favorable convergence accuracy and stability compared with GGO, SOA, GJO, WMA, and RBMO. Using 119 sets of field-measured data from mining operations, a series of RF models optimized by different algorithms are constructed. Further comparisons with conventional models, including RF, BPNN, and SVR, as well as the USBM and Ambraseys empirical formulas, indicate that the MSGGO-RF model yields the most favorable results on the test dataset (R² = 0.9641, RMSE = 0.3100, MAE = 0.2574), demonstrating high prediction accuracy. SHAP analysis reveals that DBM is the most influential variable governing PPV response, accounting for 59.5% of the model contribution, and it shows a strong inverse relationship with PPV. The remaining variables mainly exhibit nonlinear effects. Overall, the MSGGO-RF model achieves high predictive accuracy while preserving good model interpretability, offering a reliable basis for precise predictive modeling and safety management in blasting operations.
evidence_items.title: Assessment of blast-induced peak particle velocity using random forest optimized by multi-strategy greylag goose algorithm

evidence_items.summary: This study examined the relationship between World Bank-assisted intervention projects and the economic development of selected communities in Imo State, Nigeria. The study population comprised 115,465 residents across ten communities that had benefited from intervention projects. Using Taro Yamane's formula with a 6% margin of error, a sample of 278 respondents was selected; 253 completed questionnaires were returned. Primary data were collected through a structured questionnaire using a four-point Likert scale. Item responses were summarised using mean scores and compared with a criterion mean of 2.50. Ordinary least squares regression was used to examine associations between community economic development and four intervention dimensions: poverty reduction, educational infrastructure, rural development and health infrastructure. The reported coefficients were positive for poverty reduction (B = 0.262), educational infrastructure (B = 1.050) and health infrastructure (B = 0.328), but negative for rural development (B = −0.219). All four coefficients were reported as statistically significant at the 5% level. These findings suggest associations between selected intervention dimensions and perceived community economic development; however, substantial multicollinearity and inconsistencies in some reported response totals limit the strength of the conclusions. Improved project monitoring, community participation and transparent evaluation are recommended.
evidence_items.title: IMPACT OF WORLD BANK ASSISTED INTERVENTION PROJECTS ON THE ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT OF COMMUNITIES IN IMO STATE, NIGERIA

evidence_items.summary: Building-level dataset of exterior entrance accessibility for sidewalk delivery robots in Manhattan, New York City. It links the 44,319 buildings recorded as constructed in the NYC building footprint data to tax-lot, address and sidewalk data. For 6,952 buildings in seven neighbourhoods, Google Street View images of the entrance were annotated by a multimodal model for visible stairs, gates and ramps; every model-reported gate or ramp was checked by a human reviewer, and an accessibility label was derived with a transparent rule. A logistic model on non-visual attributes provides an accessibility probability for every building, with bootstrap intervals and extrapolation flags, in two versions (labels with human review; labels from the model alone). The archive contains the data records, one data dictionary per record, the blind human validation and review annotations, the model outputs and prompt, and the Manhattan subsets of the NYC Open Data inputs. Street View images are not redistributed. Code: https://github.com/lorenzorubrichi/Building-Level-AMR-Accessibility-in-Manhattan

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT: Plant-based sunscreens are gaining attention as natural alternatives to synthetic UV-protective agents due to their safety and environmental benefits. Exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation can cause skin damage, premature ageing, inflammation, and skin cancer. Plant-derived phytochemicals, including flavonoids, polyphenols, carotenoids, and tannins, offer potential UV protection through their antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. This study explores the use of plant extracts in sunscreen formulations, focusing on SPF, UV absorption, antioxidant activity, and formulation stability. It also examines the role of biocompatible nanoparticles in improving the delivery and effectiveness of natural photoprotective compounds. These plant-based formulations may provide a promising approach to developing effective and environmentally friendly sunscreens.
evidence_items.title: Plant-Derived Sunscreens: Phytochemistry, Formulation Science, Evaluation, And Emerging Therapeutic Applications

evidence_items.summary: This paper explores the evolution of localization research within Translation Studies and examines how emerging AI technologies are reshaping multilingual digital communi-cation. Through a retrospective analysis of the author’s research career, the paper maps key developments in the study of localization and its evolution through the impact of crowdsourcing and translation technologies from the early 2000s to the present AI era. The discussion highlights how localization practices challenged traditional translation models by introducing new workflows, digital genres, and collaborative environments that required novel theoretical and methodological approaches (e.g. corpus-based transla-tion studies, mixed-methods research, and socio-cognitive perspectives). It also addresses the growing integration of AI-driven tools such as machine translation, large language models, AI dubbing, and automated localization management systems into professional localization workflows. Special attention is devoted to Human-Centered AI as a promis-ing framework for balancing automation with human autonomy, professional expertise, and user needs. The paper argues that future localization research must engage critically with ethical, social, and linguistic dimensions of AI, particularly regarding low-resource languages, digital inclusion, and equitable access to multilingual digital content.
evidence_items.title: Where digital worlds and translation studies collide: from localization to AI and beyond

evidence_items.summary: This dataset accompanies the study Global urban nighttime radiance trends within fixed boundaries. It provides the city registry, numerical results and analysis code for annual satellite radiance trends from 2015 to 2023 within fixed urban boundaries observed in 2015. The registry covers 10,333 eligible urban centres and distinguishes the 10,330 centres with estimable trajectories from centres without complete trajectories. It records comparison-product availability, the primary trend classifications, alternative multiple-testing rules and seasonal sensitivity. The numerical workbook contains the results supporting the main and supplementary tables. The code archive includes frozen city-level extracts, model-ready data, analytical programs, figure-generation scripts, data dictionaries and source documentation. These materials support offline reproduction from the supplied extracts. Optional extraction scripts document how the satellite and population inputs were obtained through Google Earth Engine. The main outcome is annual VIIRS radiance aggregated using fixed 2015 population weights within each urban footprint. The comparisons use annual Earth Observation Group composites and the VIIRS-like series distributed as SRUNet. The study years fall within the observed annual VIIRS segment of that longer series. The demographic analysis relates radiance trajectories to older population share in 2010 and population change from 2000 to 2010. City-level classifications, comparison coverage and seasonal checks are supplied so that the aggregate results can be examined for individual urban centres and regions. The archive includes provider-attributed Global Human Settlement Layer source tables and urban geometry and a Natural Earth cartographic basemap. The global satellite and population rasters and proprietary fonts are not redistributed. Their sources, access instructions and reuse notices are documented in THIRD PARTY NOTICES.md and the replication instructions.
evidence_items.title: Global urban nighttime radiance trends within fixed boundaries: city registry, numerical results and analysis code

evidence_items.summary: Analysis code, intermediate result tables, supplementary tables and docking inputs for the manuscript "Division of labour in the gut–heart axis: gut-metabolite receptors occupy the non-myocyte compartment of the diabetic heart, while the cardiomyocyte carries the metabolic response" . The record contains 23 Python and R scripts, 37 result tables, the fourteen supplementary tables supplied to the journal, and the AutoDock Vina inputs and nine-pose outputs for 65 docking runs. Raw data are not redistributed: they are publicly available from NCBI GEO under accessions GSE4745, GSE6880, GSE5606, GSE267352, GSE213337, GSE116250 and GSE288708. A further human single-nucleus dataset, GSE183852, was retrieved but is not used for any inference and is therefore not listed as a source. Two corrections to the authors' own first-pass results are documented in README section 6: ligand efficiencies had been under-reported nine-fold because non-hydrogen atoms were counted across all nine Vina binding modes rather than the first, and a fixed-effect fatty-acid beta-oxidation association was withdrawn after random-effects pooling showed I-squared of 90 percent. A large language-model assistant (WorkBuddy, Tencent, desktop version 5.9.3) was used to generate and debug the analysis code and to assist with language editing; all numerical results were verified by the authors against the files in results/ . Version history. Version 1.0.0 still carried a DOI placeholder in the bundled CITATION.cff and README.md , because the archive had been packed before the DOI was issued; version 1.0.1 filled that placeholder in; version 1.0.2 points every DOI field at the concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24218227 , so that a citation of this record keeps resolving to the newest version. No analysis file, result table or docking output differs across the three versions.
evidence_items.title: Division of labour in the gut–heart axis: analysis code, result tables and supplementary data

evidence_items.summary: A new document counts as a win against a challenger if the frozen agent prefers the leading answer more strongly on this document than on the matched retrieval. Only the ordering of the two leader–challenger score gaps matters. With the answers, matching rule, and block length fixed before retrieval, the number of wins among non-tied pairs can be tested at a predetermined checkpoint. Checkpoint Sign Audit uses an exact one-sided sign test at the end of the block. Every challenger must lose its test before the agent returns the leading answer. If the leader changes or a new challenger appears, the agent discards the unfinished block and registers another comparison on fresh material. A total error allowance distributed across all registered blocks, including discarded ones, and evenly split among challengers in each block limits the chance of rejecting any true null provided the non-tied signs under that null are conditionally independent fair coins given the registration history and tie pattern. Near the stopping threshold, CSA measures how much this margin decreases when individual sources are removed from a small evidence bundle and increases the required margin when support is concentrated in one source. We outline a comparison with reading the same sign statistic after every retrieval at the same nominal allowance, using a fixed corpus and open-web search. Grouping searches by the frequency of leader changes would let us compare premature certification, answer accuracy, search calls, cost, and the number of additional sources read before a decision.
evidence_items.title: Matched Sign Tests for Adaptive Stopping a Long-Horizon Search Agent at Fixed Checkpoints

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly part of everyday life, yet there is no established way to measure how users evaluate their trustworthiness. This study introduces the Perceived Trustworthiness of LLMs scale (PT-LLM-8), a self-report psychometric instrument measuring users’ perceived trustworthiness of their primary LLM. PT-LLM-8 is developed from the TrustLLM framework and adapted as a human-centred measure. The PT-LLM-8 comprises eight items representing truthfulness, safety, fairness, robustness, privacy, transparency, accountability, and compliance with laws. Psychometric properties of the scale were tested with 752 LLM users in the United Kingdom (Mean age = 28.58, SD = 6.11, 50.3% males, 48.8% females). Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported a one-factor structure, with high internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.90, Composite Reliability = 0.91, strong item-total correlations (ranged between 0.62 and 0.75), and measurement invariance across gender. The total score measures overall perceived trustworthiness, while individual item responses may also be examined descriptively for information about the content represented by each item. For researchers, practitioners, and developers, the PT-LLM-8 offers a practical instrument for evaluating interventions, comparing groups and contexts, and examining whether technical safeguards are reflected in users’ perceived trustworthiness of LLM. The scale can also be applied to guide system design, support policy development, and help organisations monitor shifts in user trust toward LLMs over time, making it applicable across research, practice, and governance.
evidence_items.title: Development and validation of a scale assessing perceived trustworthiness in large language models
