evidence_items.summary: The development of foundation models that learn a general grammar of DNA (DNA language models) has accelerated in recent years. The vast majority of DNA large language models (LLMs), such as DNABERT-2 and Nucleotide Transformer, are pretrained almost exclusively on reference genomes. They therefore cannot represent the two sources of variation most directly tied to regulatory differences between people: genetic variants and DNA methylation. Long-read sequencing (Nanopore and PacBio) now measures both from the same native DNA molecules, but no model is designed to use this joint readout. With this in mind, we developed ModBERT, a DNA language model built on a five-letter probabilistic genome representation in which each position is a distribution over A, C, G, T, 5mC (represented with M). In pretraining, these distributions encode population allele frequencies and CpG methylation levels from 242 individuals in the 1000 Genomes Long-Read Sequencing Consortium, learned with a soft-target masked language modeling objective. We further propose probabilistic fine-tuning, in which the same representation encodes one individual's genotype and methylation. A fine-tuned model can then make person-specific predictions from a single assay. Under this novel fine-tuning framework, we show that ModBERT effectively utilizes methylation information to classify peaks from functional genomic assays, including histone mark (n=11 different marks) and transcription factor binding (n=69 TFs) ChIP-seq data, outperforming ab initio trained models and ModBERT pretrained on sequences without methylation. In silico methylation perturbations yield TF sensitivities that correlate with independent methylation-aware motif models. Using an evaluation design that separates generalization to new loci from generalization to new individuals, ModBERT predicts chromatin accessibility at held-out loci in held-out individuals (AUROC 0.88).
evidence_items.title: ModBERT: a DNA modification and genetic variant-aware DNA large language model

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Discharge instructions are an important component of the transition from hospital to home for patients with diabetic kidney disease (DKD), whose care often involves multiple comorbidities, medications, and stage-specific management needs. However, producing complete, accurate, clear, and personalized instructions can be challenging for junior physicians. Objective This study aimed to evaluate whether large language model (LLM) assistance improves the quality of DKD discharge instructions produced by junior physicians and whether its benefits vary according to chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage. Methods The study included 101 hospitalized patients with DKD. Discharge instructions for each patient were initially drafted by a group of junior residents (resident group); subsequently, another group of residents at the same level, with the assistance of DeepSeek-V3.2 (AI-assisted group), generated a separate set of discharge instructions for the same 101 patients, resulting in a total of 202 documents. Four clinical experts, including 2 nephrologists and 2 endocrinologists, independently scored both versions of the discharge instructions using a 5-point Likert scale across 5 dimensions: completeness, accuracy, safety, clarity, and personalization. Interrater reliability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Results Interrater reliability was excellent in both the resident group (ICC=0.817, 95% CI 0.763‐0.864; P <.001) and the AI-assisted group (ICC=0.860, 95% CI 0.816‐0.897; P <.001). Compared with resident-only instructions, AI-assisted instructions received significantly higher scores across 5 evaluation dimensions and the overall evaluation (all Bonferroni-adjusted P <.001), with large effect sizes ( r =0.741‐0.927).
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model–Assisted Discharge Instructions for Diabetic Kidney Disease: Comparative Evaluation Study

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The Evo2 Variant Effect Database (Evo2VED; https://dnallmved.org/) is a publicly accessible resource cataloging precomputed Evo2-derived variant effect scores, defined as allelic score differences, for 6.48 million human variants common in the gnomAD non-Finnish European population. Evo2VED includes scores from the 7B and 40B models under three scoring schemes, alongside annotations of variant function, evolutionary constraint, allele age, and disease associations. It integrates genome-wide association study (GWAS) data from UK Biobank, FinnGen, and the Million Veteran Program. Three complementary modules support variant-level interpretation, regional and region-set exploration, and trait-level analysis through flexible queries, interactive visualizations, and downloadable results. Evo2VED also catalogs associations between Evo2 annotations and per-SNP heritability across thousands of traits from these biobanks. A guided workflow connects GWAS with associated regions and individual variant evidence. Case studies of hypertension and depression illustrate how regional comparisons of Evo2 scores and GWAS signals can guide candidate variant prioritization. Evaluations using massively parallel reporter assays, molecular QTLs, fine-mapping probabilities, and clinical annotations assess associations with Evo2 scores alone and their added value beyond conservation and regulatory annotations. By providing accessible scores, contextual annotations, and comparative analyses, Evo2VED facilitates exploration and application of genomic language model predictions in human genetics research.
evidence_items.title: Evo2VED: a database of DNA large language model-derived scores for variant interpretation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Autoscalers for large language model (LLM) inference clusters that add capacity when a predicted overload probability crosses a threshold depend on the probability scale, not only on the ranking. This simulation study evaluates five such predictors under sparse telemetry and runtime anomalies on two latent-state generators and a request-level serving simulator with queueing, service-level objectives (SLOs), startup delay, and modeled power. With 3-period instead of 50-period histories, models trained on long histories became overconfident (expected calibration error up to 0.099) or conservative, whereas a Markov filter stayed calibrated and retraining on short histories removed most of the error. Temperature scaling fitted on long histories did not transfer; refitted for short histories, it cut this error by up to 68.7%, removed all 290 wrong high-confidence predictions of one model by lowering their confidence, and cut the overconfident models' idealized unmitigated overload by 59.8–82.8% at the cost of more idle capacity. With a 20-s startup delay in the request-level simulator, learned predictors used 24.0–25.3% less modeled energy than always-on scale-out, with a 1.0–1.2 percentage-point increase in the SLO-violation rate, and 95.3% of scale-out-induced violations occurred on slow new replicas. Calibration should therefore be validated per telemetry regime and checked against request-level outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Predictive Reliability and Calibration of Workload Autoscaling Models for Large Language Model Inference Clusters Under Sparse Telemetry and Runtime Anomalies

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet reliable long-horizon execution in dynamic environments remains challenging. OpenVLA supports strong task generalization and parameter-efficient adaptation, but its single-image input limits temporal modeling, while its standard framework lacks explicit use of failure experience and runtime recovery mechanisms. To address these limitations, we propose TPRVLA, which integrates temporal memory, preference learning, and closed-loop recovery. A lightweight temporal memory adapter incorporates consecutive observations into the frozen OpenVLA backbone to capture short-term dynamics. Weighted preference pairs are constructed from successful and failed trajectories under similar visual observations and identical instructions. The policy is then adapted through a joint direct preference optimization (DPO) and behavior cloning (BC) objective to favor preferred actions. During execution, a rule-based state monitor combines end-effector motion, action repetition, and visual changes to trigger checkpoint-guided recovery when anomalies persist. Evaluations across 900 rollouts on ten LIBERO Spatial tasks with three random seeds show improved task performance, particularly on tasks requiring extended execution and closed-loop adjustment, while increasing peak GPU memory usage by less than 1%.
evidence_items.title: TPRVLA:Temporal-Preference-Recovery Vision-Language-Action Model

evidence_items.summary: Grid energy storage systems are a trending technology, attracting researchers due to their significant market and need. An update is essential for this technology, as it has several drawbacks, such as improper charging, high cost, resource limitations, and weak grid stability. To overcome these drawbacks, this study presents a Solar PV system with grid stability (SPGSEV) model. This model integrates core modules, such as mobility and charging systems, charging stations, and a solar-powered photovoltaic system with battery storage and PV modules. The grid stability management system is developed to achieve effective resource utilization and, with the Multi-Objective Remora Optimization Algorithm (MOROA), to support proper decision-making and charge scheduling. The overall framework is implemented in MATLAB, and the parameters measured for result analysis include Electricity Price, Voltage, PVs Capacity, PVs Output Power, Power Loss, Voltage Magnitude, and Stay Time. The results are also compared with earlier models such as EMEVC, OEPSM, and EVESS. The outcome proves the stability of the proposed model by attaining lower loss and high PV output power, which leads to maximum energy utilization and grid stability for the energy storage systems.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Energy Management in Grid Energy Storage Systems: Design and Performance Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Widely accessible generative artificial intelligence has unsettled long held assumptions about how learning can be measured and trusted. Tools capable of producing fluent essays, functional code, and plausible solutions on demand have exposed the fragility of evaluation models that reward the unsupervised production of polished artifacts. This paper argues that the appropriate institutional response is not an escalating contest between detection software and evasion techniques, but a deliberate redesign of evaluation around authentic human competency. Drawing on established scholarship in authentic assessment, constructive alignment, and formative feedback, the paper develops a five-principle framework for evaluation that remains meaningful when capable AI is freely available. The framework shifts emphasis from the finished product toward the reasoning process, foregrounds contextual judgment that machines cannot convincingly simulate, distributes evidence of competency across a program rather than isolated high stakes events, treats AI as a declared and scrutinized instrument rather than prohibited contraband, and grounds security in thoughtful design rather than pervasive surveillance. Common assessment formats are appraised for their resilience, and implementation challenges relating to staff workload, equity of access, and institutional policy are examined. The paper concludes that the disruption introduced by generative AI, although genuinely destabilizing, presents an overdue opportunity to align evaluation with the competencies that human learners must actually develop, and to recover the formative purpose of assessment that narrow integrity policing has long obscured.
evidence_items.title: Assessment Integrity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Redesigning Learning Evaluation for Authentic Human Competency

evidence_items.summary: Emergency radiology operates at the intersection of high imaging volumes, time-critical diagnoses, and persistent workforce shortages, making it one of the most promising yet demanding environments for artificial intelligence (AI) deployment. This narrative review critically appraises the evidence on AI in emergency radiology, emphasizing diagnostic accuracy, workflow efficiency, and the strength of the underlying evidence. We searched PubMed for peer-reviewed literature published between January 2015 and August 2026 using a structured, reproducible strategy, and we classified key studies by design and outcome level. Deep learning algorithms approach expert-level performance in retrospective and reader-study settings for several high-stakes conditions, including intracranial hemorrhage (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve up to 0.991), acute pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, and skeletal fractures, for which a multicenter multireader diagnostic accuracy study found that AI assistance increased reader sensitivity by 10.4 percentage points and specificity from 90.6% to 95.6%. However, real-world evaluations report substantially lower sensitivity than development studies, and workflow evidence is mixed: in one prospective implementation, head CT studies flagged by AI for intracranial hemorrhage were interpreted sooner than routine studies (median 19 vs. 512 min), whereas a pulmonary embolism notification system produced no measurable turnaround benefit. Deep learning reconstruction can reduce radiation dose, and large language models show early promise for report error detection and communication. Prospective, multisite, patient-outcome evidence remains scarce. AI should be viewed as an augmenting technology whose value in emergency radiology depends on local validation, deliberate workflow integration, and continuous post-deployment monitoring.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in emergency radiology: opportunities, evidence, and limitations

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) sovereignty is often associated with domestically controlled infrastructure, data localisation and nationally developed models. Such measures may be valuable, but they cannot by themselves preserve public authority when consequential functions rely on AI systems that institutions cannot adequately inspect, constrain, challenge, evaluate or replace. This Perspective distinguishes ordinary technological interdependence from algorithmic dependence and proposes governed interdependence as a more practicable sovereignty objective for resource-constrained states. Drawing on scholarship on technological sovereignty and public-sector AI governance, together with documented policy developments in Somalia, we identify five tests of meaningful public control: legibility, enforceability, contestability, reversibility and independent evaluative capability. For Somalia, these tests suggest three priorities: a risk-tiered register of consequential public-sector AI systems, procurement safeguards that secure oversight and exit rights, and independent Somali-language evaluation connected to accessible human redress. These priorities are prospective policy proposals rather than findings from an empirical assessment of existing government AI deployments. The framework reframes AI sovereignty as the demonstrated capacity to govern dependence, providing a basis for comparative policy analysis and future empirical evaluation in low-resource settings.
evidence_items.title: Governed Interdependence as a Framework for Artificial Intelligence Sovereignty in Somalia

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Background A proportion of Australians encounter substantial unmet oral health needs despite eligibility for government‐subsidised care. Yet, government dental services operate within a fragmented, mixed public‐private system with limited capacity to support priority populations. The National Oral Health Plan (2015–2024) responds to this visible and measured need for priority. As the next National Oral Health Plan is developed, these priorities provide a timely basis to consider whether emerging technologies can support access and system performance without reproducing existing inequities. Methods This narrative review aims to examine the potential uses, evidence for, challenges and implementation considerations of the use of Artificial Intelligence including machine learning, in Australian public‐funded dental services, and to examine the implications for access, equity, governance, community co‐design and workforce capability. The evidence is interpreted through a multidimensional framework for access to care, while retaining the National Oral Health Plan (2015–2024) as the policy context. Conclusions Limited research conducted in Australian‐based healthcare settings shows evidence for public dental system‐level improvements for triage, risk stratification, service planning and workflow, but also identifies material concerns about opportunity cost, human oversight, non‐representative data, algorithmic bias, cultural safety, Indigenous Data Sovereignty and clinician education. Artificial Intelligence and machine learning technologies may support more responsive public‐funded dental services, but technical performance alone is not evidence of improved access or equitable care. Intentional, values‐led implementation requires representative data, Indigenous‐led governance, community co‐design, transparent evaluation, human accountability and a digitally capable workforce.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Australian Public‐Funded Dental Services

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background and Aims A major challenge in dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) care is the identification and management of individuals at risk before disease manifestation. An artificial intelligence (AI) model applied to electrocardiography (ECG) was developed to detect and predict the echocardiographic DCM phenotype (left ventricular dilatation with systolic dysfunction) and was evaluated for its ability to stratify the risk of incident DCM in familial cohorts. Methods A deep learning model was trained to detect the echocardiographic DCM phenotype and to predict its future onset, using more than 330 000 ECG-echocardiogram pairs from the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston. Model performance was validated in cohorts from the UK Biobank, Zhongshan Hospital, and Antwerp University Hospital, and compared with models based on traditional ECG features and echocardiographic traits. To assess performance in familial DCM, genetically predisposed individuals identified through cascade screening at the cardiogenetics clinics of Antwerp University Hospital (n = 166, 18% DCM positive) and Maastricht University Medical Center (n = 177, 18% DCM positive) were evaluated. Results The AI-ECG model achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of .87–.97 for diagnosing the prevalent DCM phenotype, outperforming traditional ECG parameters. AI-ECG was comparable to echocardiography for predicting future DCM (C-index .80–.87 and .80–.90, respectively). In familial cohorts, 5-year negative predictive values were 95.5% (Antwerp) and 91.5% (Maastricht), with corresponding positive predictive values of 42.4% and 39.4%, while high-risk scores were associated with a 5.1–6.4-fold increased risk of incident DCM. Conclusions The explainable AI-ECG model detects the echocardiographic DCM phenotype and predicts future disease, and supports the exclusion of short- to mid-term disease in genetically at-risk individuals.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence-enhanced electrocardiography for detection and prediction of dilated cardiomyopathy

evidence_items.summary: Purpose: This article examines the legal and governance implications of AI-assisted employee performance evaluation in Czech local government. It focuses on how such systems interact with labour law, administrative law principles, data protection requirements, anti-discrimination norms, and the emerging EU framework for high-risk AI systems.Design/Methodology/Approach: The article combines a structured literature review with doctrinal legal analysis and a limited comparative approach. Although interdisciplinary, its primary analytical focus remains legal and regulatory. It examines AI-assisted evaluation tools that process employee-related data to generate classifications, scores, recommendations, or summaries that may support managerial assessments of employee performance.Findings: The analysis shows that Czech law does not expressly regulate AI-assisted employee performance evaluation in local government, which creates uncertainty regarding transparency, accountability, lawful data use, human oversight, and remedies. It further shows that some employee-evaluation systems may fall within the high-risk employment category under the AI Act, in which case enhanced obligations concerning governance, documentation, transparency, and oversight would apply.Practical Implications: Local authorities considering the use of AI-assisted evaluation tools should adopt clear internal rules on permissible data sources, purpose limitation, documentation, explainability, human review, and complaint handling. The article identifies practical safeguards that may reduce legal and organisational risk while preserving AI’s role in supporting, rather than replacing, human judgement in personnel assessment.Academic Contribution to the Field: The article contributes to the literatureby connecting debates on algorithmic management, public administration, and AI regulation to the specific setting of employee evaluation in local government.
evidence_items.title: Using Artificial Intelligence in the Performance Evaluation of Local Government Employees

evidence_items.summary: Background Intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) has becoming indispensable for ensuring safety and efficacy during atrial fibrillation (AF) ablation. However, ICE interpretation remains highly observer-dependent, presenting a steep learning curve in rapidly distinguishing complex, dynamic cardiac structures. Objectives This study aimed to develop and validate a multi-task deep learning system (AI-ICE) for real-time, automated interpretation of cardiac structures and ultrasound views during AF ablation. Methods The interpretation task is defined as two sub-tasks, one for detecting 12 anatomical structures and the other for classifying 5 standard views. A total of 373,091 ICE images from 350 patients undergoing AF ablation across three centers were collected. The dataset was split into training/internal validation cohorts (two centers) and an independent external testing cohort (one center, 35,335 frames). The AI-ICE model combined a ResUnet backbone with an LSTM module to capture spatiotemporal dependencies across consecutive frames, reflecting the streaming nature of real-time clinical ICE imaging. The two tasks were formulated as a multi-task coupled framework with shared representations, exploiting the intrinsic interdependence between the imaging view and the visible anatomy. Results For the internal validation, the average AUC for classifying ultrasound views and detecting structures reached 0.971 (95% CI: 0.947–0.992) and 0.974 (95% CI: 0.968–0.980). For the external validation, the AI-ICE system achieved an AUC of 0.984 (95% CI: 0.974–0.993) for ultrasound view classification and 0.955 (95% CI: 0.948–0.962) for anatomical structure objection. Compared with three cardiologist experts, it achieved higher accuracy (AUC: 0.941 vs. 0.916) and superior inter-rater agreement (Kappa coefficient: 0.791 vs. 0.716). Additionally, the system demonstrated high efficiency, with an inference time of 12 milliseconds per ICE image.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence for intracardiac echocardiography interpretation and guidance during atrial fibrillation ablation

evidence_items.summary: Backpropagation has been the dominant credit-assignment mechanism behind the deep-learning revolution, yet it is global, memory-hungry, biologically implausible, and costly on hardware dominated by data movement. In parallel, predictive coding, equilibrium propagation, contrastive Hebbian learning and forward-only schemes have shown that useful credit assignment can also arise from local variables and the relaxation of an energy function. This manuscript is a review with a reproducible benchmark, not a proposal of a new learning rule. We organise existing backpropagation-free methods and continual-learning strategies under a common Local Equilibrium Learning (LEL) formulation, re-validate the core theoretical links numerically, and use a controlled continual-learning benchmark as an auditable case study within the review. The theoretical contribution is unification and verification, not priority over predictive coding, equilibrium propagation or replay. The empirical contribution is diagnostic rather than exhaustive: a benchmark of catastrophic forgetting with local networks that makes the review reproducible. We compare regularisation (EWC, SI), noise replay and generative “dreaming” across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 in two independent implementations. Generative replay with local generators turns class-incremental Split-MNIST forgetting (chance level, the same as EWC and SI) into 86.8±0.2%, which is 96% of the joint-training ceiling and 97.4% in the task-incremental setting; the same mechanism reaches 82.0% on Fashion-MNIST and 37.0% on CIFAR-10. A matched control that holds the retention mechanism fixed and swaps only the learning rule shows that backpropagation with the same generative replay reaches a comparable or slightly higher accuracy than LEL (90.3% vs.

evidence_items.summary: When using the in situ nylon bag technique to evaluate rumen degradation characteristics, if the microbial contamination in the nylon bag residue is not corrected, the degradation rate of roughage nitrogen in rumen will be underestimated. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to determine the bacterial contamination of roughages during in situ rumen culture, and to establish an equation for predicting microbial contamination of rumen culture residue. Using the nylon bag technique, a total of 30 roughages was incubated in the rumen of four Zhaowuda meat sheep. (15NH4)2SO4 was continuously infused into the rumen, and then pellets of labeled rumen solids-associated bacteria (SAB) and rumen liquid-associated bacteria (LAB) were isolated by differential centrifugation of samples of ruminal contents. The rumen degradation rate of 24 kinds of roughage nitrogen was significantly increased after microbial correction (p < 0.05), six kinds of roughage nitrogen species were increased in numerical value although there was no significant difference (p > 0.05), and there was no difference between the two labeling methods of SAB and LAB. Except for imported alfalfa hay (AH), the course of bacterial contamination of 29 roughages was described by an exponential function of the general type Ncont. = Nmax [1 − exp(−C·t)], where Nmax varied with the feed’s nutritional composition. Separate prediction models were established for straw roughages, hay roughages, and all 29 roughages combined, incorporating crude protein (CP), neutral detergent fiber (NDF), acid detergent fiber (ADF), dry matter (DM), and organic matter (OM) to estimate Nmax. The results confirm that microbial contamination systematically biases nylon bag measurements, causing a consistent underestimation of true ruminal nitrogen degradability, especially for high-fiber, low-protein feeds.
evidence_items.title: Development of Equations to Estimate Microbial Nitrogen Contamination of In Situ Roughage Residues

evidence_items.summary: Agentic healthcare platforms that combine large language models with physician oversight are growing quickly, but little is known about who uses them. We characterized 3,223 enrollees of Lotus AI, a free, physician-supervised agentic platform, who completed onboarding, messaged the agent, and had a linked health record between February and July 2026, and compared them with national benchmarks. Median age was 51 years and 62% were male. Chronic condition prevalence exceeded 2024 National Health Interview Survey estimates in every age band by 4 to 7 percentage points; 18% had a functional or symptom-defined disorder; among the 30% with four or more ambulatory visits in the prior year, care was spread across nearly five providers, with 44% meeting a threshold for high fragmentation. Users with functional disorders generated 1.8 times as many physician escalations and 2.6 times as many laboratory orders as other users, but no more prescriptions. This profile differs from the younger, predominantly female populations reported for direct-to-consumer telemedicine. It moves chronic disease management, functional disorder pathways, and care coordination from aspirations to design requirements, and we argue that deployed AI care platforms should characterize their populations against national benchmarks early.
evidence_items.title: Enrollees and Early Lessons from an Agentic Healthcare Platform with Physicians in the Loop

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Kernel-level rootkits subvert the operating system to conceal the network ports through which they maintain covert channels, and cloud tenants who cannot access the hypervisor have few reliable defences. Existing detectors stop at a verdict, leaving investigation and response to human analysts and admitting a window during which an active rootkit persists. This paper presents an agentic AI framework that both detects and autonomously responds to kernel rootkits through port-level behavioural analysis. On cloud guests hosted on Google Cloud Platform, a kernel-mode Port Enumerator and a user-mode Port Monitor produce cross-view port lists whose discrepancy, formalized here as a temporal behavioural signal, is classified by a deep ensemble of CNN-LSTM, Bi-LSTM, Autoencoder and GAN. The resulting Rootkit/Benign verdict is handed to an LLM Agent Orchestrator that executes an autonomous perceive-plan-act-reflect loop, invoking security tools under human-in-the-loop oversight for high-impact actions. A second evidence channel is released with the paper as a labelled concealment matrix of 87 kernel rootkit samples described by a binary vector over a 968-entry dictionary of concealed objects, each carrying the technique it uses to hide. We give a mathematical model of the cross-view signal, the fused decision, and the agent’s utility-driven action selection. Evaluated on a Windows Server 2025 guest, the framework detects rootkits with a mean detection latency of 1.2 s while autonomously triaging confirmed threats; on the released concealment matrix the technique of a confirmed rootkit is recovered from its hook vector at 0.846 accuracy against a 0.713 majority-class rate, with the three-way distinction among inline, SSDT and IAT concealment still limited by class imbalance. The response layer is specified and instantiated but not yet measured; Section 5.6 states the protocol by which it will be tested.
evidence_items.title: An Agentic AI Framework for Autonomous Cross-View Kernel Rootkit Detection and Response in Cloud Environments

In the present study, the prediction model for compressive strength of plain weave fabric reinforced composites (PWFCs) is developed using an analytical solution for a three-layer laminate [0°/90°/0°] under uniaxial compression (σ

Results are compared with tensile strength predictions from previous studies, and both Tsai-Hill and Tsai-Wu failure criteria are applied and benchmarked against literature values. The results revealed that for the [0°/90°/0°] layup, all compressive loading cases are governed by transverse matrix crushing in the 90° ply. The uniaxial compressive strength (136–144 MPa) is only 22–23% of the tensile strength (617 MPa). This large tension–compression asymmetry arises from the low transverse compressive strength (140 MPa) combined with stress concentration in the 90° layer. Further, under biaxial compression, failure occurs at just 28–33 MPa — a 77–80% reduction from uniaxial compressive strength and a 95% reduction from the tensile benchmark. Tsai-Wu predicts 5–14% lower failure loads than Tsai-Hill under compressive loading. The [0°/90°/0°] stacking is poorly optimized for compressive or biaxial loading; incorporating ±45° plies is recommended to improve biaxial compressive performance.

evidence_items.summary: Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) is a marine energy technology that utilizes the temperature difference between surface seawater and deep seawater to generate electricity. One of the main components in this system is the Cold Water Pipe (CWP), which functions to transport cold seawater from deep ocean layers to the power generation system. The long pipe structure with a large diameter-to-thickness ratio makes it susceptible to bending deformation. This study aims to analyze the effect of geometric imperfections on the bending capacity of CWP pipes using the Finite Element Method (FEM). The numerical model was validated through a benchmarking process against a bending formulation, with a deviation of 2.64%. A parametric study was conducted on circumferential imperfections in the form of sinusoidal waves with variations in amplitude and number of waves. The results show that increasing imperfection amplitude reduces the bending capacity, while increasing the number of waves tends to increase the ultimate moment value. This behavior is likely related to the denser wave distribution along the longitudinal direction of the pipe, which may create a local stiffness effect similar to a stiffener element, thereby improving the structural resistance against bending deformation. Variations in imperfection configuration result in changes in the UM value of up to 24.1%, indicating that imperfection characteristics have a significant influence on the bending response of the CWP structure.
evidence_items.title: Numerical Study on the Bending Behavior of OTEC Cold Water Pipes Considering Geometric Imperfections

evidence_items.summary: How does data shape language model (LM) behavior throughout pretraining? We investigate this question through a case study on entity comparison, e.g., Between France and Brazil, which country is larger?, across nine comparison tasks spanning five entity types. We begin with controlled experiments in which we train small LMs (163M parameters) on mixtures of natural text from pretraining corpora and synthetic task data. Our analysis identifies three distinct phases of learning: (1) an early phase where the LM selects entities by frequency, (2) a middle phase where the LM selects entities by position in the prompt (first vs. last mentioned entity), and (3) a late phase where the LM selects the entity that is the correct answer. We show that the emergence of these three phases is causally determined by statistical properties of the training data. With small amounts of task-specific synthetic data, we observe only the first two phases and the model fails to learn the task; with large amounts, the model jumps directly from the frequency-based heuristic to solving the task correctly. Moreover, changing the entity frequency distribution from a naturally occurring Zipfian distribution (a small number of entities are very common and the vast majority are rare) to a uniform one weakens the frequency phase and speeds up learning of the task. Lastly, we show that the three phases of training dynamics from our controlled experiments appear in the open source model OLMo-2 32B. Together, our findings demonstrate that properties of pretraining data are causal drivers of heuristic learning and show that small-scale synthetic experiments can predict training dynamics at larger scales.
evidence_items.title: Pretraining Data Statistics Shape the Phases of Learning Entity Comparison in Language Models

evidence_items.summary: The neural network model is used to estimate the permeate flux during the crossflow microfiltration process of aqueous solutions containing guar and xanthan gums at temperatures of 25°C and 40°C. For the simulations, membrane type, solution composition, filtration time, temperature, transmembrane pressure, and flow velocity were used as input variables. The model, developed in Python using the TensorFlow library, achieved an average percentage error of 2.71% for the training dataset and 5.79% for the test dataset. In addition, a graphical user interface (GUI) was developed using the Glade library, allowing users to easily and efficiently obtain permeate flux values.

evidence_items.summary: Contamination on outdoor substation insulators changes surface reflectance and, after moisture activation, produces nonuniform Joule heating. A single image band therefore provides condition-dependent evidence and can confuse light contamination with illumination variation or material aging. This study presents a multispectral gated cross-attention classifier (MS-GCA) that combines registered red-green-blue (RGB), near-infrared (NIR), and long-wave infrared (LWIR) images. The method employs multiscale modality encoders, shared-parameter iterative cross-attention, reliability gates, spectral-consistency regularization, and entropy-based uncertainty reporting. A physics-guided benchmark containing 6,000 aligned triplets was constructed from 500 distinct insulator geometries under three environmental states and four contamination grades; geometry identities were separated among training, validation, and test partitions. On the 1,200-triplet test set, MS-GCA achieved 96.8% accuracy, 96.7% macro-F1, and 99.2% macro-area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, while requiring 18.6 million parameters and 12.7 ms per triplet. The method exceeded a strong iterative cross-attention baseline by 1.1 percentage points in macro-F1 and retained 91.4% macro-F1 under an eight-pixel residual registration error. These results support multispectral classification as a robust decision-support component for inspection scheduling, while field calibration and prospective substation validation remain necessary before operational deployment.
evidence_items.title: Multispectral image classification algorithm for contamination monitoring of substation insulators

evidence_items.summary: Smaller language models (SLMs) make it feasible to deploy clinical natural language processing where large proprietary models are too costly, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning allows them to be specialised on commodity hardware. One obstacle persists after training: on medical tasks these models answer at far greater length than the clinical question requires. In clinical decision support and point-of-care use, where time is short, such verbosity is hard to act on even when the underlying reasoning is sound. Existing length-control methods depend on preference optimisation, reward models, or proprietary teachers that undercut the accessibility making SLMs attractive. We introduce Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation (PECA), which adds a single differentiable conciseness term to the QLoRA supervised fine-tuning objective. Because the token count is discrete and non-differentiable, PECA instead raises the end-of-sequence probability once generation exceeds a token budget, a smooth signal optimised during ordinary training, with no preference data, no auxiliary model, and a single commodity GPU. On a 1.7-billion-parameter model fine-tuned on the medical-o1-reasoning-SFT corpus, PECA reduces mean response length by 72.8% while improving multiple-choice diagnostic accuracy from 40.8% to 44.0%. A sweep over the conciseness strength traces an interpretable accuracy-to-length frontier for balancing brevity and diagnostic completeness.
evidence_items.title: Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation: Differentiable Length Control for Concise Clinical Reasoning in Smaller Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Large foundation models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 have recently been shown to control robots directly from visual observations. They nevertheless remain brittle on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks in real-world environments. Further progress depends on two complementary resources: demonstrations of human behavior that supervise how tasks are performed, and interactive environments in which policies can be rolled out, evaluated, and improved in closed loop. Language models have advanced along well-characterized scaling laws; the corresponding question for physical AI is how capability scales with environments and behaviors, which first requires identifying which data to scale and how to produce and reuse such data continuously. To address this question, we introduce Ropedia Xperience 2, comprising 1,589 released metric-scale 3D scans and a collection of 4,230 egocentric recordings of 74 tasks (131 hours). We further show that each capture can be repurposed for robot learning: scenes are converted into physically interactive simulation environments, human motion is retargeted to whole-body robot trajectories, and additional robot behaviors are obtained through virtual teleoperation and automated long-horizon trajectory generation. We propose this joint capture of environments and behaviors as a gold standard for physical AI data collection, laying a data foundation for establishing scaling laws over environments and behaviors.
evidence_items.title: Ropedia Xperience 2: A Gold Standard for Scaling Physical AI Environments and Behaviors

evidence_items.summary: Decision models answer a question with a typed output, such as a choice among options with a probability for each, so one model can choose an agent's actions, evaluate actions already taken, or score every action to teach a policy with reinforcement learning. Prior work has studied them mainly as actors, judging their usefulness by how well they act. We ask whether a decision model that acts poorly can still teach well. We compare three decision models and three general LLMs as actors and judges on ALFWorld, and use JEV as a teacher on ALFWorld and WebShop. As actors, all six models are pulled away from a subgoal that must come first by an easier one. As judges that see the whole trajectory, the same models credit the steps toward that subgoal, and asking whether each action helped, rather than whether the task will succeed, separates useful from useless actions. As a teacher, JEV raises a Qwen2.5-1.5B policy over GRPO from 72.8% to 82.9% success on ALFWorld and from 56.8% to 71.4% on WebShop. These results suggest that a poor actor can still teach well, because judging an action after the episode ends reveals the consequences that acting must anticipate. Code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/decision-agents.
evidence_items.title: Actor, Judge, or Teacher? Understanding Decision Models in Long-Horizon Agents

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal coding agents decouple 4D world construction from visual generation, repurposing video models from world generators toward generative renderers. This division of labor raises a fundamental question: if code builds the world, can video models just render it? A reliable generative renderer hinges on two complementary criteria: (i) world preservation, retaining prescribed 4D kinematics and camera paths; and (ii) visual realization, persistently binding text-specified target attributes over time. To evaluate this capability, we introduce WorldDraft, a benchmark of 432 strictly paired test cases across 48 executable 4D world families spanning six dynamic challenge categories. Under a 3 times 3 factorial design, WorldDraft orthogonally crosses draft granularity (abstract proxy to previs) and appearance alignment (neutral to conflicting) under identical dynamics. Extensive evaluations across 12 representative models reveal that: (I) world preservation and visual realization remain in stark operational tension; (II) richer draft scaffolding anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and (III) conflicting source cues trigger severe source leakage (up to 64%), exposing fragile cross-modal disentanglement. To mitigate these bottlenecks, we propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that consistently improves both objectives across frozen video renderers. Together, WorldDraft and WorldDraft-Primer lay a foundation for bridging programmatic 4D simulation with video generation, advancing physically grounded generative rendering.
evidence_items.title: WorldDraft: If Code Builds the World, Can Video Models Just Render It?

evidence_items.summary: GPT-6 Astra can drive a robot arm directly through a fixed harness, and scores of such robot-use agents on RoboDojo have risen quickly since. Reported systems differ in harness and test subset and often change several designs at once, so it is hard to tell which choices produce the gains. We take these designs apart and test them in one framework, along the harness around the model, the action interface, the reuse of experience and the scene geometry given to the model. A lean harness that keeps the full episode history and stops each motion early goes a long way. Reusing experience changes how the model acts but is not a free lunch, and scene geometry helps most, even when depth is predicted from RGB alone. JustRUA starts from the official L3 harness and keeps only what matters most. Even with no learned policy, self-improvement loop or task-specific tuning, this simple harness raises the score on the RoboDojo simulation benchmark substantially, from 29.7 to 50.3.
evidence_items.title: JustRUA: A Controlled Study of GPT-6 Robot-Use Agents

evidence_items.summary: Recent work suggests that pretrained image generators encode real-world understanding beyond image synthesis. Vision Banana exploits this by framing vision tasks as conditional image editing. However, its data, weights, code, and implementation details are not public. We present Open Vision Banana (OVB), a fully open and reproducible recipe for converting pretrained generators into unified multi-task perception systems. Our analyses identify the design choices that matter most for generalization, including color encoding, prompt design, parameter adaptation, and task balancing. These choices interact, so individually helpful choices can hurt when combined with others. Starting from 4B and 9B parameter open-weight base models and using 2.1M-3.8M training pairs from public datasets, OVB surpasses Vision Banana's reported Cityscapes zero-shot performance (73.9 vs. 69.9 mIoU) and rivals state-of-the-art affine-invariant depth estimators. Its non-zero-shot variants come within five points of Vision Banana on referring and reasoning segmentation but remain further behind on instance segmentation. All models largely retain the base model's image-editing abilities. With legend ensembling, we introduce a test-time scaling method for generator-based perception. It segments an image under several class-color legends and fuses the results by majority vote, correcting unstable color-class bindings and improving mIoU by up to 8.7 points on Cityscapes and 15.0 points on COCO-Object without retraining. We release the dataset construction and processing pipeline, the training and evaluation code, as well as the final, intermediate, and ablation checkpoints. Project website: https://openvisionbanana.github.io
evidence_items.title: Open Vision Banana: A Fully Open Recipe for Generative Visual Perception

evidence_items.summary: System One models promise fast, general-purpose decision-making without lengthy token generation. However, understanding their capability spectrum and decision reliability requires more than aggregate performance on current benchmarks. Existing evaluations often provide limited insight into the breadth of model capabilities and the reliability of their decisions. We introduce SO-Arena, a benchmark characterizing the capability spectrum and decision reliability of System One models across 11 domains and five capability families. For the capability spectrum, SO-Arena offers evidence-grounded evaluation through reliable sources and manual verification of reference labels against model-visible inputs; fine-grained capability assessment through domain-specific difficulty criteria; and realistic interactive evaluation, where models iteratively execute actions in sandboxes. Reasoning-intensive tasks further enable system one-two comparison. Beyond accuracy, SO-Arena assesses decision reliability through two complementary measures: decision stability under controlled option-set changes and missing-answer recognition when no valid option is available. Evaluations across 21 models reveal that the benefits of scaling and additional reasoning vary substantially across domains. More importantly, strong overall performance does not necessarily imply reliable decision-making: the best-performing System One model ranks only seventh in reliability. Together, these findings highlight the need to characterize capability spectrum and decision reliability as complementary dimensions, providing a systematic view of the strengths and limitations of System One models.
evidence_items.title: SO-Arena: Benchmarking the Capability Spectrum and Reliability of System One Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people seek and consume information, including accounts that differ across languages and regions, especially on contested topics. Supporting diverse information seeking requires models to help users navigate competing narratives across languages and information streams. We define six capabilities necessary for diverse multilingual information seeking: three foundational capabilities for narrative inclusion, narrative exclusion, and missing narrative identification; and three higher-level capabilities for presenting diverse narratives, preserving narrative coverage under confirmatory queries, and maintaining information parity across languages. To guide the development of those information seeking capabilities, we introduce NarrativeBench, a benchmark comprising 1,333 news articles in 23 publication languages across 23 contested topics and 460 Reddit-grounded queries. Evaluating 14 LLMs across 24 query languages, we find that current models lack the capabilities needed to reliably navigate diverse narratives, limiting users' control over the perspectives they receive and leaving substantial gaps in exposure to competing accounts even when diversity is explicitly requested. Information access also differs across query framings and languages, risking echo chambers, linguistic filter bubbles, and information disparities that weaken the common ground needed for democratic discourse. NarrativeBench provides a foundation for developing information systems that give users across languages and regions agency to navigate diverse narratives.
evidence_items.title: The Narrative Gap: Can LLMs Help Us Navigate Diverse Narratives Across Languages?

evidence_items.summary: Self-improving embodied agents are increasingly being developed and compared on robot simulation benchmarks. Several recent works expose the benchmark's success criteria to the learning agent, a practice we call Criteria Exposure (CE). These criteria, originally written to verify policies trained by imitation learning, often demand more than the corresponding language instructions, so a score from such a verifier may not faithfully reflect whether the instructed task was completed, especially for robot-control programs written by an agent. As embodied coding agents report ever higher benchmark scores, a natural question arises: when a coding agent is exposed to the benchmark's criteria, does it generate code that better performs the instructed task, or code that simply overfits to the verification criteria? We conduct controlled experiments with a self-improving agent with and without CE, and find that with CE the agent quickly produces code with a higher success rate under the given criteria, but this advantage disappears when the criteria are changed slightly without departing from the original instructions. More importantly, the skills the agent develops under CE transfer poorly across tasks. We further propose instruction-faithful criteria and show that they better reflect the performance of agent-generated programs.
evidence_items.title: Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier? Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are being explored to deliver health coaching across multiple contexts. However, the quality and safety of chatbot-generated advice is influenced by how prompts are constructed, and prompt design remains inconsistently described in the literature. This scoping review examined how prompt design has been applied and evaluated in AI health coaching chatbots and summarized the study designs, prompt strategies, and outcomes reported across studies. We conducted a scoping review following PRISMA-ScR guidance and searched PubMed, Embase/Ovid MEDLINE ALL, PsycINFO, IEEE Xplore, and Scopus for peer-reviewed studies published up to October 2025. Eligible studies examined prompt design in large language model–based health coaching chatbots. Data were extracted using a standardized form and synthesized narratively. Twelve studies were included, spanning mental health, medication use, physical activity, and nutrition contexts. Study designs were primarily simulation-based, with few involving real users. Prompt strategies were grouped into structural modifications, prompting techniques, and role-based approaches. Structural modifications, such as increasing specificity and adding constraints, were most common and were reported to improve response quality and clarity. Prompting techniques were reported to improve task performance but sometimes reduced focus or consistency. Role-based prompting influenced tone, specificity, and guideline alignment. Outcomes focused mainly on response quality, with fewer studies assessing safety or user experience and only one evaluating clinical outcomes. Prompt design is a key, modifiable determinant of chatbot performance. However, current evidence is limited by heterogeneous study designs and minimal real-world evaluation. Greater focus on prompt design is needed to improve the quality and safety of AI-delivered health coaching and its real-world impact on health outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Prompt design in large language model health coaching chatbots: A scoping review

organizations: Marine Monitoring and Forecasting Center of Zhejiang Province
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Typhoon-induced extreme waves pose severe threats to coastal communities, infrastructure, and maritime operations worldwide. Accurate and rapid forecasting of significant wave height is therefore critical for disaster response. Physics-based numerical wave models provide physically grounded predictions but can be computationally demanding for high-resolution forecasting, while purely data-driven models often struggle with rare, highly non-stationary extreme events. Recent time-series approaches based on large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for long-range forecasting but remain limited in explicitly representing coupled environmental variables and enforcing physically plausible predictions. Here, we develop the Typhoon Wave Large Language Model (TW-LLM), a physics-informed, domain-adapted framework for forecasting typhoon-induced coastal wave height. Building on Time-LLM, TW-LLM introduces cross-variable covariate interaction to explicitly represent dependencies between wave states and environmental forcing, structured domain-informed prompting for semantic conditioning, and a physics-informed training objective that combines magnitude-weighted Huber loss with wind-forcing consistency and temporal-rate constraints. Trained and evaluated using nine years (2017–2025) of hourly observations from eleven coastal buoys in China, TW-LLM achieves root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of ~ 0.15 m for short-term (6-h) forecasts, 0.3 m for long-term (96-h) forecasts, and 0.23 m under extreme typhoon conditions. With an inference time as low as 5 s per forecast, TW-LLM provides a computationally efficient framework for near-real-time coastal wave forecasting and early warning, with potential to enhance coastal resilience to increasingly severe climate-related hazards.
evidence_items.title: Physics-Informed Time‑Series Large Language Model for Extreme Typhoon Wave Height Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: Background: The purpose of this study is to assess the ability of generative AI and a refractive surgeon to distinguish post-LASIK Scheimpflug tomography images based on original excimer laser ablation and to recognize untreated corneas. Methods: Corneal tomography Pentacam images from 204 eyes, which included hyperopic ablations, myopic ablations, myopic astigmatic ablations, mixed astigmatic ablations, or untreated eyes, were compiled. These were individually queried in ChatGPT-5.5 using a multiple-choice prompt to obtain a response. A refractive surgeon was also tested on the same 204 corneas. Results: The clinician obtained higher overall accuracy (85.8% [95% CI 80.2–90.3]) compared to ChatGPT, (60.3% [95% CI 53.2–67.1], p < 0.001) and was significantly more likely to answer correctly overall based on McNemar’s test. Additionally, ChatGPT underperformed in the myopia with astigmatism, mixed astigmatism, and untreated categories, with sensitivities of 38%, 6.3%, and 76%, respectively. Conclusions: The overall accuracy of ChatGPT-5.5 did not meet that of the clinician while ability to identify myopic and hyperopic ablation patterns was comparable. Both the AI model and the clinician had decreased accuracy in myopic astigmatism and mixed astigmatism ablation patterns, though the clinician still performed significantly better. Further studies involving alternative AI models, multicenter data, and standardized evaluation protocols are warranted to establish the clinical applicability of these findings.
evidence_items.title: Distinguishing Post-LASIK Ablation Patterns on Corneal Tomography: Comparing Clinician Versus Large Language Model

evidence_items.summary: Emerging deep technologies create a competitive technical intelligence challenge because technical architectures, performance claims, ecosystem arrangements, and prospective markets evolve before stable adoption evidence is available. This article develops and illustrates a theory-informed, large language model (LLM)-assisted competitive intelligence (CI) process for assessing the disruptive potential of the development and commercialization of emerging quantum error-correction technologies. The process translates concepts from disruptive innovation, architectural innovation, value proposition analysis, and disruptive threat assessment into intelligence constructs, evidence questions, sequential prompt functions, source-validation criteria, and monitoring outputs. Perplexity.ai supported document discovery, organization, comparison, and preliminary synthesis; the authors evaluated sources, classified claims, and made all final interpretations. The process is illustrated through a comparative documentary analysis of Nord Quantique’s multimode bosonic quantum error-correction approach and IBM’s transmon, surface-code, and quantum low-density parity-check-oriented approach. The analysis identifies NQ as a documented architectural alternative that seeks to embed error protection within superconducting resonator modes. Its proposed reduction of error-correction overhead provides a plausible mechanism for changing system-resource requirements and deployment conditions. However, the retained evidence does not establish comparative system level advantage, lower total cost, a validated customer segment, a disruptive foothold, adoption, or incumbent displacement. The article contributes a source-disciplined and monitorable LLM-assisted CI process for emerging deep technologies.
evidence_items.title: A Theory-Informed, Large Language Model-Assisted  Competitive Intelligence Process for Assessing  Competing Quantum Error-Correction Technologies

evidence_items.summary: Objective Negative control outcomes (NCOs) help detect and correct systematic error in observational studies, yet their selection remains largely manual. The Common Evidence Model (CEM) can generate candidate lists, but researchers must still screen them for plausibility as true nulls and for sufficient observation in each institution's data. We developed and evaluated MENTOR (Multi-agent Evidence-informed Negative conTrol Outcome selection with Reasoning), a multi-agent system of large language models (LLMs) that combines CEM evidence with LLM reasoning to select institution-specific NCOs. Methods Four LLM agents operate on an institution's Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership common data model. A Curator summarizes drug labels, a Suggester assesses locally frequent candidates with CEM evidence and a first-pass LLM judgment, an Adjudicator resolves their disagreements, and a Diagnostician relaxes the patient-count threshold until a target number of NCOs is met. Using Qwen3.6-27B, we evaluated 349 candidates for three drug pairs in a Korean tertiary hospital's electronic health records (2.9 million patients) against a blinded LLM judge from a different model family, validated by three experts on 90 candidates. We compared accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), and sensitivity with CEM-only and first-pass-LLM-only selection. Results MENTOR proposed 243 NCOs versus 121 by CEM-only, with higher accuracy (0.83 [0.79-0.87] vs. 0.53 [0.48-0.58]), sensitivity (0.89 vs. 0.41), and PPV (0.86 vs. 0.79). Judge-expert agreement was κ=0.63. Adjudication, needed for 44.1% of candidates, added little accuracy, and only with reasoning mode. Concordant acceptances, which bypass it, contained about half of the false positives. Only 7%-9% of CEM-proposed outcomes had at least 10,000 patients at the institution. Conclusion Combining LLM judgments with CEM evidence and local data yielded more NCOs, with higher PPV, than CEM alone.
evidence_items.title: MENTOR: An Evidence-Informed Large Language Model-Based Multi-Agent System for Efficient Selection of Institution-Specific Negative Control Outcomes

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language models (LLMs) can extract information from unstructured clinical text, but it remains unclear whether their ability to assess current status translates into reliable predictions of longitudinal outcomes. Objective This study aimed to evaluate DeepSeek’s ability to assess baseline clinical and radiographic status in knee osteoarthritis (KOA), its performance in predicting 6-month outcomes, and its interrun reproducibility. Methods This study used a single-center, prospective observational cohort design to conduct a blinded, retrospective evaluation of the LLM. A total of 128 patients with primary KOA were enrolled, of whom 111 (86.7%) completed the 6-month follow-up and were included in the primary analysis. DeepSeek-V4-Flash and a rheumatologist independently assessed KOA diagnoses, baseline Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) scores, and Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) grading based on the same standardized interview records and imaging reports and predicted 6-month outcomes. The LLM was run independently 3 times. The actual outcomes determined by another senior physician served as the reference, and the results were compared with the physician’s predictions and the persistence model. Results The LLM showed high baseline diagnostic agreement with the physician (105/111, 94.6%) and good agreement on the WOMAC and KL, but 6-month predictions (WOMAC mean absolute error=5.92-6.58; KL exact agreement=74/111, 66.7%-76/111, 68.5%) were worse than those of the physician comparator (mean absolute error=3.86; 96/111, 86.5%) and not superior to those of the persistence model (mean absolute error=5.43). Despite high interrun intraclass correlation coefficients (0.982 and 0.965), exact agreement between runs was poor (35/111, 31.5% and 7/111, 6.3%). Conclusions The evaluated DeepSeek configuration may support structured baseline KOA assessment.
evidence_items.title: Performance of a Large Language Model for Predicting Clinical and Radiographic Outcomes in Knee Osteoarthritis: Single-Center Prospective Observational Study

evidence_items.summary: Whole-Region Comprehensive Land Consolidation (WRCLC) faces persistent evaluation bottlenecks in practice: traditional quantitative monitoring captures physical land-cover changes but fails to interpret cross-sectoral policy semantics, whereas manual administrative review suffers from high operational costs, subjective inconsistency, and severe information asymmetry. To address these challenges, this study develops a domain-adapted Large Language Model (LLM) framework for structured preliminary effectiveness assessment of WRCLC, using Guangdong Province as a case study. Following the standardization and integration of multi-source heterogeneous data across county-level units, a domain-specific model is established using a knowledge distillation framework based on a hard-constraint mechanism combined with LoRA fine-tuning. A six-dimensional evaluation system is established to evaluate project progress, factor endowment guarantee, structural optimization, value realization, bottom-line constraints, and regional characteristics. Qualitative and quantitative validation across typical county-level administrative divisions in Guangdong demonstrates high alignment with expert judgment and robust capabilities in contextual narrative generation. Rather than replacing administrative decision-making or expert review, this framework demonstrates the feasibility of generative artificial intelligence as an auxiliary decision-support tool. Operating within a human-in-the-loop governance paradigm, the proposed approach effectively bridges quantitative spatial metrics and qualitative governance semantics, significantly reducing administrative drafting burdens while enhancing process monitoring, compliance review, and adaptive land governance.
evidence_items.title: A Large Language Model-Oriented Framework for Effectiveness Assessment of Whole-Region Comprehensive Land Consolidation: A Case Study of Guangdong Province

organizations: Faculty of Management and Information Technology, Universiti Sultan Azlan Shah,33000, Kuala Kangsar, Perak, Malaysia

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is creating new opportunities for teaching materials development in higher education, yet the distribution of research attention across material types and the educational value of generated resources remains insufficiently understood. This study aimed to examine the applications, material categories, benefits, challenges, and research gaps associated with GenAI-assisted teaching materials development in higher education. A systematic literature review synthesized findings from relevant studies, with the reviewed literature identifying 31 studies in one recent review as a key evidence base for understanding current research patterns. The literature indicates that textual and written materials receive the greatest research attention, followed by assessment and evaluation materials and multimedia resources, whereas game-based and gamified materials remain comparatively underexplored. Findings also highlight GenAI’s potential to improve development efficiency and support resource adaptation, alongside persistent concerns about accuracy, bias, ethical use, and pedagogical suitability. This study contributes a structured perspective on the uneven development of research across teaching material types and identifies priorities for strengthening empirical evidence. Future work should evaluate educational effectiveness across diverse learning contexts, advance multimodal material design, and investigate human–AI collaboration to support accurate, pedagogically aligned, and responsible integration into higher education.
evidence_items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence for Teaching Material Development in Higher Education

evidence_items.summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming marketing practices through advanced data analysis and predictive capabilities. This paper examines AI driven marketing, focusing on customer behavior analysis and predictive marketing. It explores how AI technologies help businesses understand customer preferences, identify purchasing patterns, and anticipate future customer actions. The study discusses applications such as customer segmentation, recommendation systems, sentiment analysis, customer churn prediction, and customer lifetime value estimation. It also examines AI applications across commerce, banking, healthcare, travel, hospitality, and social media marketing. The paper highlights potential benefits, including personalization, improved decision making, marketing efficiency, customer retention, and demand forecasting. However, effective implementation requires attention to data quality, privacy, algorithmic bias, implementation costs, and technical expertise. Ethical considerations, including transparency, consent, fairness, security, and human oversight, remain essential for responsible AI adoption. The paper follows a conceptual approach based on secondary literature. It concludes that AI can strengthen marketing effectiveness by integrating customer insights with predictive capabilities. Successful implementation requires collaboration between human marketers and AI technologies. This balanced approach can support customer relationships, informed decisions, and sustainable marketing performance.
evidence_items.title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence for Customer Behaviour Analysis and Predictive Marketing

evidence_items.summary: Plant stress is one of the primary limitations to crop growth, yield, and quality and can result from various abiotic and biotic stresses, including drought, extreme temperatures, salinity, nutrient imbalance, pathogens, and insect pests. Early detection of plant stress is crucial for enabling timely intervention and preventing potential crop losses. In recent years, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) for automated plant health assessment has gained increasing attention through image-based deep learning and sensor-based machine learning techniques. However, single-modality approaches may have limited capability to capture the complex relationships between plant visual characteristics and environmental conditions. Multimodal AI can address this limitation by integrating complementary information from visual modalities, such as RGB, thermal, multispectral, and hyperspectral imaging, with environmental indicators, including temperature, humidity, soil moisture, light intensity, and weather conditions. In AI-based plant stress assessment, with a particular focus on multimodal data fusion and early stress prediction. AI architectures, data fusion methods, datasets, sensing modalities, and explainable AI (XAI) techniques are examined in detail. Furthermore, key challenges associated with multimodal dataset collection, sensor synchronization, environmental variability, model generalization, computational requirements, and real-world deployment are discussed. Finally, promising research directions, including temporal multimodal learning, edge AI, explainable multimodal models, low-cost sensing technologies, and foundation models for plant science, are highlighted.
evidence_items.title: MULTIMODAL ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR EARLY PLANT STRESS PREDICTION: A REVIEW

evidence_items.summary: Arid and semi-arid environments are highly vulnerable to potentially toxic element accumulation because low rainfall, high evaporation, dust transport, episodic runoff, irrigation return flow and groundwater salinity can concentrate metals in soil and water. Saudi Arabia provides a distinctive national case because rapid urbanization, agriculture, cement production, wastewater reuse, coastal development and petroleum-related activities occur across contrasting geological provinces. This review critically synthesizes published evidence on heavy-metal and trace-element concentrations in Saudi Arabian soil, sediment, groundwater, surface water, irrigation water, seawater and wastewater-influenced systems. The review follows a structured critical-review approach: peer-reviewed studies were screened for location, matrix, analytical method, concentration data, quality assurance/quality control information, guideline comparison and reported pollution or risk indices. The evidence shows strong spatial heterogeneity. Central-region datasets dominate the literature, whereas northern agricultural areas, western Red Sea coastal-industrial sites, southern wadis and landfill-affected areas, and eastern oil-related and coastal settings remain important but unevenly represented. Reported hotspots include Cd up to approximately 22 mg/kg in industrial soil, elevated Zn in Riyadh playground soils, As up to approximately 0.18 mg/L in well water and Fe up to approximately 1.45 mg/L in well water. Priority elements are As, Cd, Pb, Cr, Ni, Cu, Zn, Fe and Mn. Their interpretation requires matrix-specific guideline comparison, geogenic background assessment, and land-use context. The review identifies carbonate-evaporite aquifers, Arabian Shield-derived sediments, wadi transport, irrigation return flow, industrial emissions, wastewater inputs and petroleum-related activities as interacting controls.
evidence_items.title: Heavy metal contamination in Saudi Arabian soil and water: Regional distribution

evidence_items.summary: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in military decision-making and operational systems, developments that take a rigorous and mission-oriented approach to adversarial assessment are necessary. To this end, this research introduces an Agentic AI Red Teaming Framework for the military domain that is designed to capture the security and safety robustness together with the operational trustworthiness of AI systems. It does so by adopting a socio-technical and Systems of Systems (SoS) approach in conditions of uncertainty across four layers: goal and profiling, adversarial scenario generation, execution, and impact assessment which enables a systematic progression from threat identification to mission-level consequence analysis. To this end, the framework is including an attack taxonomy which is further instantiated on AI-enabled DSS (Decision Support Systems) and AWS (Autonomous Weapon Systems) use cases across the process lifecycle that includes phases such as threat modelling and assessment. Through this framework, the research contributes to the development of responsible and trustworthy military AI systems that account for human–AI teaming, operational constraints, and governance obligations under conditions of uncertainty.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI red teaming framework in the military domain

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language model (LLM) based agents are moving from executing well-specified tasks to Agentic Design: shaping what and how to build upstream of fabrication, integration, and deployment. However, an internally coherent but externally infeasible design propagates its compounding error downstream. The failure is easy to overlook, yet consequential and hard throughout: a design-generating loop rarely includes a check against the world, and the error surfaces only after the artifact is built. Design Grounding names the correspondence between such a design and the world it must satisfy. The mechanisms that establish it exist in adjacent fields but have been introduced into the design loop only in isolated, domain-specific forms, which leaves the same difficulty scattered across fields under different names. Studying both sides through their own corpora, the review is the first to consolidate them into one unclaimed problem. What makes the problem hard is structural: a design's referent is a system that has not been built, and the model that produces the design cannot supply it without external intervention. The review is exploratory in aim: it characterizes the problem and screens Agentic Design and Grounding in all four combinations. Reading titles and abstracts with an LLM flags roughly one in fifteen of nearly three thousand papers as closing the Design Grounding loop; only twenty survive full-text adjudication and manual review. Those twenty sort into four structural difficulties, and each becomes an open problem whose parts already exist in an adjacent field but remain unassembled.
evidence_items.title: Introducing Grounding into the Agentic Design Loop: An Exploratory Review of an Unclaimed Problem

evidence_items.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence systems extend language models with planning, memory, tool invocation, data access, and autonomous action, creating enterprise capabilities that also expand the security boundary beyond prompt-response applications. This review examines how prompt injection, tool poisoning, memory manipulation, and excessive agency threaten agentic workflows across finance, healthcare, software development, customer operations, and critical business services. It analyzes direct and indirect prompt injection through user inputs, retrieved documents, webpages, emails, databases, and multimodal content, emphasizing how untrusted instructions can override policy or redirect plans. Tool poisoning is examined through malicious descriptions, compromised connectors, deceptive outputs, dependency tampering, and excessive permissions that enable unauthorized data access or transactions. The review further evaluates memory attacks through false fact insertion, persistence abuse, cross-session contamination, sensitive-data retention, and retrieval manipulation. Excessive agency is framed as a control failure arising when agents possess broad objectives, inadequate constraints, irreversible tools, or weak human oversight. Defensive approaches include instruction-data separation, contextual trust labeling, least-privilege authorization, capability-based tool access, schema validation, content sanitization, provenance tracking, memory partitioning, transactional safeguards, runtime policy enforcement, and human approval for consequential actions. Detection methods combining behavioral telemetry, execution graphs, anomaly scoring, canary resources, and policy-violation monitoring are compared using attack success rate, false alarms, intervention latency, task utility, and operational cost.
evidence_items.title: Securing Agentic AI Enterprise Workflows Against Prompt Injection Tool Poisoning Memory Manipulation and Excessive Agency Threats

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are reshaping intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) by reducing authoring costs and enabling flexible interaction. However, effective tutoring requires more than fluent responses. It also depends on pedagogical control, domain grounding, learner modeling, interaction design, orchestration, and reliable evaluation.
