We examine these requirements through a component-centric framework that organizes LLM-based tutoring systems into four functional layers: pedagogical policy, domain and grounding, learner state, and interaction/interface. A cross-cutting orchestration layer coordinates these components, while agentic tutoring systems are treated as an emerging subset of the broader field. Drawing on representative literature on LLM-based and agentic tutoring systems, published mostly between late 2022 and mid-2026, we analyze how tutoring capabilities are implemented across system architecture, learner modeling, interaction, orchestration, and evaluation. The reviewed literature suggests that evaluation remains concentrated on response-level and model-based proxies, while direct evidence of learning gains remains limited. Learner-state modeling and interaction design also receive less systematic attention. We conclude by identifying challenges in answer leakage, pedagogy–solving trade-offs, learner-state calibration, interaction validity, and proxy validity.
evidence_items.title: What makes an LLM a tutor? A component-centric survey of LLM-based and agentic tutoring systems

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated the ability to generate parameters for variational quantum circuits without conventional optimization. However, the conditions under which this approach is effective remain unclear. Here, we investigate a frozen, general-purpose LLM that generates complete circuit parameter vectors from symbolic circuit and Hamiltonian descriptions, with optional iterative energy feedback. We evaluate the approach on general random Hamiltonians, structured parent Hamiltonians, and molecular systems. For general Hamiltonians, LLM-generated parameters exhibit larger energy errors than conventional Adam optimization, while additional feedback generally provides limited improvement. In contrast, for structured Hamiltonians, the LLM can generate promising low-energy parameter configurations, suggesting that identifiable physical and mathematical structure facilitates parameter inference. We also show that direct LLM predictions of minimum energies can violate the Hamiltonian spectral lower bound, whereas generated circuit parameters allow independent evaluation of physically realizable energy expectation values. Finally, we investigate blind circuit interpretation and find that the LLM can predict measurement outcomes even when it fails to identify the underlying quantum algorithm. These findings highlight the role of problem structure, the limitations of iterative LLM optimization, and the importance of independently verifiable predictions in quantum parameter programming.
evidence_items.title: Programming Quantum Circuit Parameters with Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text through iterative masked denoising with bidirectional attention, offering a compelling alternative to autoregressive vision-language modeling. However, each denoising step requires a full forward pass over long multimodal sequences in which visual tokens dominate the sequence length, and a fixed step budget further compounds this quadratic per-step cost. Existing inference acceleration approaches for multimodal dLLMs characterize attention redundancy implicitly, motivating designs from isolated attention visualizations rather than from measurement. We close this gap with DRAMA, a training-free acceleration framework grounded in a systematic dissection of attention redundancy in multimodal dLLMs. By probing attention tensors along spatial and temporal axes, we reveal two persistent redundancy structures: (i) attention mass consistently concentrates on a sparse subset of visual tokens, and (ii) attention distributions rapidly stabilize across denoising steps after an initial formation phase. These findings motivate two complementary mechanisms: Spatial-Redundancy-Aware Visual Token Pruning (SVTP) and Sufficiency-Guided Adaptive Stopping (SGAS). Together, DRAMA achieves an average 18.67 times inference speedup across six vision-language benchmarks without training, architectural modification, or attention caching, while maintaining competitive accuracy. Our results establish a strong, measurement-grounded acceleration baseline for multimodal dLLM inference.
evidence_items.title: DRAMA: Dissecting Attention Redundancy for Accelerating Multimodal Diffusion Large Language Models
Domain-specific large language models with chain-of-thought prompting for antibiotic prescribing: a 2×2 factorial evaluation with automated scoring assessment.

evidence_items.summary: Optional reasoning, retrieval, web search, and tool use can improve large language model responses but incur unnecessary computation when activated indiscriminately. This study investigates whether prompt optimization can compensate for limited router capacity and whether classification gains translate into downstream efficiency. The proposed framework uses prompt-driven small language models to make four independent capability decisions, allowing multiple capabilities to be selected per query. Qwen2.5 routers ranging from 1.5B to 14B parameters are compared across five prompting strategies, followed by an evaluation of capability-specific optimized configurations using a fixed GPT-OSS-120B downstream model on 127 questions. Under minimal prompting, increasing router capacity does not consistently improve classification performance. Prompt optimization narrows the capacity gap for reasoning and calculator routing, whereas RAG and web search retain larger benefits from higher capacity. Similar classification F1 scores do not necessarily imply equivalent downstream behavior: false-positive activations increase unnecessary computation, while missed capabilities can reduce answer quality. The 14B router achieves a mean BERTScore F1 of 0.8408, compared with 0.8418 when all capabilities are enabled, while reducing average downstream token consumption by 68.7\% (8,837 to 2,764 tokens) and median downstream latency by 80.5\% (9.79 to 1.91 seconds). These savings exclude router overhead, which is measured separately in a different inference environment and increases with router capacity. The findings demonstrate that the relationship between router capacity, prompt design, and downstream efficiency is capability-dependent. Consequently, router selection must consider error profiles and routing overhead alongside classification performance.
evidence_items.title: Small Language Models for Inference-Capability Routing: Effects of Model Capacity and Prompt Optimization on Downstream Quality and Efficiency

evidence_items.summary: Remasking allows diffusion language models to revisit generated text, but effective correction requires knowing when and what to revise. Our diagnosis on Sudoku reveals two gaps. Hidden states contain error information that token confidence does not reliably expose, and remasking an isolated error usually reproduces it when the surrounding context remains fixed. These findings motivate DiVR , a verifier that predicts whether a partially generated sequence will reach a correct answer. Trained on the final correctness of the model's own trajectories, DiVR decides when to regenerate a block and which alternative to retain, while the generator itself stays unchanged. On five reasoning benchmarks with LLaDA-8B-Base, DiVR raises the average accuracy of the fine-tuned generator from 35.3\% to 43.4\% at $1.9$-$3.5\times$ the cost of greedy decoding, above search baselines that use $3.8$-$7.4\times$. It also complements post-training such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, and generalizes to other generators, including Dream.
evidence_items.title: Learning When Diffusion Language Models Should Regenerate

evidence_items.summary: General-purpose language models are trained mostly on English: over open models we review, at most, non-English pretraining data makes up only a 12% share. Models built for European languages give them far more, but score well below general-purpose models of the same size. A common concern is that, in small models, languages compete for capacity. We present Lara Mini base, a model trained from scratch on 6T tokens in English and 44 other languages, which together cover all 24 official languages of the European Union. As training progresses, the 44 other languages together come to outweigh English. To give these languages enough capacity at low cost, Lara Mini base uses a mixture of experts architecture with 7.2B total and 0.6B active parameters. Among open base models with up to 2B active parameters, it achieves the highest average score across standard English, multilingual, math, and code benchmarks, ahead of models trained on 4 to 6 times as many tokens. Its margin is largest on multilingual benchmarks in the languages it supports and on math benchmarks. It supports contexts of up to 128k tokens. We find that our MoE architecture reduces capacity competition between languages. For a single user on one GPU, without quantization, it generates text at least 1.8 times faster than any model with a higher average score. We release the weights of Lara Mini base under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license. In addition, we will release T-HellaSwag, a higher-quality machine translation of the commonsense reasoning benchmark HellaSwag into 110 language variants.
evidence_items.title: Lara Mini Base: Language Diversity as a Resource, Not a Trade-off

evidence_items.summary: Multi-agent systems of language models are often motivated by an averaging argument: if the agents'errors are unbiased and independent, the error of an aggregate of N answers falls as 1/sqrt(N). Fermi estimation, whose continuous answers are aggregated on the logarithmic scale, permits a direct test. We decompose the log10 error of each answer into the mean error of its model on the item, common to all its draws on the item, and a residual, and estimate both from 2.51M answers given before any communication by 15 open-weight models (3B-72B) on realFP, with replication under a single prompt pair on realFP, Science Olympiad Fermi questions and a guesstimation set. Given the item, teammates'errors are uncorrelated and teams behave as independent draws, but the item-level component accounts for a median 0.906 of the error variance over items. Teams of thirty therefore reduce a single agent's error by a median 1.7% (at most 5.4%), whereas draws that were also unbiased on each item would reduce it by 74-79%. All models compress their estimates toward about 10^6; this trend explains a median 17% of the item-level component, and a cross-validated linear recalibration on labelled items removes the overall bias but not that component. Three rounds of debate reduce within-team dispersion by 93% and leave the item-level component unchanged; revision without peers attains the same small gain. Mixing five models of similar accuracy reduces error by 6.6% relative to their own homogeneous teams, but no mixture improves on the most accurate model. Higher sampling temperature changes team error by about 1% at most, and contrastive activation steering not detectably; per-agent scaffold prompts (not significant after multiplicity correction) and skipping one layer in a single-model screen improve it. The results are conditional on the models, benchmarks, prompts and settings tested.
evidence_items.title: Shared Item-Level Error Limits the Aggregation of Small Language Models in Fermi Estimation

evidence_items.summary: Affected-version ranges in vulnerability databases decide which deployments scanners, patching pipelines, and incident responders treat as vulnerable, yet these ranges are often incomplete, so vulnerable releases are silently treated as safe. Auditing them requires executable evidence: given a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for a listed version, show that the same vulnerability can be triggered on an earlier, unlisted version. This cross-version PoC migration combines source-code analysis, environment repair, and execution-based verification. We introduce CrossPloit, a benchmark of 127 migration instances across 45 CVEs in the Python web ecosystem. Each instance includes a version-pinned container, a reference PoC, and a vulnerability-specific oracle; two validators check that the observed effect arises from the disclosed vulnerability. Benchmark construction confirms 149 vulnerable prior versions absent from the affected-version lists of four databases, 127 of which require migration. Across 18 agent configurations (nine models and two harnesses), the best configuration resolves 58.3% of instances, compared with 8.7% for an adapted trace-guided baseline. Attack-vector shifts are particularly difficult: no configuration resolves more than 37.9% of these instances. Higher resolve rates are associated with a smaller share of missed-API failures and a larger share of incomplete executions among the remaining failures. In one configuration, withholding the reference PoC and its environment specification reduces resolve rate from 50.4% to 15.0%, highlighting the value of the supplied reference package. CrossPloit provides an execution-based measurement of under-reported exposure and of how far its enumeration can be automated.
evidence_items.title: CrossPloit: A Benchmark for Cross-Version PoC Migration in Python Web Applications

evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement learning can teach vision-language models (VLMs) to decline harmful image-text requests, but how safe the result becomes is set indirectly, through reward weights found by trial runs. Stating safety as budgets on the rate of harmful assistance and the rate of over-refusal, enforced by Lagrange multipliers inside GRPO with an off-the-shelf scorer as the cost, is the natural fix, and it fails twice. The multiplier compares the scorer's mean with the budget, and scorers built for ranking get the mean wrong: a fixed-point analysis shows that the mean bias, not the budget, then decides whether the multiplier settles, saturates or switches off. And standard GRPO standardizes the penalized reward within each group, which cancels the multiplier before it reaches the gradient. Two-channel constrained GRPO repairs both: the base reward keeps the raw score for the within-group comparison, the penalty and the constraint estimate pass through a monotone map fitted on judge-labeled training responses, and the advantage keeps the multiplier. On a Qwen3-VL-2B policy with a training-free readout of an open 4B model as the scorer, held-out harm on 1,037 adversarial prompts falls from 8.9% under standard GRPO to 4.8%, lower in every seed, where the uncalibrated budget gives 7.6%; over-refusal stays at most 2% on 400 benign queries and MMBench is unchanged. The gain is largest where the intent sits in the image (10.1% ->5.1%) and grows on the unseen HADES benchmark (28.9% ->12.8%). Order-preserving distortions of the scores reproduce each predicted controller state in every seed, and the results hold under a map fitted on another judge's labels, an image-reading judge and a human audit.
evidence_items.title: Safety as a Budget: Calibrating the Control Channel of Constrained GRPO for Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Static application security testing (SAST) tools such as CodeQL serve as security gates in continuous integration and code review, and a gate is also read in reverse. When a previously reported alert disappears after a change, developers and the tools around them often take the vulnerability to be gone. That inference holds only if the analyzer is robust to changes that keep the vulnerability. We test this robustness for CodeQL's JavaScript taint tracking with natural, vulnerability-preserving rewrites. A large language model, given only the alert CodeQL exposes and no knowledge of its implementation, rewrites one function along a reported flow as a plausible maintenance change, and we verify by manual audit and controlled experiments that the flaw survives and the alert does not. On 172 flows that CodeQL detects in real npm vulnerabilities, three rewrites per flow silence 26.2% of them, at about USD 0.51 per silenced flow. The same generator, asked only to refactor the same functions with no knowledge of the alert, silences none of them. Every silencing rewrite traces to one of seven gaps at the library-modeling boundary, and 64 of the 70 rewrites cross a gap inside an API CodeQL already models. The largest is the WHATWG URL constructor, which propagates taint to a URL's query components but not to its pathname. The boundary is not specific to CodeQL. 74% of the silencing rewrites also silence an independently built taint analyzer, and 53% escape three analyzers combined. A disappearing alert after an ordinary-looking change is therefore weak evidence that a vulnerability has been fixed, the gaps point SAST developers to narrow and concrete repair targets, and robustness to natural rewrites belongs alongside detection rate in how taint analyzers are evaluated.
evidence_items.title: Preserve the Vulnerability, Break the Alert: Testing the Robustness of CodeQL Taint Tracking with Natural Rewrites

evidence_items.summary: The Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Technical Specification 23.501 (Release 17) defines Maximum Bit Rate (MBR) enforcement at the User Plane Function (UPF) in fifth-generation (5G) networks. Supporting differentiated service-level agreements across the radio access and core networks requires the UPF to enforce MBR limits according to configured slice priorities. During overload, the challenge is to adapt these limits while preserving that differentiation and avoiding oscillations. Building on programmable enforcement and intelligent orchestration, we propose an agentic control loop combining UPF telemetry with locally hosted Large Language Model (LLM) selection from a finite set of admissible rate candidates. Deterministic logic validates each selection and derives Packet Forwarding Control Protocol (PFCP) updates. The evaluated runs show no oscillations or fallbacks and unchanged highest-priority rate limits. These observations establish configuration preservation; delivered per-class QoS protection remains unmeasured.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Orchestration for SLA-Constrained Network Slicing in Programmable Mobile Data Planes

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) inference at datacenter scale is fundamentally bottlenecked by memory capacity and bandwidth limits. Because model weights are read-only and identical across instances, conventional architectures that replicate these parameters across the local DRAM of tens of thousands of accelerators incur massive capital expenditures, significant static power dissipation, and redundant memory-fetch energy. A recent proposal to use optical fiber loops as delay-line memory alleviates these issues, but its recirculating loop must hold the whole model: loop length grows with model size, slack is fixed when the ring is built, and the layouts that serve modern Mixture of Experts (MoE) models efficiently do not fit in it. We propose Optical Broadcast Memory (OBM), an open-ended hierarchical Tap-and-Amplify fiber architecture that generalizes and replaces the optical ring paradigm. A centralized memory server continuously broadcasts weights to distributed inference nodes that passively tap the data stream using receive-only co-packaged optics, delivering parameters directly to compute units without intermediate buffering. To overcome the limitations of continuous weight streaming, we use dynamically-sized slack to accommodate large and variable context lengths. We show how removing the restrictions of the optical ring allows OBM to efficiently serve MoE models. Evaluated at a datacenter scale of 80,000 accelerators, OBM eliminates petabytes of HBM while being competitive or better in throughput and energy per token than an HBM-based system.
evidence_items.title: Broadcast, Don't Replicate: Eliminating Weight HBM in Datacenter LLM Serving

evidence_items.summary: Navigation agents use a large language model (LLM) planner to call a vision-language-action (VLA) model. Each episode needs the LLM, adding cost and delay. We distill successful agent experience into the VLA instead of distilling the planner. The VLA then navigates alone at test time. Agent sessions are not VLA demonstrations. They include motions driven by planner tools and sub-instructions, along with detours. We present H2E, a task-level experience distillation method that converts these sessions into VLA training data. Every motion becomes a VLA action under the original task instruction, with the resulting poses as targets. H2E masks the loss on steps that move away from the goal. It labels every visited state within 1 m of the goal as a stop. We then update the VLA with low-rank adaptation. The VLA learns to stop at the goal and find goals the base model never reaches. On all 3,189 REVERIE-CE val-unseen episodes, H2E raises the success rate of an 8B VLA from 35.0% to 44.9%.
evidence_items.title: What Can a VLA Learn from the Agent That Calls It? Task-Level Experience Distillation for Embodied Navigation

evidence_items.summary: Differential flatness enables efficient planning and control, but discovering explicit flat outputs for general nonlinear systems remains difficult due to the lack of general methods and supervised data. We propose FlatSeek, a framework combining backward data generation with task-specific large language model (LLM) training. By reversing the defining reconstruction of flatness, we generate system-flat-output pairs with known certificates, then fine-tune an LLM to propose symbolic flat-output candidates for unseen dynamics. On literature and synthetic benchmarks, FlatSeek outperforms both the traditional symbolic methods and the untuned reference models in flat-output discovery success, and uncovers alternative symbolic flat outputs not reported in the literature.
evidence_items.title: FlatSeek: LLM-Driven Symbolic Discovery of Flat Outputs via Backward Data Generation

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents an overview of the integrated technologies developed for the Open Platform League at RoboCup@Home 2026 in Incheon. A vision system integrated with learning-based, training-free models enables robust object recognition for both known and unknown objects. We introduce a RoomPlan-based method that semi-automatically registers furniture geometry and labels to generate semantic maps. Additionally, a large language model-based planner interprets the instructions recognized by Whisper and generates primitive skill sequences for execution. A reservoir-computing framework serves as a lightweight temporal-processing model for action recognition. Its field-programmable gate array-based implementation enables low-power, real-time operation. This is key to removing operational time constraints for service robots. Open-source releases, including task environments, dataset tools, and navigation frameworks, enhance reproducibility, reuse, and continuous progress within the RoboCup@Home community.
evidence_items.title: Hibikino-Musashi@Home 2026 Team Description Paper

evidence_items.summary: Users of artificial intelligence services, including those powered by large language models and other transformer-based models, need assurance that inference and training follow the declared computation without exposing private models or data. Zero-knowledge proofs can provide this assurance, but proof generation remains expensive. Hardware acceleration research often reports gains for individual cryptographic operations, leaving their effect on the full cost of proving neural-network workloads, particularly large transformer models, unclear. We introduce a four-layer framework linking verifiable AI workloads, proof systems, cryptographic kernels and hardware platforms, use it to review the literature, and add original measurements of six provers and seven kernels to identify which costs matter in practice. Our measurements show that the dominant cost changes with the proof system and input length. In low-rank fine-tuning, the cost of opening commitments to fixed model weights remains nearly constant across input lengths from 64 to 2048, while the work associated with intermediate values grows. A 13-billion-parameter fine-tuning configuration exceeds the capacity of a 40-gigabyte graphics processor but completes on an 80-gigabyte device, showing why capacity must be assessed alongside execution time. Our kernel profiling further identifies instruction issue and synchronization limits that a bandwidth-only model misses. We use these findings to assess graphics processors, reconfigurable logic, custom chips and existing artificial intelligence accelerators. The resulting research agenda connects proof-friendly numeric formats, reuse of fixed-weight commitments, heterogeneous execution and shared benchmarks to the measured bottlenecks. Effective acceleration requires selecting hardware and proof-system optimizations around the cost profile of the target workload.
evidence_items.title: Infrastructure for Verifiable AI: Where Proof Costs Go and How Hardware Can Help

evidence_items.summary: The increasing use of large language models (LLMs) for code generation is reshaping how programming is practiced in educational contexts. Rather than treating this shift as a replacement for traditional programming instruction, this poster frames ''vibe coding'' as a pedagogical design space in which students learn to specify, interrogate, and validate AI-generated code. Drawing on recent work in computing education and curriculum guidance on generative AI integration, we propose a structured set of classroom activities that reposition students as evaluators and refiners of model outputs rather than solely implementers of algorithms. The design space is informed by research on LLM-supported programming education, curriculum integration efforts, and known risks such as hallucinated or insecure code generation. We outline three activity types: prompt refinement tasks, multi-model comparison exercises, and failure analysis of generated code. We further propose initial evaluation dimensions for future empirical study, including specification quality, debugging reasoning, and evaluative judgement of generated artefacts.
evidence_items.title: Vibe Coding as a Pedagogical Design Space Within Programming Education

evidence_items.summary: Educators increasingly use large language models (LLMs) as student models: to summarize a learner's work, describe their understanding, and predict their next moves. For educators evaluating these tools, a fragile assumption sits underneath: a model's response can sound tailored to a student while only reflecting the programming situation. We ask whether an LLM's descriptions and predictions about novice Python programmers are tied to the specific student. We study introductory Python submissions from CodeBench, using 117 narrative cases and a matched-peer prediction audit of 310 paired comparisons. Written summaries appear personalized at the surface level: varied, behaviorally grounded, with little template language. A stricter prediction test reveals a gap. For students matched on the same exercise assessment state, predictions without process traces are roughly twice as similar in predicted activity shape (local run-count agreement) as students' real next submissions, while other granularities show smaller or uncertain effects. Adding traces reduces this collapse and adds coarse repair-magnitude and structural signal, but reliable trace-added gains for code details, edit locations, or identifiers remain absent. For educators evaluating LLM-powered tools, personalized-sounding summaries are insufficient evidence of student-specific modeling. We propose identity perturbation under matched assessment state: pair students at the same exercise and test-outcome state, then test whether predictions are correctly targeted, not merely varied. Personalization claims should specify what student-specific signal is captured, from coarse behavior to fine-grained code, so educators and tool designers can judge when LLM-based personalization is warranted.
evidence_items.title: Do LLM Student Models Track the Student or the Situation? A Matched-Peer Study in Novice Programming

evidence_items.summary: Self-directed learning is increasingly important in surgical education. Large language models may support this, however, their accuracy, reliability, and sensitivity to model generation and prompting strategy remain unclear. This study evaluated ChatGPT-generated procedural descriptions in peripheral nerve surgery using GPT-5.2, and tested robustness using a newer model, GPT-5.5. Fifteen peripheral nerve procedures were randomly selected from the Washington University in St. Louis Surgical Education Website as reference standards and coded into steps. GPT-5.2 outputs were evaluated for accuracy and other response characteristics using a structured prompt. Regression assessed accuracy against complexity, word count, steps, and step density. For five procedures, GPT-5.5 was evaluated using structured and simple prompts. Mean GPT-5.2 accuracy was 81.2% (SD 11.5%) across 90 responses, ranging from 68.5% to 91.7%. Accuracy was positively associated with word count and negatively associated with step density, though neither remained an independent predictor. Of 195 missed steps, most involved judgement-based maneuvers (86/195), major steps (56/195), or neurovascular identification (41/195). GPT-5.5 accuracy (81.4%, SD 16.2%) resembled GPT-5.2’s but was more variable, decreasing to 40.5% (SD 40.2%) under a simple prompt, shifting omissions towards major steps. GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.5 generated accurate but variable responses, inconsistently capturing judgement-dependent content. Simple prompting substantially reduced accuracy and shifted omissions toward major steps, indicating dependence on prompting strategy. The evaluated ChatGPT models may aid preliminary orientation, but should not replace expert guidance for safety–critical and judgement-required steps.
evidence_items.title: Accuracy of AI-generated procedural descriptions in peripheral nerve surgery: implications for surgical training

evidence_items.summary: Search engines and Large Language Models (LLMs) offer complementary strengths for document retrieval: lexical retrievers which rely on keyword matching are fast and energy-efficient, whereas LLMs capture semantic meaning and excel at interpreting long, context-rich queries. However, this comes at a cost that is computationally and energetically prohibitive. We propose the LLM Active Approximation Model (LAAM), a hybrid retrieval framework that introduces a lightweight learned predictor which serves as an intermediary between semantic retrieval and LLM retrieval. LAAM is refined through an active learning loop where an LLM labels a small number of documents. By concentrating LLM evaluations on the most informative documents, the framework substantially reduces inference cost while preserving retrieval effectiveness. We evaluate the proposed framework on TREC Robust 2004 using Lucene with BM25 retrieval and DeepSeek v3 as the LLM, under three levels of query verbosity. For verbose queries, LAAM achieves 87% of average P@10 achieved by DeepSeek's reranking (0.459 vs. 0.526), while requiring only 3.3% of the per-query energy consumption. LAAM is statistically significantly better than BM25 and is indistinguishable from DeepSeek on average precision, though not on MAP (Friedman test, P<0.05 with post-hoc testing). Overall, our results demonstrate that selectively approximating LLM relevance judgments through active learning enables retrieval accuracy to be controlled directly through the evaluation (and consequently energy) budget. Rather than committing to either inexpensive (and less accurate) lexical retrieval or exhaustive (and expensive) LLM reranking, our framework exposes a continuous spectrum of operating points along the energy--accuracy curve, allowing practitioners to select how to trade retrieval quality with computational budget.
evidence_items.title: Active Learning of Approximate LLM Ranking for Energy-Efficient Retrieval of Long Queries

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how biological research is done. Biological foundation models trained on millions of nucleotides, protein, and single-cell measurements predict protein structures, mutation effects, and cellular responses to genetic perturbations. Agentic systems, AI assistants built on large language models, can run multistep analyses from plain-language requests and increasingly call foundation models as tools. Yet it is often unclear when these models'outputs can be trusted. We frame this as a model's knowledge boundary: the range of inputs, tasks, and conditions over which its outputs are reliable. This review explains how foundation models are built and proposes that five design elements (data, architecture, training scheme, evaluation scheme, and post-analysis) define this boundary. We examine evidence on where current models succeed or fail and present standardized descriptions of model limits so that researchers, and the agents acting for them, can use these tools reliably.
evidence_items.title: AI for Biologists: The Knowledge Boundaries of Foundation Models in the Age of Agentic Systems

evidence_items.summary: Sharded data parallelism enables memory-efficient training of large models. While efficient training kernels favor packed, kernel-specific data layouts, optimizers may require variant data structures as optimization units. Existing sharded data-parallel frameworks couple these two choices, limiting runtime efficiency and optimization flexibility. To address this, we present \textbf{\our}, a training framework that separates runtime parameters from update parameters, allowing computation layouts and optimization units to be organized independently. Through shared data views and hierarchical sharding, \our supports this separation while avoiding redundant data movement. This design supports a broad range of optimizers, including matrix-based methods such as Muon, and performance optimizations such as fully zero-copy execution. Experiments on video and language model workloads with MXFP8 training show that \our achieves higher Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) than FSDP2, veScale-FSDP, and Megatron-FSDP. At 128 GPUs, MFU improves by up to 21.7\% over the fastest evaluated baseline, with comparable or lower peak memory usage.
evidence_items.title: SS-HSDP: Efficient and Flexible Sharded Data Parallelism via Runtime-Update Decoupling

evidence_items.summary: ZONOS3-Mini is an ultra-compact, ultra-fast, zero-shot voice-cloning TTS model. The model can run in real time on a laptop or smartphone. For its latency and size, it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and cloning fidelity. To achieve this we propose a latent MoE backbone with only 886M parameters (100M active per token) and a new audio codec, Zyphra Audio Codec 1 (ZAC-1), which represents 44.1 kHz audio at a 15 Hz frame rate. On the new ZTTS2-Eval benchmark, ZONOS3-Mini reaches a 6.71% macro-average WER over 55 language sets (35 clean and 20 in the wild), which is competitive with larger and slower state-of-the-art models. We release the model weights, inference, and training code.
evidence_items.title: ZONOS3-Mini Technical Report

evidence_items.summary: Locally deployed Small Language Models (SLMs) are attractive as educational tutors because they can keep student data inside the institution, yet they must read untrusted student input, which exposes them to prompt injection. In practice, the most troubling attacks may not be the most obvious ones. A teacher or platform reviewer can notice a message that says ''ignore all previous instructions.'' It is much harder to notice an instruction hidden in Base64, buried in a code comment, framed as ordinary help-seeking, or placed in a document-ingestion channel such as PDF metadata or annotations. As a secondary analysis of an anonymized educational prompt-injection benchmark, this poster regroups the attacks by expected detectability : whether an attack is likely to be noticed during routine educational review. Across 37 adversarial prompts and ten runs per model, Llama~3.2~3B is more vulnerable to hard-to-notice attacks than to obvious ones (50.0% strict Attack Success Rate (ASR) versus 27.9%). The opaque subset---encoded and document-ingestion payloads---reaches 44.5% ASR. Phi-3-mini shows lower confirmed attack success, but mostly because many responses drift off topic or become unusable rather than safely refusing. The pedagogical lesson is that a tutor that mishandles hard-to-notice attacks can give students inappropriate help, leak protected instructions, or produce unreliable feedback while still appearing safe under a simple success-rate metric. We argue that human reviewability should be designed, measured, and protected as part of AI-supported teaching.
evidence_items.title: Hidden in Plain Sight: When Hard-to-Notice Prompt Injections Undermine Educational SLM Tutors

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have become a powerful foundation for robotic scene understanding, task planning, and language-conditioned control. A natural question follows: can these models also decode what a human operator intends while teleoperating a robot, without any explicit instruction? We formulate this as hierarchical intent prediction, jointly inferring the ongoing atomic action and the broader mission it serves from a short visual teleoperation history. To study this, we introduce VI AMO (Vision Intention Action and Mission Ongoing), a dataset of 6,600 episodes from eleven robot sources with 13,653 temporally aligned action annotations and 9,702 mission annotations. Large proprietary models struggle with this problem: on held-out episodes, GPT-4o reaches Sentence-BERT similarities of only 0.563 and 0.470 for action and mission, and GPT-5.6 Luna achieves only 0.581 and 0.554. Fine-tuning a VLM on VI AMO yields our Vision-Intention Model (VIM), which raises these scores to 0.825 and 0.821 and still reaches 0.726 and 0.717 on the 35.4% of test actions with both labels absent from training. Finally, as a downstream application, VIM's predicted mission enables a vision-language-action (VLA) policy to take over from the operator mid-task in a real-world environment unseen during VIM fine-tuning, reducing human teleoperation time by 34.6% relative to GPT-4o and 39.8% relative to GPT-5.6 Luna, while cutting intent-prediction latency by roughly 70% on average.
evidence_items.title: I See What You Want: Decoding Hierarchical Operator Intent from Visual Teleoperation History

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming computer science (CS) education by providing immediate problem solving support and on-demand knowledge. However, commercial LLMs frequently deliver complete solutions, fostering overreliance and diminishing the productive struggle essential for deep learning. Neurological evidence further suggests that LLM dependence can significantly reduce brain activity, threatening long-term retention. In response, educators have begun customizing LLM-based AI assistants to deliver structured scaffolding. Despite these efforts, the effect of cognitive offloading in student–AI interactions on CS learning outcomes remains unclear. To address this gap, we propose Chat-Bloom (CB), a taxonomy that classifies the cognitive offloading level of both student prompts and AI responses. We validated CB through inter-rater reliability testing (Gwet's AC2 = 0.81) and trained machine learning (ML) models to achieve 81% classification accuracy for large-scale analysis. Applying CB to CS1 chat logs, we identify distinct interaction sequences, compare cognitive offloading patterns across AI assistants, and examine their relationship to student outcomes. These findings position CB as a practical framework for evaluating and improving AI-assisted learning in CS education.
evidence_items.title: Chat-Bloom: A Taxonomy for Classifying Cognitive Offloading in Student-AI Interactions in CS Education

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in programming courses to generate code, explain concepts, and support debugging. In pair programming, their use creates a new form of collaboration in which students must coordinate not only with one another but also with an AI system. Although pair programming is widely adopted in computing education, instructors often have limited visibility into how students divide work, negotiate solutions, and develop shared understanding, particularly when generative AI tools are involved. Existing evaluations typically emphasize final code quality, grades, or students' perceptions, offering limited insight into how dialogue, programming actions, and LLM use interact and evolve over time. This paper presents a multimodal framework for studying semester-long LLM-supported pair programming in undergraduate programming courses. The framework integrates three data sources: video-based dialogue transcripts, programming activity logs, and LLM interaction logs. Dialogue and LLM exchanges are qualitatively coded, while programming logs are converted into labeled action sequences. Sequence pattern mining is then used to identify recurring collaboration, programming, and LLM-use trajectories. Cross-modal analysis examines how these trajectories align at the week and semester levels, and how the resulting patterns relate to course grades and other available learning outcomes. By making these interaction processes more visible, the study aims to identify recurring patterns of LLM-supported collaboration and generate evidence for instructors that can inform the design of pair-programming activities.
evidence_items.title: Toward Understanding Collaboration and Learning in LLM-Supported Pair Programming

evidence_items.summary: This review examines how engineering educators have empirically studied generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs) in their courses since the November 2022 release of ChatGPT. From a 402-record Scopus corpus on AI in engineering education, a GenAI/LLM filter applied to titles, author keywords, and abstracts identified 184 candidates (142 paywalled, 42 open-access); 50 full-text records (42 open-access plus 8 institutionally acquired) constitute the synthesis base. Each record was coded on engineering sub-discipline, instructional application, and study design, paired with a bibliometric overview of citation anchors and venue distribution. Four findings dominate. First, the literature is overwhelmingly perceptual rather than experimental: only 6 of 50 records (12%) report controlled or quasi-experimental interventions, while 18 (36%) are surveys and 16 (32%) are perception or opinion pieces. Second, evidence is concentrated in software and computer engineering (n = 11, 22%), computing-adjacent settings (n = 9, 18%), and general engineering (n = 15, 30%); chemical (n = 4), mechanical (n = 4), civil (n = 3), and other sub-disciplines are thinly populated, and a sensitivity analysis excluding computing records leaves the principal findings unaffected. Third, application activity centres on assessment and grading (66%), perceptions and acceptance (62%), and ethics and integrity (28%), while safety and accreditation, both central to engineering as a profession, each appear in a single record. Fourth, the specific model version studied is unreported in the majority of records, and reporting practice has not improved across the review window. The six controlled studies are synthesised in detail and a framework for assessment redesign is proposed. It is argued that the most urgent contribution this review can make is to render visible the field’s methodological composition, and implications are drawn for educators, program leaders, accreditation bodies, and researchers. Not applicable.
evidence_items.title: A hybrid bibliometric and systematic review of generative AI in engineering education since the advent of ChatGPT

evidence_items.summary: As large language models (LLMs) advance toward increasingly long inputs, soft context compression offers a promising approach to efficient inference by converting long inputs into compact memory slots. Under limited memory budgets, effective context compression remains challenging because task-relevant evidence varies substantially across queries, ranging from localized evidence to multiple distant spans or information dispersed throughout the full document. Instead of compressing everything indiscriminately, we propose CoMem, a query-guided selective context compression framework that learns memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query. CoMem develops Contrastive Compressor Learning to achieve query-sensitive yet context-preserving memory representations. To inject a strong prior over query-dependent evidence distributions, we devise a same-context hard negative mining strategy by pairing a single document with multiple queries, requiring the compressor to selectively retain information according to each query's distinct evidence needs. To address the restricted information flow imposed by causal masking, we further enable bidirectional attention among memory slots. Experiments demonstrate that CoMem consistently outperforms existing context compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/scar-on/CoMem.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Compressing Everything: Contrastive Memory Learning for Selective Context Compression

evidence_items.summary: Abstract This study investigates the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to support Task-Based Language Teaching (TBLT)-oriented lesson planning in a preservice teacher education context, examining the extent to which LLM use can contribute to the mobilisation of TBLT-related competencies. The case study draws on triangulated data from surveys, interaction logs with the LLM, lesson plans produced by preservice teachers and their reflections. The module required participants to generate a lesson plan with an LLM and to compare the resulting plan with a previously created lesson plan developed without AI support. The analysis focuses on knowledge of TBLT principles and their implementation during lesson planning, and the GenAI competence activated through the interaction with the LLM. The findings reveal considerable variation in how the dyads interacted with the LLM. Some dyads formulated more precise prompts and prompt iterations, provided more contextualised input, engaged more critically with the LLM-generated output, and iteratively refined their lesson plans in ways that appeared more consistent with TBLT principles. The data suggest an association between a stronger conceptual understanding of TBLT and more purposeful interaction with the LLM. This association indicates that disciplinary knowledge may facilitate the effective use of LLMs for TBLT-oriented lesson planning. Rather than replacing pedagogical expertise, LLM use appears to be most productive when preservice teachers are able to critically evaluate and adapt the generated output in light of established TBLT principles.
evidence_items.title: Generative AI Literacies and Discipline-Specific Knowledge: Preservice Teachers Planning Task-Based L2 Lessons with GenAI

evidence_items.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as an effective post-training approach to improving fine-grained perception in multimodal large language models by amortizing costly inference-time zooming operations into a single-pass recipe. However, vanilla OPD is inherently susceptible to linguistic momentum: the teacher can follow the student's erroneous prefixes, thus weakening corrective supervision. To address this, we propose Blink On-Policy Distillation (BlinkOPD), in which the teacher"blinks"at every token: it reads the same prefix once with its eyes open and once with its eyes closed. A first-glance gain further strengthens the correction on rollouts that conflict with the teacher. By extracting more effective supervision from each on-policy trajectory, BlinkOPD achieves state-of-the-art average performance across six fine-grained benchmarks using only 500 training images (12x less data) than existing OPD methods. Beyond fine-grained perception, BlinkOPD also demonstrates strong zero-shot improvements across ten held-out benchmarks spanning general visual perception, visual hallucination, and multimodal reasoning abilities. Code: https://github.com/Supltz/BlinkOPD
evidence_items.title: Teach with Blinks: Breaking Linguistic Momentum in On-Policy Distillation for Fine-Grained Multimodal Perception

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly tested on medical exam questions, but accuracy alone does not show when an answer can be trusted. I study the calibration and uncertainty of two open-weight models, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Jais-adapted-7B-chat (both run in 4-bit precision), on 2,816 English multiple-choice questions from MedMCQA and 4,927 Arabic multiple-choice questions from MedAraBench. Accuracy was 0.561 (English) and 0.430 (Arabic) for Qwen, and 0.369 and 0.308 for Jais. Raw option probabilities were overconfident in all four settings (expected calibration error 0.242 to 0.486), and a single temperature parameter removed 82% to 93% of that error. Split conformal prediction reached its nominal coverage in all 24 settings I tested (within 0.006), but the sets were large when accuracy was low: at 90% coverage, temperature-scaled sets contained on average 63% (Qwen, English), 78% (Qwen, Arabic), 86% (Jais, English) and 89% (Jais, Arabic) of the options. The margin between the top two option probabilities separated correct from incorrect answers best for Qwen on English (AUROC 0.734) and worst for Jais on Arabic (0.579). Answering only the 20% most confident questions lowered Qwen's English error from 0.439 to 0.098. Jais showed a strong prior for option C (49% of English and 60% of Arabic predictions). Scoring Latin letters only cut the Arabic share to 29% but left accuracy, raw ECE and AUROC nearly unchanged. Because the two benchmarks differ in subject, level and number of options, I do not attribute differences between languages to language itself. Code is available at https://github.com/Mariyaaleem/arabic-english-medqa-uncertainty.
evidence_items.title: Calibration and Conformal Prediction for Medical Question Answering in Arabic and English: Evidence from Two Non-Parallel Benchmarks

evidence_items.summary: Variability is an inherent characteristic of modern GPU systems, arising from a combination of process variation, dynamic environmental conditions, and power management decisions. Prior work has characterized inter-GPU variability and found consistent performance differences across GPUs. However, we observe that modern workloads, particularly large language models (LLMs), exhibit significant intra-GPU variability. Their short-running kernels interact poorly with the coarse granularity of dynamic power management mechanisms, leading to unpredictable performance. A key source of this intra-GPU transient variability is power excursions, also referred to as electrical design power peaks (EDP$_{p}$), where power temporarily exceeds the GPU's rated power limits. While power management mechanisms are designed to ensure reliable operation despite the presence of EDP$_{p}$ sustained power peaks cause throttling that detrimentally impacts overall application performance. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to characterize the magnitude and frequency of EDP$_{p}$, showing that frequent, significant power overshoots are especially common in ML workloads, which combine high power draw, short kernels, and rapidly changing compute demands. To address this, we design and leverage hardware and firmware mechanisms to provide consistent power management behavior that reduces intra-GPU variability due to EDP$_{p}$ and improves overall performance. We evaluate our techniques across a range of popular workloads. Our approach improves performance by 3-12% over state-of-the-art GPU power management and comes within 3% of an oracular solution.
evidence_items.title: PACER: GPU Excursion Management for ML Workloads

evidence_items.summary: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) for code generation is transforming software development and necessitating a rethinking of how programming should be taught. Although AI can often produce syntactically and functionally correct code, such code is not necessarily of high quality; humans must still evaluate it for qualities such as readability, maintainability, modularity, and design. Yet introductory computing curricula often emphasize functional correctness, while code quality topics such as decomposition, modularity, and design, are postponed until upper-level software development courses. As a result, students may have little opportunity to develop the habits and vocabulary needed to assess code structure and make informed design choices. This gap is increasingly consequential as students rely on AI tools that can produce working code without making their design tradeoffs visible. We argue that introductory programming courses should teach code quality alongside functional correctness, particularly in the age of AI. From the beginning of the curriculum, students should learn why code quality matters, how to evaluate both human- and AI-generated code, and how to write programs that are not only correct but also readable, maintainable, and well designed.
evidence_items.title: The Growing Importance of Code Quality Instruction in the AI Era

evidence_items.summary: K-12 students often struggle with foundational programming concepts such as variables, data types, loops, and conditionals. Large language models (LLMs) can provide immediate help, but unconstrained AI support may act as an answer engine, revealing solutions and reducing productive struggle. This work presents an exploratory design and feasibility evaluation of answer-aware LLM hints for an interactive K-12 programming platform. The system receives structured problem context, including the correct answer as private information, and is prompted to generate progressive hints that guide reasoning without directly revealing the solution. The design is motivated by two needs: reducing the authoring burden of manually writing multiple hints for each programming question, and adding guardrails so generated hints remain age-appropriate, context-aligned, and non-revealing. We evaluated the system using post-activity surveys from 46 students ages 7-11 and 4 STEM instructors, along with automated hint-quality metrics and LLM-as-a-judge scoring. Students and instructors generally perceived the hints as useful, confidence-supporting, and preferable to direct answer display. Automated evaluation suggested that generated hints were usually grounded in the activity context while avoiding excessive reference to the correct answer.
evidence_items.title: Answer-Aware LLM Hints to Scaffold Deeper Learning in K-12 Programming Education

evidence_items.summary: Federated Learning (FL) with Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) enables efficient adaptation of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its energy and carbon costs across hardware remain poorly understood. We evaluated federated Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning on NVIDIA A40, RTX 6000 Ada, and A100 GPUs using a $2^2$ full factorial design with 135M/360M models and 10/100 local steps. CodeCarbon tracked energy and estimated CO$_2$-equivalent emissions. Descriptive allocation of variation assigned 84.8-91.2% of energy and emissions variation to local steps within these ranges. On A40 and RTX 6000 Ada, configurations with fewer steps achieved comparable accuracy with roughly 6-8-fold lower energy consumption and higher accuracy per kWh. These findings support smaller local budgets for energy-efficient federated fine-tuning within the evaluated setting.
evidence_items.title: Sustainable Federated Fine-Tuning with LoRA: Environmental Impact and Performance Footprint

authors: H. V. D. van de Wetering
evidence_items.summary: Formal verification of complex algorithms requires expertise in program specification, invariant construction, mathematical proof, and the management of automated theorem provers. Although large language models (LLMs) can generate program code and proof fragments, reliably developing complete machine-checked verifications remains challenging: it requires an iterative process of constructing and validating specifications and invariants, building proofs, diagnosing solver failures, and optimizing verification performance. This paper presents a systematic ten-step workflow for LLM-assisted verification of scientific algorithms using the Dafny verification system. The workflow integrates algorithm formalization, contract development, empirical invariant validation, proof construction, bottleneck profiling, and resource-driven proof optimization. We applied the workflow using Antrhopic's Claude Opus 5 and Opus 5.5 models, combining LLM-driven development with automated testing and verification feedback, while retaining human oversight for correctness-critical decisions and strategic interventions. We evaluate the approach on 37 complex algorithms from graph theory and labelled transition systems. Notably, we verified the Hopfcroft-Tarjan triconnectivity test, demonstrating that even highly challenging algorithmic verification tasks can be carried out through a structured LLM-assisted workflow. Many of our machine-checked verifications were obtained within hours to a few days of interactive development. Our results suggest that LLM-assisted workflows can shift the role of the human verifier from detailed proof construction toward supervision, specification review, and strategic guidance.
evidence_items.title: LLM-Assisted Verification in Dafny

evidence_items.summary: Charge and baryon stopping in Ru+Ru and Zr+Zr isobar collisions are modeled by HIJING with junction. With realistic nuclear geometry and a tuned diquark splitting, it reproduces STAR's net-baryon yield, charge difference, and scaled baryon-to-charge ratio at midrapidity. Junctions set the ratio's magnitude while neutron skins drive its centrality trend. At the LHC, large asymmetric pair production in HIJING obscures junction effects, causing apparent tension with data. This tuned generator reproduces RHIC data and predicts O+O behavior, setting a quantitative benchmark for baryon transport.
evidence_items.title: Quantitative Junction Transport Modeling of RHIC Charge and Baryon Stopping

evidence_items.summary: Watermark detectors decide whether one document came from a watermarked language model. Auditors often need a different number: the share of a corpus that did. We study this share for Gumbel-max and green-list (KGW) watermarks when every document may have been edited by an unknown amount. Without restrictions on the edits, the upper end of the identified set is 1. Combining a known least-favourable next-token distribution with a sequential coupling, we derive a power envelope indexed by three budgets: a retention floor, an entropy budget, and a budget for in-place substitutions, which for Gumbel-max make edited positions look less watermarked than human text. The envelope gives an identified set that is sharp for the alternatives it dominates, finite-sample bounds on the realized share of a fixed corpus with either the exact null or a null calibrated on an independent human sample, and confidence sequences for streams. In Gumbel-max simulations where the envelope binds, the bounds cover, and the threshold that maximizes the gap between envelope and null is generally as tight as twelve thresholds. On text from OPT-1.3B and Qwen3-1.7B, 12,000 fresh human documents scored under three keys show no robust departure from the exact null, and all bounds covered in resampling trials from finite pools of documents with random edits, substitutions and paraphrases; at a share of 0.2 the exact-null bound is about [0.14,0.38]. These results are fragile in two ways we make precise. LLM-paraphrased KGW pools fall below the envelope, yet at 2000 documents the bounds still covered in these trials. A simulated null error of 0.01, comparable to the largest deviation we observed at our thresholds, is likewise harmless at 2000 documents but breaks exact-null coverage at 100,000; a null calibrated on an independent human sample keeps coverage there, but needs a large reference sample to stay narrow.
evidence_items.title: Prevalence Bounds for Edited Watermarked Text: Power Envelopes and Calibration Sensitivity

evidence_items.summary: Video diffusion models are able to generate samples with high-quality appearance and textural qualities. However, content produced by these methods is known to exhibit significant physical errors. This is because, in a classical video generation setting, all physical reasoning must take place simultaneously and exclusively within the diffusion process.We propose to resolve these issues by redistributing the task of physical reasoning onto a language model-backed keyframe generation module, which allows for explicit reasoning in language, and fine-grained control over the appearance of the video at important moments in the video. We then condition a video generation model with these keyframes, reducing the role of the diffusion model to the simpler task of interpolating between physically-correct intermediate states, rather than inferring an entire sequence with diffusion. Results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing approaches, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Physics-IQ Verified benchmark and PhyGenBench.
evidence_items.title: K2V: Generative Keyframing For Physically Plausible Video Generation

evidence_items.summary: Whether stripes compete with $d$-wave superconductivity or promote pairing through fluctuations remains unsettled in the two-dimensional Hubbard model. Using multi-reference neural variational auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (MR-nVAFQMC) at $U/t=8$, we superpose unpaired Slater determinants across stripe periods and domain-wall positions, reaching variational energies competitive with leading benchmarks on periodic lattices up to $32\times32$ sites. For cuprate next-nearest-neighbor hopping ($t'/t=-0.2$), diagonal hopping preserves electron-doped antiferromagnetism while kinetically frustrating hole motion into Yamada stripes with a dome of short-range connected $d$-wave pairing. At $1/8$ hole doping, hole delocalization across antiphase spin boundaries outweighs on-site repulsion, splitting the filled stripes of the pure model into half-filled walls with strong local pairing. Coherently delocalizing shifted walls strongly suppresses static charge modulation yet leaves short-range pairing unchanged, showing that local pairing is intrinsic to half-filled walls rather than driven by stripe fluctuations. Across intervening antiferromagnetic domains, however, pairing correlations become unresolved at one stripe period and beyond. Both parameter transfer to larger lattices without reoptimization and deep benchmark checkpoints retain stripe spin order without resolving long-range pairing, within uncertainties allowing weak superconductivity. Half-filled antiphase walls thus generate local $d$-wave pairs, whereas suppressing static stripe order alone yields no resolved coherence across stripes in the states studied.
evidence_items.title: Multi-reference variational states resolve stripe selection and local $d$-wave pairing in the Hubbard model

evidence_items.summary: Accurate plant disease recognition is essential for intelligent agriculture, but few-shot settings provide limited labeled samples that may not capture diagnostic symptoms and intra-class variations. Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP, offer transferable visual-semantic knowledge. However, existing CLIP-based methods often rely on coarse class semantics and global visual representations, overlooking disease-specific diagnostic information and fine-grained local cues. Excessive few-shot adaptation may also cause over-specialization and weaken the generalization ability of large-scale pre-training. We propose a description-guided, two-stage CLIP adaptation method to address these issues. Symptom and comparative descriptions enrich class semantics with typical visual symptoms and discriminative cues between similar diseases. The enhanced semantics guide the aggregation of class-relevant patch evidence to calibrate global image-text matching with fine-grained cues. For adaptation, we first update the vision-language encoders with lightweight parameters, then freeze them and train a linear classifier. At inference, the classifier is used for in-domain prediction, while class prototypes from the adapted text encoder support cross-domain prediction and retain vision-language transferability. Experiments with two backbones show that our method achieves the highest mean accuracy in most few-shot settings on PlantVillage, Cassava, and Pear, reaching 93.16%, 79.30%, and 96.56%, respectively, with ViT-L/14 under 16-shot. On class-aligned cross-domain evaluation across 21 shared PlantDoc classes, it achieves 56.96% accuracy, outperforming all compared methods. These results demonstrate its effectiveness in fine-grained few-shot plant disease recognition and cross-domain generalization.
evidence_items.title: Description-Guided CLIP Adaptation with Local Evidence Calibration for Few-Shot Plant Disease Recognition

evidence_items.summary: This report summarizes the Mobile Unified Multimodal Understanding (MUMU) track of the 8th Large-scale Video Object Segmentation (LSVOS) Challenge, held in conjunction with ECCV 2026. MUMU asks for a single unified model that jointly performs multi-concept image tagging over quality, scene, and event vocabularies, open-vocabulary object detection, and concise image captioning, within a budget of 0.5B parameters and 8 GB of peak inference memory. Submissions are ranked by a weighted task score scaled by an efficiency factor. We describe the tasks, rules, and evaluation protocol, report the final results, and review the methods of the top three teams. All three leading solutions build on the compact Florence-2-base model, but extend it in different ways: lightweight tagging heads with cross-task inference refinement, a shared low-rank adapter trained on coverage-aware multi-source data with task-dependent decoding, and a training-free pipeline that maps captions to tags and applies detection test-time augmentation. The results show that a compact prompt-based vision-language model can serve all three outputs when supervision, decoding, and cross-task cues are designed for each task, while open-vocabulary detection on novel categories remains the main bottleneck.
evidence_items.title: Report of the 8th LSVOS Challenge: Mobile Unified Multimodal Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Fine-tuning foundation models on financial data has a wide range of applications, including identifying event types from news, monitoring risk and compliance language, and answering questions over filings and earnings calls. In this setting, the main challenge is to improve task performance without degrading the generalization capabilities of the model. In this paper, we present an extensive set of ablations for fine-tuning Qwen3-8B with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). We compare three training regimes: (1) response-only LoRA, where the supervised response is the label alone; (2) single-adapter reasoning, where reasoning traces from a teacher model are included alongside the labels in the training loss; and (3) dual-adapter composite training, where separate LoRA adapters are trained on traces and labels. Response-only LoRA improves in-domain performance and leaves general capabilities near those of the frozen model. The in-domain change is largest for calibration and argmax accuracy. Under single-adapter reasoning, the in-domain metrics remain behind those of the response-only regime, while MMLU-Pro can rise slightly and the other retention benchmarks stay within ordinary variation. Dual-adapter composite training remains on the same side of this comparison and yields no further gain. Finally, we compress the teacher traces by summarizing them before training, and show that shorter summaries move calibration toward the response-only regime without reaching it.
evidence_items.title: Reasoning Supervision and Capability Retention in LoRA Domain Adaptation

evidence_items.summary: Remote sensing change detection usually relies on large collections of temporally aligned, pixel-level annotations, which limits its scalability across regions, imaging platforms and application domains. Recent zero-shot approaches reduce the need for supervision, but they often localize fine-grained changes poorly because their features are coarse or inconsistent across time. We present SpotDiff, a training-free, plug-and-play framework for zero-shot change detection built by composing complementary vision foundation models. SpotDiff uses DINOv3 for semantically robust features, AnyUp to reconstruct them at pixel resolution, and SAM 3 for text-guided region-of-interest proposals, which an inference-time multi-scale strategy (SWIMS) makes reliable on small objects. Change is then measured by comparing the reconstructed features of the two dates inside the proposed regions, with no learnable components, fine-tuning or change labels. To our knowledge, SpotDiff is the first change detection method to use a universal feature upsampler, which alone adds 13.8 F1 over bilinear upsampling of the same features. On LEVIR-CD, SpotDiff reaches 82.46 F1, 2.06 points above the strongest prior training-free method, and on the multi-class SECOND benchmark it improves building change detection by 10.3 IoU and the six-class average by 2.2 IoU. Qualitative results on PlanetScope (3 m) and Sentinel-2 (10 m) imagery show that the same pipeline transfers across resolutions without modification. Our results indicate that composing modern foundation models is an effective route to scalable, label-free change detection.
evidence_items.title: SpotDiff: A Plug-and-Play Framework for Zero-Shot Change Detection in Remote Sensing Imagery

evidence_items.summary: Graph neural surrogates for granular flow can resolve the motion of individual grains, but propagating information across a large amount of grains requires repeated, costly updates on the full particle graph. This study introduce a Hierarchical Coarse-Grained Graph Neural Network (HCG-GNN) that couples direct interactions between neighboring grains with information exchange on two coarser graphs of occupied spatial cells. In discrete element method (DEM) benchmarks of granular flows down incline planes, HCG-GNN captured key flow characteristics, including front propagation, lateral spreading, deposition morphology, free surface evolution, internal shear behavior, and energy conversion. Results also show that preserving grain-specific features as coarse information returned to the particle graph and integrating predicted accelerations to advance particle motion both improved multi-step accuracy. With 5 of its 7 message-passing steps performed on coarse graphs, HCG-GNN achieved accuracy comparable to a conventional particle-level GNN with a 6.47-fold training speedup and 46.2% lower GPU memory use. A model trained on up to 5000 grains predicted a 2 s release of 10000 grains in 31 s, compared with 2000 s for DEM under the benchmark conditions. This combination of speed and grain-scale resolution supports particle-resolved inverse design, with prescribed runout or discharge targets guiding the search for suitable geometries and grain dynamics revealing the basis for differences in performance.
evidence_items.title: A hierarchical graph neural network for efficient particle-resolved prediction of granular flow dynamics

evidence_items.summary: As computer science (CS) education evolves, emerging technologies — including virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), artificial intelligence (AI), gamification, and mobile learning — are increas- ingly reshaping instructional practices and learning environments. This systematic literature review synthesizes empirical findings from 75 peer-reviewed studies to critically evaluate the pedagogi- cal value, effectiveness, and implementation challenges associated with integrating these technologies into CS classrooms. Drawing on thematic analysis across five research questions, this review examines how immersive environments foster deeper conceptual understanding, how AI-driven tutoring systems enable adaptive and personalized learning experiences, and how game-based and mobile learning tools enhance student engagement and intrinsic motivation. Key themes emerging from the literature include the benefits of interactivity, accessibility, and learner-centered per- sonalization, alongside persistent barriers such as infrastructural limitations, cost constraints, and insufficient instructor professional development. The review further highlights how blended learning models and social technologies support flexible, student-centered pedagogical approaches, while identifying critical gaps in longitu- dinal evidence, standardized assessment frameworks, and equitable access across diverse learner populations. To address these gaps, this paper presents a structured set of future research directions spanning longitudinal effectiveness, K–12 applications, inclusive design, ethical governance, and the emerging convergence of im- mersive environments with large language models. The insights offered are intended to inform educators, researchers, and policy- makers seeking to advance evidence-based, scalable, and inclusive technology integration in CS education.
evidence_items.title: Immersive and Interactive Technologies in Computer Science Education: A Systematic Review
Implications of Image-Level Duplication in Public Glaucoma Datasets.

organizations: TOBB University of Economics and Technology
evidence_items.summary: This paper aimed to conduct a systematic search within a scoping review framework and provide a critical narrative appraisal of the current literature on artificial intelligence (AI) applications for tympanic membrane (TM) image analysis in the diagnosis of ear infections, with a focus on methodological rigor, dataset characteristics, and clinical applicability. A comprehensive search was performed across various online databases (Scopus, PubMed, Google Scholar, Embase, IEEE Xplore, and SPIE Digital Library) to identify studies published up to June 30, 2024. Studies employing AI for the analysis or classification of TM images in ear disease diagnostics were included. Inclusion and exclusion criteria were predefined. Data extraction covered dataset properties, imaging modalities, AI models, validation strategies, and performance metrics. The level of evidence, potential sources of bias, and methodological rigor were assessed qualitatively. Eighty-three studies met inclusion criteria, encompassing 90 experimental results. Considerable heterogeneity was observed regarding dataset size, image quality, device types, labeling protocols, and AI models. Most studies relied on small, private datasets, limiting model generalizability. While deep learning methods-especially convolutional neural networks-achieved high classification accuracies, methodological limitations included inconsistent data augmentation, imbalanced datasets, and lack of external validation. Few studies employed multidisciplinary teams or standardized protocols. Despite notable advances in AI-driven TM image analysis, direct comparison of studies remains challenging due to substantial heterogeneity and methodological shortcomings. A meta-analysis or systematic review was not performed, as quantitative synthesis would be misleading due to substantial data and labeling heterogeneity, wide methodological diversity, and a widespread lack of external validation across the included studies. Future research should prioritize larger, diverse, and well-annotated datasets, adoption of standardized protocols, and interdisciplinary collaboration to improve the clinical translation and reliability of AI-based diagnostic tools for ear infection management.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Otoscopy for Tympanic Membrane Pathologies: A State-of-the-Art Scoping Review.

evidence_items.summary: Ethnic music education is a vital vehicle for cultural heritage, yet traditional teaching relies heavily on teachers’ subjective judgment, making it difficult to objectively quantify learners’ performance development across dimensions such as pitch accuracy, rhythmic accuracy, dynamics control, and expressiveness—a challenge especially pronounced in culturally specific genres such as Hua’er, Jiangnan sizhu, and Mongolian music. To address this, this paper proposes ProgressEthno, a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN)-based model for sequence-based performance assessment in AI-augmented ethnic music education. Building on a dilated causal convolutional backbone, ProgressEthno incorporates a Style-Aware Feature Fusion (SAFF) module and a Multi-task Progression Scoring Head (MPSH), jointly modeling style-conditioned representations and multidimensional learner-performance patterns. The model is trained and validated on a traditional Chinese folk music dataset (2374 samples, 78-dimensional MFCC features) and a music teaching effectiveness dataset (2000 student records). Experimental results show that ProgressEthno achieves 96.8% accuracy and 96.5% macro-F1 on style classification, and 93.8% accuracy with 93.4% macro-F1 on teaching effectiveness classification, outperforming LSTM, GRU, standard TCN, and Transformer baselines, while maintaining 89.7% teaching-effectiveness classification accuracy under the high-noise condition. Ablation studies confirm the contributions of the SAFF and MPSH modules. These results demonstrate the potential of ProgressEthno as a style-aware, sequence-based framework for intelligent assessment in ethnic music education, while genuine long-term learner progression tracking remains to be validated using prospectively collected longitudinal data.
evidence_items.title: A temporal convolutional network for sequence based performance assessment in artificial intelligence augmented ethnic music education

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
Community-wide active case-finding is being increasingly implemented as a tuberculosis elimination intervention. However, conventional site selection strategies can result in low screening yields. We aimed to evaluate whether geographical targeting using artificial intelligence (AI) software can improve detection of tuberculosis during screening in comparison to conventional approaches for site selection, within the programmatic setting in Pakistan.


METHODS
