We conducted a pragmatic, stepped wedge, cluster-randomised trial across all four provinces of Pakistan, and was embedded within The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria-supported active case-finding activities implemented by Pakistan's National TB Control Program and private sector partners. 30 mobile x-ray van teams operating in 68 districts were randomised to transition from conventional site selection approaches (based on field team knowledge, experience, and historical data) to an AI-guided targeting strategy using the Mapping and Analysis for Tailored disease Control and Health system strengthening-Artificial Intelligence (MATCH-AI) software. All individuals attending community active case-finding camps were eligible for participation except those excluded as per the national guidelines. The primary outcome, camp positivity yield, was defined as the number of individuals diagnosed with bacteriologically confirmed tuberculosis per camp. The primary analysis was by intention to treat and camps conducted within a 5-km radius of AI recommended locations were included in a validated per-protocol analysis. This trial is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06017843, and has been completed.


FINDINGS
Between Aug 1, 2023, and Sept 28, 2024, 3936 screening camps were conducted (2046 [52·0%] control, 1890 [48·0%] intervention), screening 269 254 individuals. In the intention-to-treat analysis, camp positivity yield was 7% higher in the intervention group, but not statistically significant (adjusted risk ratio 1·07, 95% CI 0·94-1·22; p=0·27). In the validated per-protocol analysis, the camp positivity yield was 32% higher in the intervention group (1·32, 1·12-1·54; p<0·0001). Yields were highest in districts with moderate yields at baseline before the trial and in rural districts.


INTERPRETATION
AI-guided targeting was associated with substantially higher detection of bacteriologically confirmed tuberculosis during active case-finding in the validated per-protocol analysis and could improve efficiency of community-based tuberculosis case-finding interventions in high burden countries. Routine programmatic data did not capture all implementation or process-quality indicators, limiting assessment of implementation fidelity and variation across sites.


FUNDING
Gates Foundation, the Global Fund through Mercy Corps, Pakistan.
evidence_items.title: Geographical targeting of active case-finding for tuberculosis in Pakistan using artificial intelligence software (SPOT-TB): a pragmatic, stepped wedge, cluster-randomised control trial.

evidence_items.summary: This study examines the flow characteristics of tetra-hybrid Jeffrey nanofluids in a porous medium through a vertical channel. The use of a tetra-hybrid nanofluid enables the synergistic integration of four distinct nanoparticles, yielding superior thermophysical characteristics, enhanced thermal transport, and improved suspension stability compared with conventional hybrid and tri-hybrid nanofluids. The effects of thermophoresis, Brownian motion, and slip boundary conditions are analyzed along with viscous dissipation, Joule heating, thermal radiation, and heat flux. Homogeneous and heterogeneous chemical reactions are incorporated into the mathematical model, where partial differential equations (PDEs) are converted into ordinary differential equations (ODEs). The transformed equations are solved numerically in MATLAB using the shooting method under the assumptions of low Reynolds number and long wavelength. A graphical analysis explores velocity, temperature, and concentration distributions. The results reveal that buoyancy, magnetic, and porous-medium effects govern the velocity field, while Prandtl number, thermophoresis, Brownian motion, homogeneous reaction heat, and thermal radiation significantly modify the temperature distribution; meanwhile, Schmidt number, thermophoresis, Brownian motion, and homogeneous reaction strongly influence the nanoparticle concentration. Additionally, artificial neural networks (ANNs) are employed to predict nanofluid behavior under varying physical conditions, including the influence of viscous dissipation, heat flux, and magnetic fields. The Levenberg-Marquardt backpropagation algorithm is applied for estimating key transport properties such as the Sherwood number, Nusselt number, and skin friction coefficient. ANN predictions are validated through training accuracy, performance metrics, regression analysis, and error histogram evaluations. The findings confirm that the ANN model provides highly accurate predictions, optimizing computational efficiency. This research has significant applications in energy systems, thermal regulation, chemical processing, biomedical advancements, vehicle cooling, nuclear reactors, and transportation system optimization. For the Nusselt number, the ANN predictions exhibit an average absolute percentage error of 2.9680% and a coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.9130, demonstrating good agreement with the numerical results. The maximum prediction error is 15.1120% for Case 8, followed by 8.1079% for Case 10. These results confirm that the developed ANN model can effectively reproduce the nonlinear numerical predictions over the investigated range.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted analysis of reactive tetra-hybrid Jeffrey nanofluid flow with thermal radiation and Joule heating

evidence_items.summary: As higher education institutions increasingly adopt Artificial Intelligence (AI) to support curriculum mapping, these pipelines rely heavily on text embedding models to align internal module/course learning outcomes (LO) with degree programme outcomes and external accreditation standards. However, a critical assumption remains largely untested: do general-purpose text embedding models used to compare LO similarity adequately represent the unique, multidimensional semantics of pedagogical texts? In educational theory, an LO is not an ordinary sentence; it strictly binds a disciplinary topic to a specific cognitive process (e.g., Bloom's Taxonomy). General-purpose models risk conflating these orthogonal dimensions, prioritising topical overlap while ignoring pedagogical rigor. Using a dataset of 6,790 authentic LOs from a UK higher education institution, this work investigates whether current text embedding models capture this bipartite structure in their vector embeddings. Through a controlled semantic perturbation methodology: comparing verb ablation against cognitive tier changing, we quantify how vector spaces distort pedagogical intent when distinct cognitive actions share identical subject matter. Preliminary findings indicate that standard embedding models are overwhelmingly dominated by topical context, effectively rendering cognitive verbs invisible in the latent space. This systematic fusion poses severe false-positive risks for automated curriculum auditing, highlighting the need for pedagogy-aware text embeddings.
evidence_items.title: Can Text Embeddings Distinguish Cognitive Depth in Learning Outcomes?

evidence_items.summary: We update our 2022 mapping of 441 quantum technology (QT) companies and examine how the industry has developed. The principal dataset now includes 1,092 companies founded with a QT focus, of which 935 remain active. Public sources and archived company websites provide evidence on company formation, technology fields and geography, alongside acquisitions, closures, valuations and involvement in artificial intelligence, defence and space. Company formation continued beyond the apparent 2018 peak in the earlier study. Computing software and applications remain the largest field, with suppliers and supporting businesses accounting for almost a third of active companies. Countries with similar company totals can have different technological profiles, and regional comparisons reveal concentrations obscured by country rankings. The first companies generally preceded the selected national policy milestones. Supporting businesses usually followed technical companies in the same jurisdiction. AI is more prevalent than defence in current company activities, while defence shows the larger increase from the earliest assessed evidence. Space relevance is documented for more than a quarter of active companies, often alongside defence involvement.
evidence_items.title: The landscape of quantum technology companies in 2026

evidence_items.summary: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may provide personalised and dynamically adjustable support for chronic disease self-management. However, previous studies have largely focused on isolated questions and a limited range of evaluation dimensions. Objective To compare the quality of self-management advice generated by GenAI and primary care physicians (PCPs) across multiple stages of chronic disease management and evaluation dimensions. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional, source-blinded comparative evaluation using 15 standardised vignettes of diabetes and hypertension derived from authentic primary care follow-up records. Each vignette comprised three sequential management stages, with medical accuracy, readability, and behaviour-change potential assessed across the three simulated stages; individualisation and multidisciplinary integration at plan initiation; contextual adaptability during acute adjustment; and empathy during long-term maintenance. The GenAI system and 22 PCPs independently generated advice which was independently rated by three cliniciansone each from general practice, endocrinology, and cardiology. across seven dimensions. Linear mixed-effects models were used for the primary comparisons, and case-level paired and physician-distribution analyses were conducted as robustness analyses. Results The GenAI system achieved estimated marginal means above 4.0 in all dimensions except readability. It scored significantly higher than PCPs in six of the seven dimensions, with adjusted mean differences ranging from 1.16 to 1.56 points (P<.001). Readability was the only exception, with no significant difference between GenAI and PCPs (-0.22, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.11; P=.19). The GenAI mean exceeded the individual means of all recruited PCPs in the six dimensions but ranked at approximately the 23rd percentile for readability. Conclusions Our findings indicated the GenAI system may generate more highly rated self-management advice than PCPs across most evaluated dimensions but offered no advantage in readability. These findings provide pre-implementation evidence for GenAI as a potential source of structured and adaptive chronic disease self-management support. Patient-level pilot studies and subsequent randomised trials are needed to determine its acceptability and effects on behaviour and clinical outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Generative AI Versus Primary Care Physicians from Plan Initiation to Long-Term Maintenance of Chronic Disease Self-Management: A Vignette-Based Validation Study

evidence_items.summary: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping the technology labor market and raising fundamental questions regarding the adequacy of traditional Computing Undergraduate Programs (CUPs) in preparing graduates for evolving software development practices. Historically, entry level software development roles have served as a critical transition between academic study and professional practice. However, the increasing integration of GenAI-based tools automates routine coding tasks, thereby reducing the relative importance of basic programming. At the same time, it elevates the need for higher-order competencies, including system level reasoning, architectural design, system integration, and the critical evaluation of AI-generated outputs, as well as concerns of security and reliability. Correspondingly, graduates face increasing difficulty in securing initial positions. These developments raise the question of whether existing CUP structures provide an adequate foundation for early-career competencies. In response, this spotlight proposes a staged modular structure organized into coherent packs, each pack includes courses, defined learning outcomes and competences alongside integrative projects. In addition, the proposed modular structure identifies the appropriate point, recognized by the institutions that will grant professional certificates, with which students can begin engaging in entry-level professional roles while continuing their academic studies. Such parallel engagement may create a feedback loop between academic learning and professional practice: practical experience can deepen the relevance and value of academic study, while continued coursework can support more reflective, informed, and theoretically grounded professional development.
evidence_items.title: Toward Industry-Aligned, Flexible, Computing Undergraduate Programs in the AI Era

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly central to computing education, yet its environmental implications are largely absent from curricula. While students learn to optimise predictive performance, efficiency, and correctness, the energy consumption and carbon footprint of AI systems remain peripheral concerns. This omission risks normalising unsustainable practices among future computing professionals. We introduce the Sustainable Computing in AI (SCAI) framework, a structured approach for embedding environmental responsibility into AI education. SCAI integrates three interrelated layers: (1) the Lifecycle Layer, which identifies environmental impact across data, training and fine-tuning, deployment and inference, and maintenance stages; (2) the Evaluation Layer, which extends traditional performance metrics to incorporate energy, computational efficiency, and model appropriateness; and (3) the Pedagogical Layer, which specifies learning outcomes, instructional activities, and assessment strategies that foreground sustainability. By connecting technical decision-making, assessment, and pedagogy, SCAI transforms sustainability from an abstract principle into an explicit, assessable component of coursework.
evidence_items.title: Sustainable Computing in AI (SCAI) Framework: Integrating Environmental Responsibility into AI Education

evidence_items.summary: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence in programming education has intensified concerns about the transparency and reproducibility of empirical studies involving code generation, automated feedback, and AI-assisted tutoring. Existing research frequently underreports critical methodological details such as prompt design, development environments, evaluation protocols, and mechanisms for validating AI-generated code, limiting interpretability and replication. While the Reporting AI Studies in Education (RAISE) framework provides a comprehensive structure for improving reporting quality, its generic educational wording does not consistently specify the technical and methodological details required for programming education studies, where executable artefacts, development toolchains, and debugging processes are central to study design. This paper proposes RAISE-Prog, a domain-specific extension of RAISE for AI-supported programming education studies. It retains RAISE's ten-domain, thirty-item structure while adapting and extending individual reporting requirements, including reproducible coding environments, prompt and workflow specification, code validation practices, and academic integrity considerations in AI-assisted programming tasks. The paper outlines the rationale for the extension, presents the adapted checklist, and discusses directions for future validation through community consensus and empirical evaluation.
evidence_items.title: RAISE-Prog: Extending the Reporting AI Studies in Education Framework for Programming Education

evidence_items.summary: Computing students experience challenges with negative perceptions toward writing and communicating technical ideas. While generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) writing tools provide immediate support, they often generate complete written content, which may reduce students' active participation and sense of ownership. ProseSpark is introduced as a consent-based agentic AI writing companion designed to support computing students without writing on their behalf. ProseSpark is grounded in human-centered AI and self-regulated learning theory to maintain student autonomy and encourage active engagement throughout the writing process. This poster presents ProseSpark's design principles, platform, and responsible-AI safeguards. Future evaluation will examine how workflow-oriented AI support influences computing students' motivation, engagement, and writing self-efficacy.
evidence_items.title: ProseSpark: Preserving Student Agency in Computing Writing with an Agentic AI Companion

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is quickly expanding the capacity of organizations to produce and analyze data. We argue that this expansion shifts the leverage of data scientists from performing individual analyses to assessing the credibility and importance of findings and determining when evidence generalizes across contexts. Drawing on a roundtable of academic researchers and industry practitioners, we examine three ways in which data scientists who work on causal inference and experimentation can help organizations turn more analytical capacity into better decisions: preserving and accumulating the learning value of experimentation beyond individual tests; choosing and combining experimental, observational, and synthetic evidence; and ensuring evaluation keeps pace with AI as its capabilities and uses evolve. In each area, we distinguish established practice from open questions. We conclude with implications for the training and practice of data science and for organizations.
evidence_items.title: From More to Better: Causal Inference and Digital Experimentation in the Age of AI

evidence_items.summary: In today's technology-driven world, data and artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is critical across all different job sectors. While curricula in science and engineering disciplines are updated routinely to reflect the need for data and AI literacy, this is not the case for liberal arts disciplines. In fact, coursework within most liberal arts disciplines does not explicitly emphasize improving students' data and AI literacy. In this work, we use occupational-skill data and domain-expert interpretation to identify potential data and AI literacy gaps in selected liberal arts curricula. Our study finds that current LA coursework provides limited explicit training in the data and AI literacy skills demanded by many LA-oriented careers. We also describe how integrating data and AI literacy projects into existing coursework can support students' development of these skills and present preliminary evidence of promise from a mixed formative evaluation across four projects.
evidence_items.title: Improving Data and AI Literacy in Liberal Arts Curriculum: A Project-based Approach

evidence_items.summary: Lung cancer screening (LCS) with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) significantly reduces mortality among high-risk individuals, yet implementation remains limited at national and European levels. The Strengthening the Screening of Lung Cancer (SOLACE) Project aims to facilitate the implementation of equitable LCS. While considering the overall impact of LCS, we identified a lack of systematic evaluation on the impact on the workload of radiology professionals, including radiologists and radiographers. This multicentric, European-wide study prospectively examines the effects of LCS on radiology healthcare workers. A survey-based cross-sectional study was conducted among European radiology professionals engaged in LCS to evaluate their experiences across seven domains: impacts on workload, workflow specifics, reporting practices, artificial intelligence (AI) use, participation in training programmes, potential professional development, and overall support for LCS. We evaluated 56 responses (mean age 46 ± 10.8 years; 27 men) from 14 countries. About half of respondents (53.6%; n = 30) reported increased working hours, but only 21.6% (n = 11) felt overworked due to LCS. No significant factors were directly associated with feeling overworked. Most respondents (86.7%; n = 39) perceived increased expertise in assessing LCS LDCTs throughout screening, and 91.1% (n = 51) expressed support for the implementation of LCS. Although LCS increased workload for many radiology professionals, few reported feeling overworked. Despite the added demands, there may be added benefits for radiology professionals. Taken together, these findings emphasise the importance of continuously evaluating and monitoring how LCS affects the workload of radiology healthcare professionals. Question As wider implementation of lung cancer screening occurs in Europe, it is critical to consider its impact on radiology professionals’ workload and associated workforce demands. Findings Although lung cancer screening increased workload for many radiology professionals, few felt overworked, and the majority perceived increased diagnostic confidence and support for screening implementation. Lung cancer screening via LDCT plays a critical role in detecting cancer earlier and improving survival. With growing support for the broader implementation of LCS, it is essential to consider its potential impact on the workload of radiology professionals.
evidence_items.title: Impact of lung cancer screening on the workload of radiology professionals

evidence_items.summary: Artificial Intelligence is developing at a rapid pace resulting in rising concerns relating to the ethical implications of this technology. AI professionals are in greater demand alongside a concomitant increase in interest in studying this topic. AI educational programs primarily teach the technical components of this domain, with ethical and socio-technical concerns seen as an optional extra. Therefore, a change in pedagogical approach is imperative to ensure the future AI workforce are critical and socially responsible practitioners. We propose a critical pedagogical methodology to interweave intersectionality, ethics and social responsibility into AI education to address the inequalities of AI in society. Tangible approaches to a critical AI curriculum are outlined in this paper including incorporating algorithmic social impact assessments, datasheets for datasets and embedding ethics within technical assessment to demonstrate to students the intrinsic socio-technical nature of AI.
evidence_items.title: CAP: Critical AI Pedagogy

evidence_items.summary: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly integrated into EFL writing instruction, little is known about how learners perceive emotional changes during engagement with AI-generated feedback. Guided by Complex Dynamic Systems Theory (CDST) as an interpretive framework, this qualitative study explored 50 Chinese university EFL learners' retrospective perceptions of emotional change during a 16-week GenAI-assisted writing course. Post-course semi-structured interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis. Participants described relief and curiosity at the outset, greater enjoyment and confidence as familiarity increased, and increasingly reflective engagement with AI feedback. Immediate, accessible, and less face-threatening feedback reduced writing pressure and encouraged revision, whereas suggestions perceived as inappropriate, mechanical, or difficult to evaluate produced uncertainty and concerns about dependence and authorial voice. Learners' evaluative decisions and teacher guidance appeared to support calibrated trust and a stronger sense of agency. Overall, participants described a broadly positive pattern of emotional development, in which enjoyment and confidence coexisted with concerns about AI reliability, dependence, and authorial voice-a configuration we describe as positive emotions under tension. The study extends CDST-informed research by interpreting L2 emotion in relation to GenAI affordances, evaluative judgments, learner agency, and instructional guidance, and highlights the need to combine the emotional benefits of GenAI feedback with critical AI literacy.
evidence_items.title: Positive emotions under tension in GenAI-assisted L2 writing: A complex dynamic systems perspective.

evidence_items.summary: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more prevalent in daily life, developing AI literacy and computational thinking (CT) in K--12 students is increasingly important. Recent AI education programs focus heavily on machine learning (ML), but rule-based systems lie at the intersection of CT and symbolic AI, offering an opportunity to teach both. The recent interest in neuro-symbolic AI highlights the continued relevance of symbolic reasoning. To address this need, we developed RuleRunners, a novel web application that teaches rule-based systems through a gamified parkour environment. In this work, our research questions were: (RQ1) How does RuleRunners impact student learning of rule-based systems?; (RQ2) How do students compare rule-based systems and machine learning models?; and (RQ3) How engaging is the two-player collaborative and competitive design of RuleRunners? We evaluated RuleRunners at an in-classroom AI Expo event with 8th grade students, collecting qualitative and quantitative data to assess student learning and engagement. Our results show that RuleRunners effectively helped students understand the fundamentals of rule-based systems and some advantages over ML models. Furthermore, we found that interaction with RuleRunners led to a statistically significant improvement in performance on a matched pre- and post-survey item about rules. These findings suggest that RuleRunners can be adopted to support K--12 AI education initiatives, as it fosters AI literacy and CT through a collaborative, engaging experience.
evidence_items.title: RuleRunners: A Two-Player Collaborative Software Tool for Introducing Rule-Based AI Systems to Middle School Students

evidence_items.summary: 1. Monitoring plant biodiversity requires identifying large numbers of plants across space and time. Although artificial intelligence (AI) can now identify plant species from images with high accuracy, most existing systems rely on users manually submitting images. As ecological monitoring increasingly generates large image collections from cameras, drones, robots and online platforms, there is a growing need for plant identification services that can be directly integrated into automated data-processing workflows. 2. Here, we present Pl@ntNet's machine-to-machine AI plant identification service. This service uses an application programming interface (API) to provide programmatic access to Pl@ntNet's plant recognition models and the associated taxonomic processing. This service enables the implementation of automated identification workflows without human intervention and can thus directly link large image collections and automated observation systems to an AI-based plant identification system. 3. We establish that this service, which covers 85,000 species from around the world, (1) has a species prediction accuracy of 0.89, (2) process images up to 666 times faster than workflows requiring human intervention, (3) and has processed over 84 million identification requests since its launch, including more than 40 million in 2025 alone. We demonstrate how it has already enabled the implementation of a new generation of ecological workflows: identifying plants from images of insects to reconstruct the plant-pollinator interactions, analysing geolocated images from social media to study plant distribution, detecting invasive plants using images taken at the roadside, and identifying weeds using agricultural robots. Finally, we illustrate its application using a reproducible example: identifying plants from insect photos on iNaturalist. In approximately 30 min on a standard laptop, 2,424 images were processed to generate a dataset of 708 plant-pollinator interactions, with a weighted precision of 0.98 for flower detection and an accuracy of 0.88 for genus plant identification. 4. In conclusion, this machine-to-machine species identification is already operating on a considerable scale and meets a genuine need. All of this paves the way for a new paradigm in biodiversity monitoring, in which automated sensors and image collections can be directly connected to AI-based identification services.
evidence_items.title: Pl@ntNet machine-to-machine identification service with Pl@ntNet API: enabling automated biodiversity monitoring through large-scale plant identification

evidence_items.summary: Cross-view pose estimation estimates a ground camera's geographic pose by matching onboard sensor data with geo-referenced overhead imagery. This is particularly relevant when GNSS is unreliable, for example under forest canopy or in urban canyons. Existing metric cross-view benchmarks, such as VIGOR and cross-view KITTI, are dominated by urban and road scenes with strong human-made structure without off-road terrain. We introduce GOOSELoc, a multimodal benchmark for ground-to-aerial localization in unstructured environments, including forests, fields, and rural tracks. GOOSELoc comprises 9,356 scenes recorded across all four seasons around Munich, Germany, pairing geo-referenced aerial orthophotos with surround-view RGB imagery and 3D LiDAR point clouds. Paved/unpaved labels enable analyzing the impact of terrain structure, while the seasonal recordings allow studying the appearance gap to mostly summer-captured orthophotos. To assess the transferability of existing methods, we adapt and fine-tune four state-of-the-art cross-view localization baselines on GOOSELoc. Despite task-specific fine-tuning, the performance degrades substantially in off-road environments. We therefore propose a multimodal baseline combining surround-view imagery and LiDAR geometry, improving localization performance and providing a stronger reference for future work. Data and baselines are released at https://gooseloc.github.io.
evidence_items.title: GOOSELoc: A Multimodal Benchmark for Ground-to-Aerial Localization in Unstructured Off-Road Terrain

organizations: University of Information Technology and Sciences
evidence_items.summary: Urban landfill activities can significantly alter the quality of nearby water systems through the release of metal-enriched leachate, raising concerns for environmental sustainability and public health in rapidly urbanizing regions. This study assesses heavy metal contamination in urban water systems in Dhaka, Bangladesh, using an integrated approach that combines Water Quality Index (WQI), GIS-based spatial analysis, and exploratory data-driven modelling. Twelve water samples were collected from three major landfill-influenced zones (Matuail, Amin Bazar, and Kodda) during a post-monsoon field campaign in October 2025. Samples were analyzed for key physicochemical parameters and selected heavy metals, including iron (Fe), manganese (Mn), and lead (Pb). Water quality conditions were evaluated using WQI, while spatial mapping was applied to identify contamination patterns and high-risk zones associated with landfill proximity. Exploratory statistical and machine-learning-assisted analyses were used only to examine potential inter-parameter relationships under severe data constraints. WQI values ranged from 45 to 185, with 67% of sampling sites classified as poor to unsuitable for drinking purposes. Spatial analysis revealed pronounced contamination gradients radiating from landfill zones, with metal concentrations generally decreasing with distance from waste-disposal sites. Lead emerged as the most critical concern, exceeding the WHO guideline value (0.01 mg/L) at 75% of sampling locations, with a maximum concentration of 0.18 mg/L in landfill-proximal zones. Iron and manganese showed exceedance rates of 58% and 50%, respectively, reflecting mixed geogenic and anthropogenic influences. Although predictive performance of the data-driven models was constrained by the limited sample size (Model performance indicated limited predictive generalization under data constraints, while still providing useful insight into controlling factors), exploratory feature-importance analysis indicated that electrical conductivity, organic load (BOD, COD), and site-proximity factors were among the most influential variables in model outputs under data-limited conditions; these patterns should be interpreted as preliminary signals rather than confirmed causal controls. Overall, the findings indicate that integrated WQI-GIS assessment, supported by exploratory modelling, provides a preliminary basis for contamination hotspot screening and targeted water quality monitoring in landfill-impacted urban environments. The findings should be interpreted with caution due to the limited sample size (n = 12), single-season sampling, and uncertainty associated with spatial interpolation. The study highlights lead contamination as a priority public-health concern requiring immediate monitoring and mitigation in Dhaka’s landfill-adjacent communities.
evidence_items.title: Heavy metal contamination in landfill-impacted urban water systems: a GIS-based WQI and spatial risk assessment in Dhaka, Bangladesh
Time and Accuracy of Manual Protected Health Information Redaction in Biospecimen and Clinical Research Workflows: An Exploratory Pilot Benchmark Against Automation.

evidence_items.summary: In July 2026, the European Commission (EC) set out the anonymization measures Alphabet must implement to share Google Search data with competing search engines under Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act. As the first concrete illustration of how the EC operationalizes anonymization under the EU digital rulebook, this methodology could become a regulatory benchmark. In this paper, we show why it should not. We critically review the anonymization measures proposed by the EC, from the characterization of residual risk to the suppression thresholds and the reliance on contractual safeguards. For each of those issues, we highlight significant conceptual flaws, and, where applicable, we illustrate these flaws with empirical observations from real Google Search data provided by Alphabet and protected under the EC's measures. Importantly, we present examples of low-effort reidentification, record linkage, and confidential attribute inference achieved through straightforward and automatable attack patterns. Our findings show that the approach of the EC relies on unjustified heuristics rather than formal privacy guarantees, underestimates the risks inherent in free-text search queries, and sacrifices data utility without achieving meaningful protection. We also demonstrate that the proposed measures do not meet any of the three anonymization criteria established by the European Data Protection Board (EDPB): no record isolation, no linkage, and no inference. Practitioners and regulators are therefore cautioned against treating these measures as a sound anonymization practice.
evidence_items.title: Anonymous in Name Only: A Critical Review and a Reidentification Exercise on the European Commission's Anonymization Measures for Google Search Data under Article 6(11) of the DMA

evidence_items.summary: Mangrove forests are essential in improving coastal resilience, biodiversity, and carbon sequestration. However, they are increasingly threatened by anthropogenic pressures, particularly pollution such as oil contamination, which can induce long-term physiological stress in mangrove vegetation. Yet, monitoring the health of such ecosystems across large areas is difficult due to the scarcity of ground-based data and the spatial resolution-coverage trade-off. In light of this, we propose a scalable deep learning framework that incorporates hyperspectral imagery and transfer learning to classify mangrove species and retrieve canopy-level biochemical traits, including pigments, sugars, and phenols. The framework is a Multi-Task Convolutional Neural Network (MTS-CNN) organized in a teacher-student architecture with pseudo-labeling. The teacher model, trained on airborne hyperspectral imagery at 0.5 m resolution, generates pseudo-labels and transfers its learned weights to student models developed on satellite datasets from PRISMA (5 m, pansharpened) and EnMAP (30 m), enabling knowledge transfer from high- to lower-resolution sensors. Despite differences in spatial resolution, the predicted biochemical patterns remained spatially consistent across sensors. Results show accuracies above 95% for airborne data, approximately 70% for PRISMA, and 60% for EnMAP. Spectral analysis additionally confirmed that the predicted classes retained key absorption features characteristic of the target biochemical compounds. Furthermore, the resulting maps could distinguish biochemical signatures associated with oil contamination from those caused by other stressors. These results demonstrate that cross-scale transfer learning can support broad monitoring of mangrove ecosystems by propagating biochemical information from high-resolution observations to satellite hyperspectral imagery.
evidence_items.title: Retrieving mangrove biochemical traits under oil pollution using hyperspectral data and transfer learning.

evidence_items.summary: Micro aerial vehicles that operate without GPS often run SLAM on ARM-based edge boards, yet there is little published data on how standard RGB-D SLAM systems behave on such hardware. We benchmark RTAB-Map and ORB-SLAM3 on the Raspberry Pi 5 using six TUM RGB-D sequences at three image resolutions, recording tracking coverage, trajectory error, time per frame, memory, CPU load and temperature for every run, and we profile both systems at the stage and function level. RTAB-Map was configured to process and keep every frame, so its back end runs on every frame rather than at its default rate of 1 Hz. On the sequences that every configuration tracked, its front end takes 38-74 ms per frame and its full pipeline 150-462 ms, compared with 13-45 ms and 26-62 ms for ORB-SLAM3. RTAB-Map's main cost is optimizing a pose graph that keeps growing, because its working memory is unbounded by default; ORB-SLAM3's local bundle adjustment costs about as much as its tracking but runs in a parallel thread. At quarter resolution, both systems lose tracking on most sequences, and runs that lose tracking finish sooner and report lower error on the poses they keep, so time and accuracy must be read alongside coverage. Timing is repeatable to within 1-5%, but trajectory error varies by up to 27% between identical runs, so the accuracy differences between the two systems are inconclusive. No thermal throttling occurred.
evidence_items.title: RGB-D SLAM on the Edge: Benchmarking and Profiling RTAB-Map and ORB-SLAM3 on the Raspberry Pi 5

evidence_items.summary: To investigate local erosion in split-frame aqueducts under sediment-laden flow, a three-dimensional water–sediment two-phase numerical model was developed using the RNG k–ε turbulence model, the Discrete Phase Model (DPM), and the Neilson–Gilchrist erosion model. The model was validated against flume-test data for pier erosion. The effects of discharge, sediment concentration, and particle size on erosion at different aqueduct sections were then examined, and pier-end aspect-ratio schemes were compared in terms of velocity distribution and erosion response. The mean relative error between simulated and measured erosion thicknesses under four benchmark inlet velocities was 6.76%. The inlet split-frame pier region, upstream aqueduct body, and turning zones of the outlet transition section were identified as the main high-erosion regions. Within the tested range, erosion generally increased with discharge, sediment concentration, and particle size. A combined scheme with AR₁ = 1.5 at the inlet and AR₂ = 2.0 at the outlet produced a smoother velocity transition, reduced the outlet wake-affected region, and yielded lower model-predicted erosion rates than the original semi-circular configuration in most cases. These results provide numerical support for erosion-risk identification and preliminary pier-geometry selection in similar water-conveyance structures.
evidence_items.title: Numerical simulation of water-sediment two-phase erosion in a split-frame aqueduct and comparison of pier geometry schemes

evidence_items.summary: Background: Over 3.5 million US men are living with prostate cancer (PCa). Certain per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are carcinogenic and impair cardiometabolic health. Due to comorbidities and treatment, men with PCa may be uniquely susceptible to PFAS. Objectives: To develop and validate a model for drinking water perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS), and perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA), and study associations of each PFAS with all-cause, PCa, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality in PCa survivors. Methods: We conducted a cohort study of 51,289 men with PCa diagnosed from 2006 to 2017 and followed through 2024 from the New Jersey (NJ) cancer registry. PFAS monitoring data (n=26,161 results) were obtained from NJ government evaluations and Community Water Systems (CWS) compliance reports and were used to estimate PFAS concentrations using a two-phase XGBoost model with 67 predictors of PFAS contamination across 566 CWS. PFAS predictions between 2006-2024 were linked to participant address histories. Adjusted hazard ratios (aHR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were estimated from Cox models with sociodemographic, clinical and time-varying neighborhood covariates. Results: There were 19,749 deaths, including 3,778 PCa deaths, and 4,972 CVD deaths over 466,843 person-years. Higher PFOA exposure was associated with all-cause mortality in certain quintiles (aHRQ2vsQ1: 1.07, 95% CI: 1.07-1.12; aHRQ3vsQ1: 1.06, 95% CI: 1.01-1.11) and with CVD mortality (aHRQ5vsQ1: 1.12, 95% CI: 1.01-1.24). Higher PFNA exposure was suggestively associated with all-cause mortality (aHR[≥]3.8ng/L vs <2ng/L: 1.22, 95% CI: 0.98-1.50) and PCa mortality (aHR[≥]3.8ng/L vs <2ng/L: 1.42, 95% CI: 0.96-2.10). Associations were strengthened when applying five-year lags. For example, higher PFOA (aHRQ5vsQ1: 1.15, 95% CI: 1.06-1.25), PFOS (aHRQ5vsQ1: 1.16, 95% CI: 1.07-1.25) and PFNA (aHR[≥]3.8ng/L vs <2ng/L: 1.57, 95% CI: 1.06-2.31) were associated with higher all-cause mortality. Discussion: Exposure to CWS-level PFAS was associated with higher mortality in PCa survivors. Replication is needed to confirm findings.
evidence_items.title: Associations of drinking water per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances with cause-specific mortality in men with prostate cancer

evidence_items.summary: Aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) is a mycotoxin, or fungal toxin, that contaminates maize, peanuts, and tree nuts grown in warm regions of the world. It causes liver cancer and is synergistic with chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection to multiplicatively increase cancer risk. Peanuts (also called groundnuts) are a major source of aflatoxin exposure in many populations worldwide. We conducted a systematic data review to examine the occurrence of AFB1 in peanut food products in 106 nations. We then conducted a dietary exposure assessment based on this occurrence dataset and consumption of peanuts in these nations, to compare trends across the time periods from 1990 to 2024. 22 nations experienced a substantial increase in aflatoxin exposure through peanut consumption, and 22 nations experienced a substantial decrease. Changes in exposure are largely driven by changes in intake levels. Many sub-Saharan African populations have alarmingly high levels of aflatoxin exposure, due to high contamination coupled with high consumption. Detection methods are shown to demonstrate recent improvements in sensitivity. These findings are important given the health risks of high aflatoxin exposure; most notably liver cancer.
evidence_items.title: Aflatoxin B1 exposure through peanuts worldwide: national level occurrence and exposure assessment.

evidence_items.summary: Reference-frame stabilization registers every frame of a hovering-drone video onto one reference frame, keeping object positions comparable. The registration pipelines it relies on are selected on feature-matching benchmarks in which only the camera moves. Over a busy intersection, vehicles moving together supply mutually consistent correspondences that can draw the robust homography estimate toward their motion: consensus capture, which inlier statistics cannot flag. A two-part benchmark measures it and the object masking meant to prevent it. A static protocol scores ten pipelines under exactly known homographies on 4K aerial frames, tuned on a site-disjoint split at a matched resolution and feature budget. A dynamic protocol scores them at an offline and a real-time budget on hovers selected from the video alone to span the amount and coherence of moving foreground, plus a stationary control. It measures background alignment, object position error and the share of a moving group's displacement an estimate follows, against a pseudo-ground-truth reference audited with manually annotated ground control points, which also score every candidate. On static scenes, tuned AKAZE, RootSIFT, SIFT and BRISK lead, retuning the matcher thresholds raises the mean average accuracy (mAA) by at most 0.0062, and masking costs less than 0.005. Unmasked ORB is captured on 28 of 304 real-time dynamic pairs and on 6 offline; its real-time captured estimates have a median corner error of 18.8 px yet typical inlier counts and ratios. Masking removes capture for every pipeline and leaves the leading pipelines unchanged. Code, data and results are released.
evidence_items.title: Consensus Capture in Reference-Based UAV Video Stabilization: A Benchmark on Dynamic Urban Scenes

evidence_items.summary: Existing adaptive-reasoning methods shorten the explicit reasoning a model writes, or skip it by switching modes; either way the answer is still written out token by token. Rather than deciding how much to think, we explore a different paradigm, zero-or-T thinking: a single model either answers from the implicit thinking inside one forward pass, generating no token, or performs full autoregressive reasoning at a cost of T tokens when that is worth paying. We realise it in a hybrid decision model (HDM), where one frozen backbone serves both modes and a lightweight self-routing block chooses between them. The block estimates the value of thinking, the utility the slow mode is expected to add over the fast one, from what that implicit thinking has already produced, and the slow mode runs only where that value exceeds a price λ set per request. Where no per-decision label exists, as in episodic agentic tasks, we introduce Calibrated Decision Policy Optimisation (CDPO), a reinforcement-learning recipe that trains the block from episode-level returns. We evaluate HDM on MMLU-Pro, AGIEval, GPQA-Diamond, JevBench, BANKING77 and MiniWoB. Specifically, on JevBench HDM-4B scores 0.857 against Jev's 0.851 (+0.7%) at a median 0.179\,s against 0.652 (-72.5%). On the agentic venue MiniWoB HDM-27B cuts token cost by 80.1%.
evidence_items.title: The Value of Thinking: Learning When to Reason in Hybrid Decision Models

evidence_items.summary: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.
evidence_items.title: Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding

evidence_items.summary: Decoder-only Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) with KV-cache have recently achieved state-of-the-art quality by regressing novel views from neural networks without reconstructing 3D geometry, while Test-Time Training (TTT) layers save computation but sacrifice quality. We propose Test-Time Baking (TTB), a strategy that learns to bake global scene information from cross-view attention into a lightweight MLP, enabling fast and high-fidelity novel-view decoding. The first key is to repurpose the fast-weight MLP of TTT to learn the cross-view attention mapping explicitly from its input-output pairs, rather than replacing attention entirely, achieving the same rendering efficiency as TTT while delivering substantially higher quality. The second key addresses a modality misalignment between context prefilling and novel-view rendering: we disentangle context tokens into camera-only context rendering tokens to serve as TTB input, and context ground-truth tokens with image content to serve as the TTB mapping target, ensuring the baked MLPs are relieved of the modality generalization challenge between context and novel-view processing. Our method achieves up to **23x** rendering speedup with quality on par with the state-of-the-art across several benchmarks. Project page: https://test-time-baking.github.io
evidence_items.title: TTB: Test-time Baking for Efficient Rendering of Decoder-only View Synthesis Models

evidence_items.summary: Transferring LLMs into System One decision models typically replaces the language modeling head with a decision head while retaining the full backbone, making every decision pay for all layers. Yet it remains unclear how much depth such decisions require. We find that decision information is concentrated in intermediate layers, with early layers building essential features and the final six layers removable without loss, while independently trained smaller models largely mimic the full model rather than developing specialized decision capabilities. These findings suggest that efficiency requires not simply smaller backbones, but shared computation across different depths. Building on this, we propose , which jointly trains a full model with prefix sub-models that share its final layers and decision head through self-distillation. A lightweight gate reads the hidden state at each exit to determine whether additional computation is needed, allowing one model to operate at multiple layers. Across seven decision benchmarks, our approach matches or outperforms independently trained models at every depth, while achieving better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs through adaptive computation.
evidence_items.title: From Large Language Models to Efficient System One Models via Adaptive Computation

evidence_items.summary: Medical imaging is essential for diagnosing disease, guiding treatment and monitoring patients over time. Although artificial intelligence has advanced image interpretation, existing medical models often address restricted tasks, while general-purpose proprietary models lack access to private clinical imaging required to achieve medical expertise. Developing models that can interpret complex examinations and communicate their findings in the context of clinical decisions remains a major challenge. Here, we show that Neuro-VL, a vision-language model trained on nearly one million neuroimaging studies from routine clinical care, can interpret complete imaging examinations and engage in natural language conversations about their findings. Across internal and international datasets, Neuro-VL outperformed frontier general-purpose and specialized medical models in diagnosing, localizing, and describing abnormalities, as well as generating comprehensive radiology reports. The model also compared serial examinations to assess disease progression and more reliably resisted misleading clinical assumptions than leading frontier models from OpenAI and Google. These results extend health system learning beyond individual predictions to interactive image interpretation and longitudinal disease monitoring. They demonstrate how the collective clinical experience of health systems can be used to develop medical AI with specialized expertise and broad clinical capabilities.
evidence_items.title: A frontier machine intelligence for human neuroimaging

evidence_items.summary: Recent work shows that multimodal agents increasingly self-improve without recurring human annotation. However, each self-improvement mechanism is designed and evaluated within a single scenario, leaving its preconditions unverified under cross-scenario transfer. This survey investigates the structural source of asymmetric mechanism transfer across four scenarios: multimodal reasoning, multimodal generation, GUI and Web navigation, and embodied manipulation. We first formalize the self-evolving multimodal agent by four criteria and a differentia of self-reference, and adopt the three-stage self-evolving loop of experience generation, feedback acquisition, and update consolidation as our analytical framework to position the scenarios along ceilings on rollout count and feedback fidelity. Comparing self-evolving with fixed loops within each scenario separates the limitations that the scenario imposes from those inherent in the self-evolving design. We then recast each mechanism as a trade-off that raises a scarce factor by presupposing a task-structural resource, such as output equivalence or checkable outcomes, and judge it portable, conditional, blocked, or redundant across scenarios. We attribute the asymmetry to divergent combinations of scarce factors and resources across opposite transfer directions, and identify the matched-budget measurements that could overturn these still untested verdicts.
evidence_items.title: A Cross-Scenario Survey and Analysis of Self-Evolving Multimodal Agents

evidence_items.summary: Adversarial training is often plagued by "pseudo-attacks", perturbations that significantly increase the loss value but fail to truly alter the model's confidence structure. To address this, we propose two complementary approaches to directly attack and defend against confidence structure deformation. First, building upon the traditional loss maximization perspective, we introduce a hybrid objective that integrates cross-entropy and KL divergence, encouraging adversarial examples to simultaneously disrupt prediction accuracy and distribution consistency. Second, we geometrically reconstruct adversarial training by generating perturbations that maximize the distribution distance on the confidence manifold. Theoretical analysis shows that the optimal perturbation direction aligns with the principal eigenvectors of the Fisher information matrix. We also propose an efficient algorithm to avoid high-dimensional matrix computations. Experiments on multiple datasets and model architectures demonstrate that our method outperforms existing methods in adversarial robustness and robust transferability, particularly excelling in structural perturbations within high-confidence regions.
evidence_items.title: Structured Confidence Perturbation via Fisher Geometry for Adversarial Training

evidence_items.summary: Driving world models aim to simulate how a scene unfolds under different ego actions. This requires plausible motion of surrounding vehicles as well as precise ego-trajectory control. Learning vehicle motion from perspective video alone is challenging because motion is entangled with appearance and vehicles can be occluded. Prior work therefore conditions video generation on layouts that specify vehicle motion, providing control over surrounding vehicles but requiring their future trajectories as inputs. We introduce BirdDreams, an autoregressive driving world model that jointly generates perspective video and a schematic bird's-eye-view (BEV) video, making scene layout part of the predicted future. The BEV, rendered from scene annotations for training, depicts roads and vehicles as simple shapes at a fixed metric scale, providing a top-down view of their positions and motion with reduced occlusion between vehicles. Perspective video, by contrast, retains scene details that the BEV omits, such as traffic signals and object appearance. Joint attention between two video diffusion transformers, one per stream, lets each stream inform the other during generation. The predicted BEV also provides a geometric interface for ego control: we translate and rotate its latest frame along an input ego trajectory and use the resulting frames as a soft condition that shows how the scene would appear to move if only the ego vehicle moved. At inference, BirdDreams generates both videos from a single camera image without requiring an HD map or vehicle-state inputs. On PhysicalAI-AV and nuScenes, BirdDreams follows input ego trajectories more faithfully than prior driving world models and generates more plausible ego motion without ego-action conditioning. Human evaluation shows that BirdDreams outperforms a perspective-only baseline in generating realistic surrounding-vehicle behavior.
evidence_items.title: BirdDreams: Joint Perspective and BEV Video Generation for a Plausible, Reactive Driving World Model

evidence_items.summary: As multimodal agents accumulate increasingly long interaction histories, effectively retrieving and utilizing past information becomes critical for long-term interaction. Existing memory systems typically rely on semantic retrieval over compressed memories and expose predefined representations, which may miss relevant memories and overlook heterogeneous evidence needs across queries. We introduce \hivemem, a multimodal memory framework that interleaves \textsc{H}or\textsc{i}zontal Memory Expansion with \textsc{Ve}rtical Evidence Composition. For horizontal memory expansion, \hivemem organizes memory episodes into a relational graph using textual and visual anchors, expanding semantically retrieved seeds with related neighbors to recover complementary information. For vertical evidence composition, each retrieved memory retains multiple evidence forms, including compact summaries, captions, grounded visual views, raw images, and interaction history. A lightweight trainable selector independently composes an evidence subset for each retrieved memory, enabling query-adaptive utilization of heterogeneous multimodal information. This two-dimensional design jointly broadens memory coverage and adapts the evidence contributed by individual memories. Experiments across three multimodal memory benchmarks show that \hivemem consistently improves task performance across base models while reducing token consumption by about 90\% compared with the most efficient competing multimodal baselines.
evidence_items.title: HiVe-Mem: Interleaving Horizontal Memory Expansion and Vertical Evidence Composition for Multimodal Agents

evidence_items.summary: Discrete autoregressive models offer a scalable framework for image generation. However, they face a fundamental trade-off: long token sequences preserve representation quality but slow generation, while aggressive spatial compression reduces representation capacity. Based on product quantization, we show that, under a fixed nominal information budget, group size should scale quadratically with the per-axis spatial compression factor. Building on this principle, we propose GSTAR, a spatial--group co-scaling framework that enables \(32\times\) and even effective \(64\times\) compression while preserving strong reconstruction, understanding, and generation performance. Since larger groups introduce intra-group dependencies that must be modeled efficiently, we analyze their impact on inference latency and generation quality and introduce a semi-autoregressive decoder that combines parallel feature computation with lightweight causal modeling. With these designs, our highly compressed models perform competitively with leading models across five representative text-to-image benchmarks (GenEval, DPG-Bench, PRISM, LongText-Bench, and Qwen-Image-Bench). At \(1024\times1024\) resolution, our model delivers a \(20\times\) speedup over prior discrete autoregressive models, generating each image in 2.5 seconds on a single NVIDIA H200. Together, these results show that highly compressed discrete representations can enable high-quality autoregressive generation at low latency.
evidence_items.title: G-STAR: Group-Scaled Token Capacity for Deeply Compressed Autoregressive Generation

evidence_items.summary: Tool timeouts can leave AI agents facing ambiguous tool outcomes and partial execution: an action may have failed, committed or remained in flight while other workflow steps have already completed. We formulate evidence-guided task recovery over approved obligations, provider capabilities and states compatible with public evidence. A shared admissibility check handles key expiry, authorization timing, dependencies and residual effects; a terminal certificate separates actual goal satisfaction from publicly supported safe completion. The known-model implementation combines standard observation-contingent planning with a separately implemented effect-history adjudicator. In a finite study of 37 assignments, planning and three active controls each certify 28 completions; four saved synthetic fee units incur additional computation. A preregistered assignment-held-out comparison then evaluates planning advice against evidence prompting with two local model bundles. Across 58 paired units in 19 previously developed task families, advice certifies 30 completions versus 9, a 36.2-percentage-point difference (exact family sign-flip p=0.0078), using 272 proposals versus 399. All 116 trajectories pass independent replay. Both models exhibit a positive completion difference. The comparison measures the evaluated advice interface under a common shield; search-versus-rule advice requires a separate matched comparison. Unknown and handoff outcomes remain explicit, with guarantees tied to the declared provider capabilities rather than arbitrary third-party exactly-once execution.
evidence_items.title: Evidence-Guided Recovery for AI Agents with Ambiguous Tool Outcomes and Partial Execution

evidence_items.summary: A spectrum can be given to a model as a table in nanometers or as a plot in photon energy, and the decision should not depend on which one it sees. When the data needed for an answer are missing, the model should say so. We test representation invariance and abstention on measured optical spectra of silicon metasurfaces (MOCLIP) and gold nanoparticles, with labels computed from the data. Each spectrum is shown as four tables (nm, μm, scientific notation, eV) and two plots (nm, eV), and partial spectra remove data inside or outside the queried range. We evaluate the decision models d3-nano and Jev 1.13, three GPT-6 Luna configurations and the Qwen3.5-2B base model. Changing only the representation moves accuracy by up to 41 percentage points within one model, mostly on photon-energy tables and plots. With the same evidence, asking in photon energy instead of wavelength helps some model-view pairs by 16-50 points and hurts others by up to 25. When the relevant extremum is removed, unadapted models rarely answer "undetermined". LoRA fine-tuning of d3-nano improves comparisons on the trained table formats, but much of its gain on unanswerable questions comes from a shortcut: it abstains whenever the input is truncated. Training with answerable truncations avoids the shortcut in all six seeds, with a 90-100 point gap between abstention after inside and outside cuts on held-out structures; with the same amount of extra original-task data, five of six seeds keep the shortcut. On gold spectra the two training sets perform similarly. Multimodal language models used for scientific decisions should be tested on equivalent representations and on missing evidence, not only on average accuracy. We release the tasks, per-response results and analysis code.
evidence_items.title: Do Multimodal Models Decide Consistently on Equivalent Optical Spectra?

evidence_items.summary: AI "humanizers" rewrite machine-generated text so that detectors classify it as human-written. Public leaderboards score evasion and embedding similarity, but not whether checkable details survive. We check whether numbers, dates, person and organization names, and quoted spans survive each rewrite, using a rule-based checker validated by two AI annotators (precision 0.84-1.00, recall 0.93-0.95; no human annotation). In the October 2026 cycle of a public humanizer leaderboard, all 11 commercial tools changed or dropped at least one of these units in 35-65% of the documents that contained one. Most changes were to quoted spans; counting numbers and names alone, 10 of the 11 tools still altered at least one in 20% or more of the documents. The September 2026 cycle was similar (19-50%). An open 12B humanizer kept at least 97% of numbers and names in fact-dense U.S. federal agency text, but reworded 67-78% of the quoted spans, against its own prompt. Unit retention and detector evasion were not clearly related across tools (Spearman rho = -0.46, 95% CI -0.65 to 0.08), and the open model's four released files (two of them quantization-aware low-bit files) did not show the pre-registered monotone trade-off. On federal texts with matched human, AI-styled and humanized versions, a general-purpose decision model, Jev, asked a single zero-shot question, separated human originals from humanized rewrites with AUROC 0.864 (0.827-0.902), 0.18-0.22 higher than Binoculars, Fast-DetectGPT and the adversarially trained RADAR, while calling 24% of the human originals AI at a 0.5 threshold. On the AI-styled rewrites by 2026 models, both perplexity-based detectors scored below chance (AUROC 0.37 and 0.39), also with line breaks removed. Hypotheses, data rules and analyses were frozen before the main runs; two earlier data contacts are disclosed. We release the checker and the per-item results.
evidence_items.title: Humanized but Still True? Auditing Facts and Detection in AI-Text Humanizers

answers.plain_english: Treat this feed as a prompt to tighten evaluation practices, not to replace benchmarks blindly. If you use Ragas, test its update before deployment because its release note reports installation, security, and model-provider compatibility fixes. Lock exact dataset and evaluation versions, record fingerprints, and rerun comparisons when inputs change. For agents with privileged access, test for unintended actions and explicit boundary crossings.
answers.question: What should someone building or evaluating AI systems do differently today?
answers.signal: Operationally relevant items emphasize maintenance and reproducibility: most captured records are releases, while benchmark, evaluation, and dataset tags are common and overlapping.

answers.takeaway: Review dependencies and benchmark provenance before the next evaluation run. answers.question: What does today's evidence fail to show, and what would change the reading?
answers.signal: The captured evidence cannot establish field-wide direction, benchmark quality, growing adoption, or whether differences from other days reflect reality rather than collection changes.

answers.takeaway: The reading would change with repeated comparable windows using stable connector coverage and the same taxonomy, restored missing connectors, metric movement confirmed by multiple sources, and independent hands-on validation of highlighted releases and benchmarks. cards.blurb: PromptLeaks identifies a specific contamination risk in safety evaluation: offensive jailbreak tools and defensive guardrails may draw from overlapping human-authored prompt collections, so a guardrail can be tested on material present in its own training data.
